Equivalent to con- +‎ nūbō (“I marry”) +‎ -ium. Per De Vaan, the cō-n- (found also in other words that are on the surface composed of con- + a stem starting with n-) has been explained as a development from previous *com-sn-.[1] Weiss reconstructs the word as going back to an original form *kon-snoubii̯om.[2] It is not simple to determine the usual length of the vowel in the second syllable using poetic evidence (see below). Long ū would be the regular outcome of a diphthong derived from the e- or o-grade of the Proto-Indo-European root (and would get analogical support from the long ū in nūbō); on the other hand, the related words prōnuba and innuba can be cited to support the possibility of a pronunciation with short /u/, which would come from the zero grade of the Proto-Indo-European root.

Uncertain. Perhaps related to Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”). De Vaan, however, doubts the possibility of a semantic connection between the Latin term, meaning "to support," and the Proto-Indo-European term, meaning "to swell." The root *bʰelg- has been proposed based on a possible connection with Ancient Greek φᾰ́λᾰγξ (phắlănx), Old High German balko, and Icelandic bjálki, although De Vaan rejects such connections. Rix posits, albeit uncertainly, the root *bʰelḱ-, from which a form *bʰl̥ḱ-yé-ti may have emerged,[1] whence   fulciō.[2] However, the only other evidence for such a root is Ancient Greek φάλκης (phálkēs), which Beekes considers to be of Pre-Greek origin.[3]

Thank you for you generous donation.

vocabList.etym: Borrowed in the 17th century, and provided with a paragogic -t, from French (vin) sec (literally “dry wine”), which is also the original sense in German. The sense “sparkling wine” is believed to originate from an anecdote in 19th-century Berlin. The actor Ludwig Devrient supposedly ordered a bottle of wine using the phrase “Bring [er] mir Sekt, Schurke!”, based on the German translation of the line “Give me a cup of sack, rogue!” from Shakespeare’s Henry IV. He was served sparkling wine, his usual order, and this sense was given to the word Sekt when the phrase and anecdote caught on.

From Middle High German lest, a contraction of lezzest, from Old High German lezzist (also lazzōst), itself superlative of laz (cognate to English late). The modern German form with -tz- is of northern origin; two separate origins have probably met in it: Firstly, there is a general tendency in some Central German dialects of inserting -t- before comparative and superlative endings. (Compare for this, for example, Ripuarian fröh → fröhter, fröhtste). Secondly, Middle Low German lest, contracted superlative of lat (“late”), had a regular or regularized variant letst, which is very rare in writing, but may have been more common in spoken dialects. (Compare modern German Low German lättst.) Related forms are Dutch laatst and lest, English latest and last, Luxembourgish lescht, Hunsrik letst.

29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 4.296–297:
At rēgīna dolōs – quis fallere possit amantem? – praesēnsit [...].

Compare Proto-Indo-Iranian *grā́mas (“bunch”), Ancient Greek ἀγείρω (ageírō, “to gather”), Proto-Slavic *gromada (“heap, pile”), Lithuanian grùmulas (“lump”), Proto-Germanic *krimmaną (“to push, crumble”).[1] See also grex (“flock, herd”).
From dēlu(ō) (“to cleanse”) +‎ -brum, from de- + lavō (“I wash”).
From Proto-Italic *wātis, from Proto-Indo-European *wéh₂t-i-s (“seer”), from *weh₂t- (“to be excited”).

From Proto-Italic *swādejō, itself from a Proto-Indo-European causative verb in *-éyeti from the root *sweh₂d- (“sweet”),[1][2][3] hence literally, “to make sweet, sweeten”. The stem of the original verb may have been either the zero-grade *suh₂d-éyeti,[2] as in Sanskrit सूदयति (sūdáyati, “to make tasty”), or the o-grade *swoh₂d-éyeti,[3] but in the end it was secondarily replaced with the full grade by influence of the related adjective suāvis (“sweet”).[2][3]

The -ss- would be expected to go back to original *-t-t- or *-d-t-, hence pre-forms such as *vici-dtim (a compound with the root of dō, dare, dedī, datum) or *vici-cessim (a compound with the root of cēdō,  cēdere, cessī, cessum) have been proposed.[1] Compare anteclassical vicissātim.

From überzeugen (“to convince”) +‎ -ung (“-ing”).
Univerbation from earlier adverbial genitive ebenen Falls (literally “just the same case”).

From Middle High German verbieten, from Old High German firbiotan, from Proto-West Germanic *furibeudan, from Proto-Germanic *furibeudaną. Equivalent to ver- +‎ bieten. Compare Dutch verbieden, Low German verbeden, English forbid, Danish forbyde, Swedish förbjuda, Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌱𐌹𐌿𐌳𐌰𐌽 (faurbiudan).
vocabList.usage:
Ich verbiete Ihnen, in diesem Ton mit meiner Frau zu sprechen.
I forbid you to talk in that tone of voice with my wife.

vocabList.etym: be- +‎ zweifeln

Compound of aller (genitive plural of alle (“all”)) +‎ Dings (genitive singular of Ding (“thing”)) (compare schlechterdings). Before the 19th century, the full form aller Dinge (“of all things”), with the plural Dinge, was used.
vocabList.usage:
Es wird allerdings die Vermutung ausgesprochen...
It is, however, conjectured...

vocabList.etym: From fähig (“capable, able”) +‎ -keit.

From Middle High German pfanne, from Old High German phanna, from Proto-West Germanic *pannā, from Proto-Germanic *pannǭ, from Late Latin panna, from Latin patina (“bowl, platter”). Doublet of Patina.
Alster +‎ Wasser, after the tributary of the Elbe River.
Of uncertain origin. Attested since the 15th century. Several etymologies have been proposed.[1]
verfügen +‎ -bar
verstehen +‎ -nis
From Middle High German vegen, from Old High German fegōn, from Proto-West Germanic *fegōn.

Coined in the 15th century after the model of wahnwitzig which uses as its first part the word wahn, which came from Old High German wan "missing, empty", which came from Proto-Germanic *wanaz. Not cognate with Wahn. Cognate with English wane.
vocabList.usage:
Sind Sie wahnsinnig?
Are you insane?

vocabList.etym: un- +‎ berechenbar
From Middle High German māz, from Old High German māza, from Proto-West Germanic *mātu. Compare Dutch maat (“size, measure”), Old English met (“measure, amount, limit”). More at mete.
vocabList.usage:
Ehrlichkeit ist das wahre Maß eines Mannes.
Honesty is the true measure of a man.

vocabList.etym: From gemein +‎ -schaft. Cognate to German Low German Gemeenschopp (Gemeenschop), Middle Low German Gemeinschopp (in 16th century, used by Joachimus Magdeburgius).
Außenseite +‎ -er
From Middle High German niderslahen, from Old High German nidarslahan. Equivalent to nieder- +‎ schlagen.

From Middle High German īseren, īserīn, from Old High German īsarnīn, from Proto-Germanic *īsarnīnaz. Equivalent to Eiser (“iron”), older variant of Eisen +‎ -en. Now reanalysable as Eisen (“iron”) +‎ -ern, but historically eisern is itself one of the words that contributed to the development of this extended suffix -ern (see there).
From mit- +‎ Gefühl. Cognate with Dutch medegevoel.
From horchen.
vocabList.usage:
Sie gehorchten ihren Eltern nicht.
They didn't obey their parents.

vocabList.etym: ur- +‎ Sünde
ge- +‎ schwätzen
Univerbation of so +‎ genannt.
From Middle High German vergeben, from Old High German fargeban, from Proto-Germanic *fragebaną. Analyzable as ver- +‎ geben. Cognate with Dutch vergeven, English forgive, Icelandic fyrirgefa.
Compare Dutch oneerbiedig.
um- +‎ krempeln
From Middle High German gewaltec, from Old High German giwaltīg, equivalent to Gewalt +‎ -ig.
erdenken +‎ -lich
From Middle High German zuobringen, from Old High German zuobringan. Equivalent to zu- +‎ bringen.
From Middle High German verræter.
From versagen +‎ -er.

vocabList.definition: to bleed to death, to bleed out
vocabList.etym: ver- +‎ bluten, compare English forbleed.
From Middle High German zuolāzen, from Old High German zuolāzan, from Proto-West Germanic *tōlātan. Equivalent to zu- +‎ lassen. Cognate with Dutch toelaten.
From Treue +‎ -los.
Niedertracht +‎ -ig. Also analyzable as nieder- +‎ -trächtig.

vocabList.definition: to lie to, to tell someone a lie, to tell someone lies
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German beliegen, from Old High German biliogan, from Proto-West Germanic *bileugan. Equivalent to be- +‎ lügen.

vocabList.definition: to set against, to make a stand against

vocabList.etym: From Schupp (“push”) +‎ -s (“intensive nominal ending”). Schupp (15th c.) is deverbal from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German schuppen, from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną, intensive form of *skeubaną, whence German schieben and English shove. See schubsen for more.
er- +‎ folgen
vocabList.usage:
Der Angriff Steiners ist nicht erfolgt.
Steiner's attack did not occur.

vocabList.etym: Borrowed from French masser, probably from Arabic مَسَّ (massa, “to touch”), or from Portuguese amassar. The Arabic verb was, in French, associated with and perhaps reinforced by unrelated Ancient Greek μάσσειν (mássein, “to knead”), but direct derivation from this latter is now considered unlikely.

vocabList.definition: attack, offensive, strike, assault, onslaught, raid, offence
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German angrif, anegrif, from Old High German *anagrif, from Proto-West Germanic *anagripi, equivalent to an- +‎ Griff. Related to German angreifen.
From Old High German in zuiskēn, from Old High German zuiski, from Proto-Germanic *twiskaz (“twofold, double”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwís (“twice, doubly; in two”).
vocabList.usage:
die Schere zwischen Arm und Reich
the gap between the poor and rich

vocabList.definition: to break something in two [auxiliary haben]
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German durchbrechen, from Old High German duruhbrehhan, from Proto-West Germanic *þuruhbrekan; analyzable as durch (“through”) +‎ brechen (“to break”).
From Middle High German vīant, from Old High German fīand, fīant, from Proto-West Germanic *fijand, from Proto-Germanic *fijandz.
vocabList.usage:
Er ist mein größter Feind
He is my greatest enemy.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German bevel, synchronically analyzed as a deverbal noun from befehlen (“to order, command”). Compare also Dutch bevel.

From Italian tasto (“key”), from the verb tastare, from Vulgar Latin *tastāre (“to touch, feel”), from *taxitāre, from Latin taxāre (“to touch sharply”), from tangere (“to touch”). Related with older German tasten, which is from the same Latin verb through Old French.
From Konto +‎ Auszug.
From Middle High German herūzkomen. Equivalent to heraus- +‎ kommen.
From Fehler +‎ Meldung.
From auszahlen +‎ -ung.

vocabList.definition: to choose, to select, to pick
vocabList.etym: aus- (“out”) +‎ wählen (“pick, choose, select”).  Compare English pick out.
aus- +‎ drucken
From Middle High German abebruch. By surface analysis, deverbal from abbrechen.
A Central and Low German verb, from Middle Low German klappen, from Old Saxon **klappōn, probably from Proto-West Germanic *klappōn, from Proto-Germanic *klappōną.
From ein +‎ -sam, probably on the model of gemeinsam.
From zu- (“to, at”) +‎ gleich (“equal, same, alike”).
vocabList.usage: an mehreren Stellen zugleich ― at multiple points simultaneously

vocabList.etym: 16th century, originally in the longer form bissolang, a univerbation of bis (“until”) +‎ so (“so”) +‎ lang (“long”). The word was at first chiefly restricted to vernacular High German in northern Germany. It established itself more widely in the 19th century, but remains rare in Austria, Switzerland and South Tyrol.
da (“there”) +‎ gegen.

vocabList.definition: accessories, fittings, paraphernalia, equipment, supplies, belongings
vocabList.etym: 17th century, northern alteration of the above form, itself from Middle High German zuogehœr(d)e, under influence of the equivalent Middle Low German tôbehö̂re, literally “to-belongings”, thus “that which belongs to something else”. The northern behören for gehören see also in Behörde; compare Dutch behoren.
From the obsolete verb bereichen (“to extend; to cover”, literally “bereach”).
From Middle High German anevart, from Old High German anafart. By surface analysis, deverbal from anfahren.
Verwendung (“use”) +‎ -s- +‎ Zweck (“purpose”)
vermieten (“to rent”) +‎ -er (“-er”)
From über- +‎ weisen.
vocabList.usage:
Sie müssen den Betrag sofort überweisen.
You have to transfer the amount immediately.

vocabList.etym: Ca. 1500, from Latin rata, perhaps through Italian rata and/or Middle French rate.
mahnen +‎ -ung
Last +‎ Schrift

vocabList.definition: to take care, to look after
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German kumbern, derived from the noun kumber, probably from Old French *combre (“obstruction, barrier”), itself probably from Gaulish. See Kummer for more.
vocabList.usage:
Wer kümmert sich um die Ausbildung der Lehrlinge?
Who takes care of training the interns?

vocabList.etym: Konto +‎ Stand

From Middle High German enphāhen, from Old High German intvāhan, from Proto-Germanic *andfanhaną. Equivalent to emp- +‎ fangen and further ent- +‎ fangen. Cognate with Dutch ontvangen, Old Saxon antfāhan.
ein- (“in-”) +‎ zahlen (“to pay”)
From Dauer +‎ Auftrag.
From Middle High German īngeben, from Old High German ingeban. Equivalent to ein- +‎ geben. Compare Scots ingive.

Borrowed from Middle Low German beschênigen (14th c.), extended form of beschênen, from be- +‎ Proto-West Germanic *skainijan (“to make appear”). This latter verb is a causative of *skīnan, whence German scheinen (“to shine, appear”). It was borrowed along the Lower Rhine in the 15th century and fully established itself in High German during the 16th. Due to the merger of West Germanic ai and ī, it appears to be derived as be- +‎ Schein +‎ -ig +‎ -en. In truth, the noun Schein is closely related, but does not underlie directly.
From Middle High German anelāzen, from Old High German anelāzan. Equivalent to an- +‎ lassen.

vocabList.definition: to come off, come loose, to wear off, to be deducted
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German abegān, from Old High German abagān. Equivalent to ab- +‎ gehen.
ab- +‎ buchen
From Middle High German ūzvüeren, from Old High German ūzfuoren. By surface analysis, aus (“out”) +‎ führen (“to lead”). Compare Dutch uitvoeren.
vocabList.usage:
Heute früh habe ich meinen Hund ausgeführt.
I took my dog for a walk this morning.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German *ersūfen, from Old High German irsūfan. Equivalent to er- +‎ saufen.
fernsehen +‎ -er
herunter- +‎ fahren
From Middle High German geil, from Old High German geil, from Proto-West Germanic *gail ("wanton, lustful"), from Proto-Germanic *gailaz ("frothing, arrogant, tempestuous, violent, wanton").
erleben +‎ -nis

From Middle High German wels, from Old High German *wals, *walis, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaliʀ, from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷálos (“sheatfish”). Cognate with German Low German Wels (“catfish”), Dutch wels (“catfish”), Old High German walira (“whale”), German Wal (“whale”).
From Middle High German wec, from Old High German weg, from Proto-West Germanic *weg. Cognate with Dutch weg, Afrikaans weg, English way.
vocabList.usage:
Der Wald kann gefährlich sein, also bleib auf dem Weg.
The forest can be dangerous, so stay on the path.

vocabList.etym: Ca. 1600, deverbal from nach +‎ richten. Compare Dutch naricht.
vocabList.usage:
Die Nachricht von seinem Tod hat mich tief erschüttert.
The news of his death shocked me deeply.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German mittel, from Old High German mittil (akin to Old Saxon middil), from Proto-Germanic *midlą, *midilą, *medalą (“middle”), *midil-. Compare Dutch middel, English middle. See also Mitte.
From fern (“far away”) +‎ Verkehr (“traffic”).
Univerbation of ob +‎ wohl, from the older use of ob as a conditional and concessive conjunction, reinforced with an adverb. Compare obgleich, obschon, obzwar and also gleichwohl.
vocabList.usage:
Frau Anna, unsere Empfangsdame, flirtet mit Patienten, obwohl sie Mutter von drei Kindern ist.
Ms. Anna, our receptionist, flirts with patients, although she is the mother of three children.

vocabList.etym: Univerbation of trotz +‎ dem. Compare Middle High German tratz, traz, truz (“anyhow, nevertheless”).
vocabList.usage:
Ich verstehe deine Sichtweise. Trotzdem bin ich anderer Meinung.
I understand your point of view. Nevertheless, I have a different opinion.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German kleit, from Old High German *kleid, from Proto-Germanic *klaiþą, from Proto-Indo-European *gleyt-. Cognate with Dutch kleed, Low German Kleid, English cloth. Possibly related to klettern, Klette, Klei.

vocabList.definition: to gather, draw, bring or collect (together), assemble, pick up; contract, draw up, compress, concentrate; harvest
vocabList.usage:
160 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Adelphoe 5.3.59–63:
DĒMEA. Ego istuc vīderō,atque ibi favīllae plēna, fūmī ac pollinis
coquendō sit faxō et molendō. Praeter haec
merīdiē ipsō faciam ut stipulam colligat.
Tam excoctam reddam atque ātram quam carbō est.
DEMEA. I'll see to that,
and full of soot, smoke and flour
from the cooking and grinding I'll make her. And, besides that,
I'll make her collect the straw at noon.
I'll render her as burnt and black as coal.

vocabList.definition: abandoned, having been abandoned, forsaken, relinquished, having been relinquished, left behind
vocabList.etym: Perfect passive participle of relinquō (“abandon, relinquish”).
From Proto-Italic *wenjā, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”). See also Latin Venus, veneror and English wish.

vocabList.definition: to wait, await, expect a person or thing
vocabList.etym: See experior.

vocabList.definition: to come in contact with, touch
vocabList.usage:
c. 52 BCE, Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.1:
[…] ; attingit etiam ab Sēquanīs et Helvētiīs flūmen Rhēnum, vergit ad septentriōnēs.
[…] ; it borders also the Rhine River on the side of the Sequani and the Helvetii, [and] stretches toward the north.

vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *pretjom, from  Proto-Indo-European *pr-é-ti, *pr-ó-ti, from *per- (“in front”) perhaps in the meaning of “equivalence, recompense, compensation”. Compare Proto-Slavic *protivъ (“contrary, against”), Ancient Greek πρός (prós) from older προτί (protí, “in the direction of, towards, near”), Sanskrit प्रति (prati, “towards, near; against”).[1]
From Proto-Italic *frūgməntom, equivalent to fruor (“I use, enjoy”) +‎ -mentum (instrumental suffix); ultimately, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰruHg-mn̥-to-m.

vocabList.definition: (in the plural) three each; three at a time
vocabList.etym: From ter (“thrice”) +‎ -nus (adjective-forming suffix), compare the older trinus.
Present active participle of flagrō.

vocabList.definition: a tract of land, a demos, a deme
vocabList.etym: Borrowed from Ancient Greek δῆμος (dêmos, “[the common] people”).
From Middle High German tol, from Old High German tol, from Proto-West Germanic *dol, from Proto-Germanic *dulaz (“dazed, foolish, crazy, stupid”).
Perfect passive participle of pandō (“I spread out [to dry]”).
From petō (“I assault, attack, demand”) +‎ -tiō.
From coniūrō +‎ -tiō.

From Old Latin āsa, from Proto-Italic *āzā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs-.
Cognate with Sanskrit आस (ā́sa, “ashes”) and English ash.
From herstellen +‎ -er.
From Proto-Italic *ātros, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₁ter- (“fire”) (whence Proto-Iranian *HáHtr̥š (“fire”), Umbrian 𐌀𐌕𐌓𐌖 (atru), Oscan 𐌀𐌀𐌃𐌝𐌓𐌉𐌉𐌔 (aadíriis), Old Irish áith (“kiln”)).
From sonder- (“special”) +‎ Angebot (“offer”).
From Middle High German urloup. Related to erlauben. Cognate with English leave (“time off, permission to be away”).
From Late Middle High German koffer, from Middle Dutch coffer, from Old French cofre.
From in- +‎ ūsitātus.
From Middle High German sō, from Old High German sō, from Proto-West Germanic *swā, from Proto-Germanic *swa, *swē, compare with Old Dutch so and Dutch zo.
From per- (“through”) +‎ speciō (“observe, watch, look at”).
Perfect passive participle of prōiciō.
Perfect passive participle of prōdō.
From iuvō (“to delight, please”) +‎ -cundus. -undus should be considered for etymological origins.
Future active participle of videō (“I see”).

vocabList.definition: to ask, beg, request, look for, inquire, petition, entreat
vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Fasti 1.465:
unde petam causās hōrum mōremque sacrōrum?
Where shall I look for the reasons and practice of these sacred rites?

vocabList.definition: collectively, all together; the whole, entire
vocabList.etym: Uncertain. Proposals include:
From Proto-Italic *tom, from Proto-Indo-European *tóm, accusative of *só. Cf. its feminine form Latin tam, as in tamquam. Cognate with Ancient Greek τότε (tóte).
vocabList.usage:
Tum Caecilius in horto sedet.
Then Caecilius sits in the garden.

vocabList.definition:
(pronoun) this or that man, woman or thing; he, she, it, they (previously introduced)
Picks up the subject or object after an intervening clause, to avoid repeating the relative pronoun quī, or substitutes syntactically fronted expressions
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *is, from Proto-Indo-European *éy. Cognate with Oscan 𐌉𐌆𐌉𐌊 (izik), Umbrian 𐌄𐌓𐌄 (ere), and further with Lithuanian jis, Proto-Slavic *jь.

vocabList.definition: (interrogative) of what kind, sort, description, nature; what kind of
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Indo-European *kʷo- (“interrogative, relative stem”) and maybe *h₂el- (“to grow”) (cf. the sense of indolēs, from this root). Cognate with Ancient Greek πηλίκος (pēlíkos).
From Proto-Italic *nām, a feminine accusative singular.[1] There are multiple proposals for the root:
From quid +‎ Proto-Italic *-im (emphatic marker); morphologically compare idem, from is (“he”).
From ad- +‎ pōnō (“put”).
vocabList.usage:
Nōn gladium corporibus hostium, sed arborum truncīs secūrim appōnit.
He doesn't put his sword to the bodies of foes, but his axe to the trunks of trees.

vocabList.definition: to run into; to go to meet

vocabList.etym: ad- (“to, towards”) +‎ eō (“there; so much”)
vocabList.usage:
c. 52 BCE, Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico VII.25:
Quod [...] nec facile adire apertos ad auxiliandum animadvertebant
Because [...] they perceived that [our soldiers] being militarily undefended could not easily go to give assistance

vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *magjōs, from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂yōs, from *meǵh₂- (“great”) +‎ *-yōs (comparative suffix).
Same source as aut.

From older hec, from Proto-Italic *hoke, from *ho (from Proto-Indo-European *gʰo (“indeed”, emphatic clitic)) + *ke (from *ḱe (“here”, deictic particle)). Reconstructed forms with o are made likely by the Old Latin form hoi (“this”).
From inter- +‎ iaceō (“lie”).
From re- (“back-”) +‎ vorsus, earlier form of versus (“towards, -wards”).
From Middle High German nie, from Old High German nio.
From Middle High German selten, selden, from Old High German seltan, from Proto-West Germanic *seldanā.
From Middle High German ofte, oft, uft, from Old High German ofta, ofto, oftu, from Proto-Germanic *ufta, *uftō (“often”). Cognate with Dutch oft, English oft and often.

vocabList.usage:
c. 347 CE – 420 CE, Hieronymus, Vulgate Exodus.20.12:
Honōrā patrem tuum et mātrem tuam, ut sīs longaevus super terram, quam Dominus Deus tuus dabit tibi.
Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.

vocabList.definition:
superlative degree of posterus
last
next, following (coming after)
vocabList.etym: From earlier *postrezmo- < *posterezemo- < *posterisemo-, from Proto-Italic *posterisemos. Equivalent to posterus +‎ -issimus. Same development as extrēmus and suprēmus. Compare with postumus.
From the noun Mal (“time”). Partly shortened from einmal, which is also derived from the noun.
vocabList.usage:
sechs mal sieben ist zweiundvierzig
six times seven is forty-two

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German gehalt, deverbal from gehalten (“to keep still, retain, preserve, imprison”), itself from halten (“to hold”). The earliest attested sense of the noun is “custody, prison”. In some southern dialects it also means “room, container, closet”. The modern sense develops in the 15th century, at first in the context of coins and metal alloys.

vocabList.definition: chocolate bar, bar of chocolate, candy bar
vocabList.etym: From Schokolade +‎ -n- +‎ Tafel.

vocabList.definition: to donate, to give as charity
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German spenden, from Old High German spentōn (“to consume, use, spend”), from Proto-West Germanic *spendōn (“to spend”), from Latin expendō.
vocabList.usage:
Blut spenden.
to donate blood.

vocabList.etym: Future passive participle of levō.

vocabList.definition: carried, having been carried, borne, having been borne; worn, having been worn
vocabList.etym: Perfect passive participle of gerō (“carry, bear; wear”).

vocabList.definition:
(Old Latin, chiefly Late Latin) punishable, liable, guilty, referring to:
(rare) the injured party

(with dative, ablative or genitive) a fault

a punishment
vocabList.etym: From ob- (prefix meaning ‘against; towards’) +‎ noxa (“harm, hurt, injury; crime, fault, offence”) +‎ -ius (suffix forming adjectives). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *neḱ- (“to disappear; to perish”).
From locus +‎ -ālis.
From ex- (“out of, from”) +‎ rapiō (“grab, seize”).
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 2.289:
“‘Heu fuge, nāte deā, tēque hīs, ait, ēripe flammīs.’”
[Aeneas recalls Hector’s dire warning:] “‘Alas! Flee, goddess-born,’ [Hector] says, ‘and deliver yourself from these flames!’”

vocabList.definition: to go among, become lost in
vocabList.etym: From inter- (“between, among”) +‎ eō (“go”).
Present participle of licet.
From Ancient Greek μνᾶ (mnâ).
From nītor +‎ -tus.
Syncopic form of validē.

vocabList.definition: to be away, to be absent, to be distant
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 2.620:
“‘Nusquam aberō, et tūtum patriō tē līmine sistam.’”
“‘I will never be distant [from you], and will set you safe at your father's doorstep.’”(Venus reassures her son, Aeneas.)

vocabList.definition: to be allowed; to be permitted
vocabList.etym: Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Italic *likēt, from Proto-Indo-European *lik-eh₁-yéti, from a root of the shape *leyk-,[1] though there are no certain cognates outside of Italic.[2] Cognate with liceor, liceō, Oscan 𐌋𐌝𐌊𐌝𐌕𐌖𐌃 (líkítud, “it is permitted”); outside of Italic, compare perhaps Lithuanian reikė́ti (“to need”).[3]
vocabList.usage:
c. 52 BCE, Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.7:
[…] quī dīcerent sibi esse in animō sine ūllō maleficiō iter per prōvinciam facere, proptereā quod aliud iter habērent nūllum; rogāre ut ēius voluntāte id sibi facere liceat.
[These envoys] were to say that they intended to make a journey through the province without any harm, for the reason that they had no other route; [and] they were to ask that it be permitted to do so with his consent.

vocabList.definition: about to move, set in motion
vocabList.etym: Future active participle of moveō (“I move, set in motion”).

vocabList.definition: to take back, (i.e., regain possession of something)
vocabList.usage:
27 BCE – 25 BCE, Titus Livius, Ab Urbe Condita 26.1:
Ea tum cura maxime intentos habebat Romanos, non ab ira tantum, quae in nullam unquam civitatem iustior fuit, quam quod urbs tam nobilis ac potens, sicut defectione sua traxerat aliquot populos, ita recepta inclinatura rursus animos videbatur ad veteris imperii respectum.
This concern in particular troubled the mindful Romans at the time, not so much because of anger, which has never been more justified against any other city, rather because a city so noble and powerful, in the same way that it had attracted the support of a number of communities by its revolt, was thought would again turn attention back towards respect for the previous government once recaptured.

vocabList.definition: to drive or thrust out or away

vocabList.definition: to look or gaze at, behold, watch, view
vocabList.etym: Uncertain. De Vaan and Rix both postulate a root of the shape *tewH-. However, De Vaan suggests that the original meaning of the term was "to protect," which evolved into the meaning "to look." If this theory is accepted, then a connection with the root *tewh₂- (“to be strong”) becomes tenable. In either case, according to De Vaan, the term may derive from a Proto-Indo-European causative *towH-éye- or *towh₂-éye-. This verb would become Proto-Italic *tawe-, which may have developed into tueor via the reintroduction of -ow-. Alternatively, De Vaan postulates that *tetówh₂e, the stative form of the root *tewh₂-, could have produced the Latin verb via the same reintroduction of -ow-. Rix alternatively postulates an original Proto-Indo-European verb *tuH(h₁)yéti, which he considers to be a possible source of the Latin verb. Mallory suggests a possible derivation from a root of the shape *tew- (“to look upon favorably”).

The garden was full of many different kinds of plants.

vocabList.etym: From prae- (“before”) +‎ serō (“I join or bind together”) +‎ -tim (forms adverbs).

vocabList.definition: to leave, depart, abandon, retire (with ablative)
vocabList.etym: From dis- +‎ cēdō.
vocabList.usage:
63 BCE, Cicero, Catiline Orations Oratio in Catilinam Prima in Senatu Habita.18:
Quam ob rem, discēde atque hunc mihi timōrem ēripe; sī est vērus, nē opprimar, sīn falsus, ut tandem aliquandō timēre dēsinam.
On account of this concern, depart and take away this fear from me; if it is true, so that I may not be attacked, but if false, so that finally, at last, I may cease to fear.

vocabList.definition: longing, desire, wish (especially for something once possessed)
vocabList.etym: From dēsīderō (“want, desire, wish for; miss, lack, need”) +‎ -ium.

vocabList.definition: to be accustomed, used to, in the habit of
vocabList.etym: PIE word*swé
From earlier cunde, from a declined form of quī (“which, what, where”) and a demonstrative suffix *-de. See ubi for the loss of c and compare ali-cunde and sī-cunde.

From Proto-Italic *swordi- (“dirt”) or *swordo- (“dirty”)[1] + -ēs. Cognate with Proto-Germanic *swartaz (“black”), which could also go back to *sword-; within Latin, suāsum (“dirty gray color”) could be from the same root,[2] but this relationship is not certain since it is phonetically problematic.[1]

vocabList.definition: to lift up or raise (from underneath)
vocabList.etym: From sub- +‎ levo.
vocabList.usage:
c. 347 CE – 420 CE, Hieronymus, Vulgate John.6.5:
Cum sublevasset ergo oculos Jesus, et vidisset quia multitudo maxima venit ad eum, dixit ad Philippum: Unde ememus panes, ut manducent hi?
When Jesus raised his eyes, and saw that a huge crowd came to him, he said to Philip: From where shall we buy bread, so these people may eat?

vocabList.definition: to be sad or mournful; mourn, grieve, lament
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *maizēō; further origin uncertain. Possibly related to miser (compare with misereō), and possibly related to Ancient Greek μῖσος (mîsos) by means of Proto-Indo-European *mēwdʰ- (“to complain, be emotional about”). De Vaan hesitantly suggests a connection to Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”).[1]
Present active participle of amō (“love”).
Back-formation from nequeō, itself related to the irregular verb eō.
vocabList.usage:
166 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Andria 804–805:
CRĪTŌ: Quid vōs? Quō pactō hic? Satin rēctē? MȲSĪS: Nōsne? “Sīc / ut quīmus,” aiunt, “quandō ut volumus nōn licet.”
CRITO: What about you all? How are things going here? Well enough?MYSIS: Us? “We do what we can,” as they say, “since we can’t do as we wish.”
(More literally: “since what we want is not possible.”)

vocabList.etym: Perfect active participle of contestor.
From ex- (“out of”) +‎ veniō (“come”).
vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Fasti 4.775:
quae precor ēveniant
[Those things for] which I am praying: May they happen.

vocabList.etym: Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *éy and *só. Compare ita and itidem.

vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Fasti 1.157–158:
tum blandī sōlēs, ignōtaque prōdit hirundōet luteum celsā sub trabe fīgit opus
Then is the sunshine refreshing; and the stranger swallow comes forth, and builds her fabric of clay beneath the lofty rafter.
1851. The Fasti &c of Ovid. Trans. & notes by H. T. Riley. London: H. G. Bohn. pg. 13.

vocabList.etym: From dēlinquō (“fail, be wanting”).

vocabList.definition: to owe something, to be under obligation to and for something
vocabList.etym: Contraction of *dēhibeō, from dē- +‎ habeō (“have”), though "I hold away (from someone)".[1] See the same contraction in dēbilis. Compare the later formed dēhabeō.
vocabList.usage:
c. 4 BCE – 65 CE, Seneca Minor, Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium 1.1.3:
[...] nēmō sē iūdicet quicquam dēbēre quī tempus accēpit, cum interim hoc ūnum est quod nē grātus quidem potest reddere.
[Yet] no one who receives [a gift of] time judges himself to owe anything [in return], when meanwhile this one [thing] is in fact what not even a grateful [person] is able to repay.

vocabList.etym: Present participle of cū̆nctor.
From dē (“from, away or down from”) + decus (“glory, honor, dignity”).
Perfect passive participle of permoveō.

From Proto-Italic *rē(z)mos, from a Proto-Indo-European root *h₁reh₁- shared with Ancient Greek ἐρετμός (eretmós, “oar”), ἐρέτης (erétēs, “rower”), τριήρης (triḗrēs, “trireme”), and possibly English oar.

vocabList.definition: to pay attention, attend, focus, concentrate, give heed to, consider, regard, observe
vocabList.etym: From animus +‎ advertō.
vocabList.usage:
166 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Andria 767:
DĀVUS: Ō facinus animadvertendum!
DAVUS: Oh, such an outrage ought to be punished!

vocabList.definition: desire, longing, especially amorous desire, eagerness
vocabList.etym: From cupiō (“to desire”) +‎ -īdō.

vocabList.definition: to beg, to demand, to request, to desire
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *porskō (“to ask for; request; demand”), from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥(ḱ)sḱéti (“to keep asking; to question”), from *preḱ- (“to ask; to ask for”) +‎ *-sḱéti (“imperfective suffix”).[1] Latin -ēscō (inchoative suffix) derives from this ending.[2]
vocabList.usage: Poscor aliquid. ― Something is asked of me.

vocabList.definition: which is to be examined, contemplated, observed
vocabList.etym: Future passive participle of īnspiciō.
See vās. The word is pre-Classical. In Classical Latin it is only used in the plural.

vocabList.definition:
to take away, take off, bear away, bear off, carry off, remove, withdraw
  to bear or carry away, sweep away by wings, the winds, waves, or any other quick motion
vocabList.etym: From au- (“from, away, off”) +‎ ferō (“to bear, carry, bring”). Whether the prefix au- is identical to ab- is the source of much controversy; see au- for more.
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 4.28-29:
“Ille meōs, prīmus quī mē sibi iūnxit, amōrēsabstulit; ille habeat sēcum servetque sepulchrō.”
“That [man], who first joined himself to me, he has taken away all my love; may that [man] hold [it] with him, and guard [it] in his grave.”
(Dido speaks of her dead husband, Sychaeus.)

vocabList.etym: Disputed.
vocabList.usage:
Cato the Elder:
Cēterum cēnseō Carthāginem esse dēlendam
Furthermore, I recommend that Carthage must be destroyed

vocabList.definition: which is to be created, which is to be made, which is to be produced
vocabList.etym: Future passive participle (gerundive) of creō (“create”).
From late Middle High German nuor, contracted from older niwer, newære, from Old High German niwāri, ni wāri (“were it not”). Cognate with Yiddish נאָר (nor), Dutch maar, Old English nǣre.
vocabList.usage:
Nur reife Kirschen dürfen auf den Kuchen.
Only ripe cherries may go on the cake.

vocabList.etym: From ent- +‎ werfen. Compare Dutch ontwerpen.
Equivalent to nach dem, an inflected form which has been used together as a conjunction from Old High German nâh diu.
From adeō (“approach, attend, undertake”) +‎ -tus (action noun forming suffix).
From hiems (“winter, rainy season”).
From exig(ō) (“to demand”) +‎ -uus.

vocabList.usage:
166 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Andria 60–61:
Nōn iniūria; nam id arbitror / adprīmē in vītā esse ūtile, ut nēquid nimis.
Not without reason; for I believe that it is an especially useful [rule] in life, that nothing [be done] in excess.

vocabList.definition: to move away, leave, withdraw, break away
vocabList.usage: ab aliqua re deficere ― to break away from something

vocabList.etym: From per- (“through”) +‎ -dō (“put”).
vocabList.usage:
166 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Andria 642:
PAMPHILUS: Chārīne, et mē et tē, imprūdēns — nisi quid Dī respiciunt — perdidī!
PAMPHILUS: Charinus, me and you both, unintentionally — unless the gods care about what [has happened] — I’ve ruined [us]!(In the comic context, Pamphilus is being hesitant to admit any responsibility to his friend Charinus.)

vocabList.etym: Perfect passive participle of spoliō.
Disputed.
From iste + -ce.
From ob- +‎ sacrō (“consecrate”).
vocabList.usage:
166 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Andria 351:
Obsecrō tē: quam prīmum hōc mē līberā miserum metū!
I beg you: free me in my misery from this fear as soon as possible!

163 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Heauton Timorumenos 1.77:
Homō sum, hūmānī nihil ā mē aliēnum putō.
I am a human, I consider nothing that is human alien to me.

vocabList.definition: to look back, around, continuously or intently
vocabList.etym: From re- +‎ spectō, cf. respectus.

vocabList.definition: to fill up, fill full, fill out; make up, complete
vocabList.etym: From con- +‎ pleō.
vocabList.usage: Pōculum complēvit et hausit. Aquam et vīnum miscuit. Collāpsus est. ― He filled the cup and drank it. He mixed water and wine. He collapsed.

vocabList.etym: From cāssus with regular degemination after a long vowel, for cadō (“to fall, happen”) +‎ -tus (“action noun suffix”), from Proto-Italic *kadō, Proto-Indo-European *ḱh₂d- (“to fall”). The grammatical sense is a semantic loan from Ancient Greek πτῶσις (ptôsis) (whence also calqued Old Church Slavonic падежь (padežĭ) (Russian паде́ж (padéž)), German Fall).
Perfect passive participle of corripiō (“to seize”).

Unknown.[1] De Vaan is skeptical of the proposal that it originally referred to the hair on an animal's back and was derived from a Proto-Indo-European *(s)ter- (“to be stiff”)[1] (compare *tr̥nós, *sterbʰ-). It has been speculated to be connected to one or more of Ancient Greek τράχηλος (trákhēlos, “neck”), Ancient Greek τρέχω (trékhō), or Latin trahō, with a debated connection to the root of English drag, draw.

From Proto-Italic *wetos (“year”), from Proto-Indo-European *wétos (“year”). The Latin underwent semantic shift "year" > "having accumulated (many) years" > "aged, old", with the Latin term for year being annus, from a different root.[1]
From nec + opinatus.
From the ablative of fors (“chance, luck”).
From Proto-Italic *dūm (adverb), from *dweh₂- (“long”) +‎ *-m (adverbial suffix). Compare dūdum.[1]

vocabList.usage:
59 BCE, Cicero, Pro Flacco 26:
Quod quidem ego nōn modo nōn postulō, sed contrā, iūdicēs, vōs ōrō et obtestor ut tōtam causam quam maximē intentīs oculīs, ut aiunt, acerrimē contemplēminī.
But I not only do not ask that, gentlemen, but on the contrary, I beg and beseech you to the best of your ability to examine the whole case most closely and with steady eyes, as the saying goes.

vocabList.etym: From mora (“delay”) +‎ -or (deponent verb-forming suffix).
vocabList.usage:
c. 4 BCE – 65 CE, Seneca Minor, Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium 1.2.1:
Prīmum argūmentum compositae mentis exīstimō posse cōnsistere et sēcum morārī.
The first proof of a well-ordered mind, I believe, [is] the ability to remain in one place and to linger with itself.

vocabList.etym: From ne (“not”) + usquam (“anywhere”).

vocabList.definition: put in motion, moved, stirred, shaken; quick, swift, rapid; having been moved
vocabList.etym: Perfect passive participle of cieō (“put in motion”).

vocabList.definition: to have an aversion towards, to hate, dislike
vocabList.etym: Inherited from Proto-Italic *ōdai, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃e-h₃ód-e ~ h₃e-h₃d-ḗr, reduplicated perfect from the root *h₃ed- (“to hate; to start hating?”).[1][2]
vocabList.usage:
63 BCE, Cicero, Catiline Orations Oratio in Catilinam Prima in Senatu Habita.13:
Quid est enim, Catilīna, quod tē iam in hāc urbe dēlectāre possit? — in quā nēmō est extrā istam coniūrātiōnem perditōrum hominum, quī tē nōn metuat, nēmō quī nōn ōderit.
For what is there, Catiline, that can now delight you in this city? — in which there is no one outside that conspiracy of desperate men who does not fear you, no one who does not hate you.

29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 4.143-144:
Quālis ubi hībernam Lyciam Xanthīque fluentadēserit ac Dēlum māternam invīsit Apollō, [...].
Just like Apollo when he leaves Lycia in winter, and the flowing waters of Xanthus, and visits his mother’s [island,] Delos, [...].

vocabList.etym: From puer (“male child, boy”) +‎ -itia.

vocabList.definition: to kill, murder (especially without physical wounding such as by poison or hunger)
vocabList.etym: From nec- +‎ -ō (denominative verb suffix), from Proto-Indo-European *neḱ- (“perish, disappear”).
vocabList.usage: aliquem igni necare ― to kill someone by fire (fire burning)

vocabList.definition: to press down upon; to suppress

vocabList.etym: Frequentative of horior. See -tō.
vocabList.usage:
c. 37 BCE – 30 BCE, Vergilius, Georgicon 4.266:
[…] ultro / hortantem et fessas ad pabula nota vocantem
[…] freely / calling them and exhorting the weary insects to eat their familiar food.

vocabList.definition: to remember, recollect, recall, call to mind, think of
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *memonai, from Proto-Indo-European *memóne (“to remember”), perfect of the root *men- (“to think”). Compare mēns (“mind”).
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 1.203:
“forsan et haec ōlim meminisse iuvābit”
“Perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember [even] these [things].”

vocabList.definition: to wander through; to rove about
vocabList.etym: From per- +‎ vagor.

vocabList.definition: to lay waste, ravage or devastate, destroy or ruin
vocabList.etym: From populus (“community, people”). According to De Vaan, the meaning developed from an earlier sense "to have an army pass through".[1]
vocabList.usage:
c. 52 BCE, Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.11:
Helvetii iam per angustias et fines Sequanorum suas copias traduxerant et in Haeduorum fines pervenerant eorumque agros populabantur.
The Helvetii had by this time led their forces over through the narrow defile and the territories of the Sequani, and had arrived at the territories of the Aedui, and were ravaging their lands.

vocabList.definition: to go before, precede (walk on ahead)
vocabList.etym: From ante- +‎ eō. Forms in antid- are part of the same analogy as redeō, antideā, to avoid hiatus.

From earlier *well, from Proto-Italic *wels (“you wish”), thus originally the second-person singular present active indicative form of volō (“I will, I wish”). The semantic development may have been helped by the fortuitous similarity to -ve.
From Proto-Italic *enim, accusative singular of *eno (“that one”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁enos (“that”). Cognates include nam, nē (“truly”), Ancient Greek νή (nḗ), ναί (naí).
vocabList.usage:
Id enim ferendum esse negat.
It was truly not to be endured.

vocabList.definition: surrounded, enclosed, having been fenced in.
vocabList.etym: Perfect passive participle of saepiō (“surround, enclose”).
Perfect passive participle of pervagor.
Inherited from Middle High German spil(e)n, from Old High German spilōn, from Proto-West Germanic *spilōn.
vocabList.usage:
Die Kinder spielen draußen.
The children are playing outside.

vocabList.etym: From manch +‎ Mal.

From Middle High German iemer (also imer, immer), from Old High German iomēr (“always”). From io (“always”) +‎ mēr (“more”). Cognate with Dutch immer, German Low German immer, ümmer, jümmer, jümmers, Middle English a mare, aa mare (“evermore”).
vocabList.usage:
Irgendwo scheint immer die Sonne.
The sun is always shining somewhere.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German ëzzen, from Old High German ezzan, akin to Old Saxon etan, compare Dutch eten.
vocabList.usage:
Das Trinken lernt der Mensch schon früh, und später erst das Essen.So soll der Mensch aus Dankbarkeit das Trinken nicht vergessen.
Man learns to drink early on, and only later to eat.So man will not, out of gratitude, forget to drink.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German kochen, from Old High German kohhōn, from Proto-West Germanic *kokōn (“to cook”).

vocabList.usage:
c. 4 BCE – 65 CE, Seneca Minor, Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium 1.2.2:
Certīs ingeniīs immorārī et innūtrīrī oportet, sī velīs aliquid trahere quod in animō fidēliter sedeat.
You must linger among certain distinguished writers, and nourish yourself [upon their books], if you wish to derive anything that will be held reliably in your mind.(Note the possible dual meaning: initially to extract words or meaning from a text, and also to ponder something memorable.)

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German kleidunge, from kleiden (“to clothe”), from Kleid, from Old High German *kleid, from Proto-Germanic *klaiþą (“cloth”). Cognate with Dutch kleding, English clothing.
From Middle High German sëhen, from Old High German sëhan, from Proto-West Germanic *sehwan.
From Middle High German schuo, levelled variant of schuoch (inflected schuo(h)-), from Old High German scuoh (“shoe”), from Proto-West Germanic *skōh. More at shoe.
From Middle High German vile, from Old High German filu (“many”), from Proto-West Germanic *felu, from Proto-Germanic *felu, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁-. More at fele.
vocabList.usage:
Es ist viel passiert.
Much has happened.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German lernen, from Old High German lernēn, lirnēn, from Proto-West Germanic *liʀnēn. Cognate with Old English leornian (Modern English learn). Related to lehren.
fahren (“drive/ride”) +‎ Rad (“wheel”). Compare Dutch rijwiel.
From an (“on”) +‎ Statt (“stead”). Compare English instead.
vocabList.usage:
Anstatt mich anzurufen, ging er mit seinen Freunden ins Kino.
Instead of calling me, he went to the movies with his friends.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German maht, from Old High German maht. Cognate with Dutch macht, English might.
vocabList.usage:
Die Kanzlerin übernahm die Macht im Jahr 2005.
The Chancellor took power in 2005.

vocabList.definition: to make, to produce, to create
vocabList.etym: Inherited from Middle High German machen, from Old High German mahhōn, from Proto-West Germanic *makōn, from Proto-Indo-European *mag- (“to knead, mix, make”). Cognate with Dutch maken, Low German maken, English make.

From Middle High German noch, nog, from Old High German noh, from Proto-West Germanic *noh, from Proto-Germanic *nuh, from Proto-Indo-European *nu (“now”) + *-kʷe (“and, also”). Cognate to Dutch nog and noch (which are etymologically the same word).
From Middle High German ieweder, from Old High German ioweder, from io + wedar. Compare English either, Dutch ieder.
Borrowed from French passer. Compare English pass.
vocabList.usage:
Wie konnte das nur passieren?
How could that have happened?

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German dāheim, dāheime, darheime, from Old High German dārheime (“at home”), equivalent to da +‎ heim. Compare Middle High German heime (“home, at home”, adverb), Old High German heime, heimi (“home, at home”, adverb).

From Middle High German warumme, war umme, warumbe, war umbe, from Old High German wār umbe. Equivalent to wo (“where”) +‎ um (“in order to, for the purpose of”), thus “for what purpose”. Doublet of worum, but with the older vocalism preserved. Compare Dutch waarom, which has both meanings.
15th century, equivalent to regieren (“to reign”) +‎ -ung.

vocabList.definition: to, towards,Contraction of zu der (“to the (feminine)”).
vocabList.etym: A contraction of zu + der. Compare Dutch ter.
Inherited from Middle High German eigenlīche, equivalent to eigen +‎ -lich. Compare Dutch eigenlijk.
vocabList.usage:
Das wird zwar oft behauptet, aber das stimmt eigentlich gar nicht.
People often claim that, but that's actually wrong.

vocabList.etym: By surface analysis, an +‎ fechten.
vocabList.usage:
Hunderte Händler des unter Gläubigerschutz arbeitenden US-Autobauers Chrysler wollen ihre Vertragsauflösung anfechten.
Hundreds of trade companions of the US car manufacturer Chrysler which is under bankruptcy protection, want to contest the dissolvement of their contract.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German ērest, from Old High German ērist, from Proto-West Germanic *airist.
From Middle High German [Term?]. Deverbal from berufen (literally “calling”).

vocabList.definition: (among nations, states, or rulers) treaty, compact, alliance, truce, league
vocabList.etym: Inherited from Proto-Italic *feiðos (“faithful”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ-os, from *bʰeydʰ- (“to trust”). Same root as fīdō, fidēs, fīdus, and Proto-Germanic *bīdaną. Perhaps a corruption from an o-stem.[1]
From com- (“together”) +‎ -es (“-faring”).

vocabList.definition: to lay straight; arrange in lines (especially in military contexts)
vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Fasti 1.466:
dīriget in mediō quis mea vēla fretō?
Who will guide my sails amidst the sea?

vocabList.etym: From Proto-Indo-European *Hrew- (“to tear up, dig up”). Related to rudus.
From Proto-Italic *wiks sg (nom.), *wiksu pl (“a turn, bend”, loc.), from Proto-Indo-European *weyk-.[1]
According to Michiel De Vaan's Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), probably from the same root as pariō.

vocabList.definition: to have respect for, revere, stand in awe
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *werēōr, from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to cover, heed, notice”). Cognate with Ancient Greek ὁράω (horáō, “see”) < ϝοράω (woráō), and English aware [1] and wary.

vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 2.56:
“Troiaque, nunc stārēs, Priamīque arx alta, manērēs.”
“And Troy, you would be standing now, and high citadel of Priam, you would remain!” – Aeneas

vocabList.etym: Earlier *tlātus, from Proto-Italic *tlātos, from Proto-Indo-European *tl̥h₂tós, from the root *telh₂-.

vocabList.definition: each one, each person, each individual
vocabList.etym: From quis +‎ -que (“each”). Compare to quoque and quisquam, and a parallel development in Gothic 𐍈𐌰𐌶𐌿𐌷 (ƕazuh).
From cārus (“dear, expensive”) +‎ -tās.
From quī +‎ vīs.
Apocopated form of neque.
From Proto-Italic *pākslā, from Proto-Indo-European *pak-slo-, from *peh₂ǵ- (“to attach, fasten”). See pangō, pāgus, pacīscor, pāx, pāgina.[1]

vocabList.definition: to cry out, shout, scream, exclaim
vocabList.etym: From vōcifer.
From older seive, from sei (“if”) +‎ -ve (“or”). Equivalent to sī (“if”) +‎ -ve (“or”). Collateral form seu by apocope.

vocabList.definition: to keep busy, keep at work, drive on; occupy, practise, employ, exercise (something in a form of action)
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 1.430–431:
Quālis apēs aestāte novā per flōrea rūraexercet sub sōle labor [...].
Just like [a colony of] honeybees [which], in early summer, through flowery meadows, keeps busy under the sun, [such was the] toil [of the Carthaginian builders] [...].

vocabList.etym: Apocope of sīve.
Possibly for *provillium, *produillium from bellum, duellum.

Shortened from Middle High German enwec, from Old High German in weg, corresponding to modern in +‎ Weg. The first syllable is still seen in dialectal forms with e-; compare Luxembourgish ewech. Cognate with Dutch weg, Hunsrik wech, English away.

vocabList.definition: at length, at last, finally, eventually
vocabList.etym: From tam (“so”) +‎ -dem (“new interpreted particle from īdem”). Compare with its earlier doublet: tamen. Both with original meaning supposedly "so(much)ever".

vocabList.definition: to be astonished at, marvel at, admire, be amazed at, wonder at
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 1.421–422:
Mīrātur mōlem Aenēās, māgālia quondam;mīrātur portās, strepitumque, et strāta viārum.
[Upon his first sight of Carthage,] Aeneas marvels [at such] massive construction, [where] once [was only] huts; he admires its gateways, and such noisy activity, and the pavement of its streets.
(Exemplifies anaphora.)

vocabList.etym: From ante (“before”) + ea (“these things”).

vocabList.definition: to delight, charm, please (+ accusative the person, who is delighted)
vocabList.etym: Frequentative of dēliciō, or else from dē- +‎ lactō.
Probably from ut +‎ -quam (“any”), with intermediate Proto-Italic *utVs (“so that, as”) plus indefinitizing quam. Compare uspiam.

vocabList.definition: pleasantness, pleasurableness, delightfulness, loveliness, agreeableness, charm
vocabList.etym: From amoenus (“pleasant, delightful, lovely”) +‎ -tās.

From Proto-Italic *rāros, probably from Proto-Indo-European *h₁r̥h₁rós, from *h₁reh₁- (“to separate”) (though Schrijver and de Vaan are skeptical). Cognate with Ancient Greek ἐρῆμος (erêmos, “lonely”).

vocabList.definition: without a doubt, no doubt, of course
vocabList.etym: Univerbation of nī, mīrum ("if not, that would be odd").
Perfect active participle of sequor (“to follow”) (for expected *sectus, proven by sector, possibly after volūtus, solūtus etc.).

vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Fasti 5.652:
montibus hīs pōnunt spemque laremque suum
on these hills they place their hope and their home

vocabList.definition: scarcely, hardly, by no means, not, not at all
vocabList.etym: Possibly from the same Proto-Indo-European root as Cornish gow (“lie”).[1]

vocabList.definition: to go, move, proceed, go along, move along
vocabList.usage:
c. 191 BCE, Plautus, Pseudolus 4.1.44–45:
SIMŌ. Illīcine est? PSEUDOLUS. Illīc est. SIMŌ. Mala merx est, Pseudole. Illūc sīs vidē,ut trānsvorsus, nōn prōvorsus cēdit, quasi cancer solet.
SIMO. Is he there? PSEUDOLUS. There he is. SIMO. He's a bad piece, Pseudolus. Look at that,
how he goes sideways, not forwards, as a crab does.

vocabList.etym: quot +‎ -iēns
Reduplication of  quis.
For *propiter, from prope. Compare with inter (“between”) and subter (“beneath”).
vocabList.usage:
Ibi angiportum propter est.
There hard by is an alley.

vocabList.definition: to perish, pass away, die, be ruined
vocabList.etym: From per- (“through”) +‎ eō (“go”).
vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Fasti 5.267–268:
‘flōrē semel laesō pereunt viciaecque fabaeque,et pereunt lentēs, advena Nīle, tuae.’
“Once the blossom has been damaged, the vetches and the beans perish, and your lentils perish, oh foreign [River] Nile.”
(The poetic voice is that of Flora (mythology).)

29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 1.232–233:
“quid Trōēs potuēre, quibus, tot fūnera passīs,cūnctus ob Ītaliam terrārum clauditur orbis?”
“What have the Trojans done, for whom, having suffered so many losses, the whole circle of the lands has been closed. [And all] for the sake of Italy.”
(Venus, speaking to Jupiter, laments the plight of the Trojans as they wander the Mediterranean shores.)

vocabList.etym: Uncertain. Ultimately from the root *demh₂- (“to domesticate, tame”).

vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 4.382–384:
“Spērō equidem mediīs, sī quid pia nūmina possunt,supplicia hausūrum scopulīs, et nōmine Dīdō
saepe vocātūrum. [...]”
“But I hope [that], in the midst [of the sea] — if the just gods do what they are able — [you] will drink [your] punishments on the reefs, and to the name ‘Dido’ you will cry out often.”
(hausūrum = [tē] haustūrum esse: figuratively, may you suffer what you deserve; literally, may you drown when you are shipwrecked “mediīs scopulīs” — among underwater rocks)

vocabList.etym: From sōlor (“to comfort, console, solace”) +‎ -āx +‎ -ium.
From pateō (“be open”) + faciō (“make, construct”).
From in + ops (“power, ability, wealth”).

vocabList.definition: that which flees, has fled, fugitive
vocabList.etym: From prōfugiō (“I flee, run away or escape”).

vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 1.1:
Arma virumque cano […]
I sing of weapons and a man […]

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German wër, from Old High German wër, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaʀ. Related to wo.
From Middle High German sich, from Old High German sih, from Proto-Germanic *sek. Compare Yiddish זיך (zikh), Dutch zich. Unrelated to sicher.

From Middle High German hiute, from Old High German hiutu, a contraction of earlier *hiu tagu, from Proto-West Germanic *hiu dagu, from Proto-Germanic *hinō dagō (“on this day”, from *hiz + *dagaz). Cognate with Old English hēodæġ (“today”) and Dutch heden (“today”).
Compare German heuer from hiu (“in this”) +‎ jāru (“year”).
vocabList.usage:
Heute ist Montag
Today is monday

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German tisch, from Old High German tisc, from Proto-West Germanic *disk (“dish”).
vocabList.usage:
Kommt, der Tisch ist gedeckt!
Come, the table is set!

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German durst, from Old High German durst, thurst, from Proto-West Germanic *þurstu, from Proto-Germanic *þurstuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”).
Inherited from Middle High German gelīch, from Old High German gilīh, from Proto-West Germanic *galīk, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, from *ga- + *-līkaz.
vocabList.usage:
Zwei plus zwei ist gleich vier.
Two plus two is equal to four.

vocabList.definition: even as, as, just as, like, as if
vocabList.etym: From vel +‎ ut.
From Proto-Italic *flēō, from earlier *flējō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁- (“to bleat, cry”).[1]

vocabList.definition: to groan, moan or sigh (at or over)
vocabList.etym: From in- +‎ gemō.
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 4.691-692:
[...] oculīsque errantibus altō / quaesīvit caelō lūcem, ingemuitque reperta.
And with wandering eyes [Dido] searched for high heaven’s light, and having found it, she groaned.

vocabList.etym: From sīc (“thus, so”) +‎ ut (“how, as”).
From pateō (“to be open”) +‎ -ulus.
From sēmi- +‎ ustus. For the contraction of /i/ and /u/ through internal sandhi as well as etymologically, compare sēmustulō.
From dēlu(ō) (“to cleanse”) +‎ -brum, from de- + lavō (“I wash”).

Perhaps from praes (“surety, bondsman”) +‎ -ium.
Others refer it to praehendō.
For quid (“what, why, well!”, interjection) +‎ -pe, the same corroborating particle seen in nempe; see also quispiam.
Perfect passive participle of prōruō.
From pro- +‎ ruo.
im- +‎ mēnsus.[1]

vocabList.definition: to go or march on; to advance
vocabList.etym: Frequentative verb from gradior.

From Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃-, the root of sternō (“I spread, bestrew, scatter, fell”), with a *-g- extension. Cognate with Ancient Greek στόρνυμι (stórnumi, “scatter”), στρατός (stratós, “army, people, body of men”), Old English strewian (English strew).

vocabList.definition: some sort of snare or trap
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *tenos, from Proto-Indo-European *ténos, from *ten- (“to stretch, draw”). Cognate with  Sanskrit तनस् (tánas), Ancient Greek *τένος (*ténos) (attested in ἀτενής (atenḗs)), also with German Dohne which has the same meaning. More at teneō (“hold, grasp”).[1]
Unknown.[1][2] Maybe from earlier *verstīgium, from verrō (“to sweep”).[3] Or, possibly from vē- +‎ *stīgō, from Proto-Indo-European *stéygʰeti (“to walk”).
From lacer.

vocabList.definition: Covered, concealed, hidden; having been covered, hidden or concealed
vocabList.etym: Perfect passive participle of tegō (“cover; shelter”).

vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Fasti 5.263–266:
‘sī bene flōruerint segetēs, erit āreā dīves;sī bene flōruerit vīnea, Bacchus erit;
sī bene flōruerint oleae, nitidissimus annus,
pōmaque prōventum temporis huius habent.’
“If the crops blossom well, the threshing floor will be rich; if the vineyard blossoms well, Bacchus will be [pleased]; if the olive trees blossom well, the year [will be] most polished [with oil], and fruits [will also] have the prosperity of this season.”
(Translating the Latin future perfect tense as English present tense. The poetic voice is that of Flora (mythology).)

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German and Old High German māl, from Proto-West Germanic *māl, from Proto-Germanic *mēlą. See also Mahl (“meal”), which is ultimately the same word. Cognate with English meal.

vocabList.definition: to ask, to beg, to plead, to request ,third-person singular present

vocabList.etym: A contraction of in + das.
vocabList.usage:
Ich bin ins Kino gegangen.
I went to the cinema.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German offanlīh (“open, public”) and offanlīhho (“openly, publicly”). Equivalent to offen +‎ -lich.

From Middle High German bewegen, from Old High German biwegan, from Proto-West Germanic *biwegan, derived from Proto-Germanic *weganą (“to move”),[1] which stems from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. Compare English beweigh.

vocabList.definition:
will, to be going to,  From Middle High German wërden, from Old High German werdan, from Proto-West Germanic *werþan, from Proto-Germanic *werþaną. Cognate with Dutch worden, obsolete English worth, Swedish varda, Norwegian Nynorsk verta, and also with Latin vertō (“to turn”).
,third-person singular present of werden
vocabList.etym: Inherited from Middle Scots word, from Middle English word, from Old English word (“word”), from Proto-Germanic *wurdą (“word”), from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰh₁om (“word”).
From sē +‎ -cum (“with”).
vocabList.usage:
Duxit secum virginem.
He led the girl with himself.

vocabList.etym: From in- (“within”) +‎ signum (“a sign, an emblem”) +‎ -is (suffix forming an adjective); so formed because the subject qualified by this adjective has been revealed, specifically by means of a sign, to be exceptional relative to ordinary examples of its kind.
From quis +‎ -dam (indefinite adverbial suffix). Compare quondam (“at one time”).

vocabList.definition: long, a long while, a while, for long, for a long time
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *djowe, from Proto-Indo-European *dyéw(i) (“during the day”), locative case of *dyḗws, with d possibly imported from diēs. Cognate with Old Armenian տիւ (tiw), Sanskrit दिवा (divā, “by day”).
From ob- (“to, against”) +‎ iūrgō (“dispute, chide”).
vocabList.usage:
166 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Andria 141–143:
Rēctē putās; / nam sī illum obiūrgēs vītae quī auxilium tulit, / quid faciās illī quī dederit damnum aut malum?
You’re corrrect; for if you were to scold someone who brought help, what would you do to someone who gave harm or evil?(Second person singular present active subjunctive, used in a future less vivid conditional clause.)

vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *plousisemos. Suppletive superlative of multus (“many”).

vocabList.definition: to esteem, prize, love, have regard, to delight in (something)
vocabList.etym: From dis- (“apart, asunder”) +‎ legō (“to choose, to take”), or from dis- (“utterly, exceedingly”) +‎ Proto-Italic *legō (“to care”).
vocabList.usage:
c. 84 BCE – 54 BCE, Catullus, Carmina 72.3-4:
Dīlēxī tum tē nōn tantum ut vulgus amīcam,sed pater ut gnātōs dīligit et generōs.
I loved you at the time, not merely as an ordinary man does his girlfriend, but as a father loves his sons and sons-in-law.

vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *kʷoizā, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys- (“to heed”).
From Middle High German gesuntheit. By surface analysis, gesund (“healthy”) +‎ -heit (“-ness, -hood”). Compare Dutch gezondheid.

vocabList.definition: to imply, to mean, to signify, to indicate, to spell, to betoken
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German bediuten, betiuten, from Old High German bidiuten. Equivalent to be- +‎ deuten.
From Middle High German heiȥen, from Old High German heiȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *haitan, from Proto-Germanic *haitaną.
vocabList.usage:
Ich werde Lutz genannt, aber ich heiße Ludger.
They call me Lutz, but my name is Ludger.

vocabList.etym: Inherited from Middle High German nëmen, from Old High German nëman, from Proto-West Germanic *neman, from Proto-Germanic *nemaną, from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to give or take ones due”).
vocabList.usage:
Wer hat meinen Hut genommen?
Who took my hat?

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German klingen, Old High German klingan, from Proto-West Germanic *klingan, from Proto-Germanic *klinganą. More at clink.

vocabList.definition:
to understand
to hear and interpret

to comprehend, make sense of

to take, to see, to gather 

to know, have knowledge or understanding of
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German verstān, virstēn, vorstēn, ferstān, from Old High German firstān, firstēn, from Proto-Germanic *frastāną, equivalent to ver- +‎ stehen. Cognate with Bavarian versteh, Dutch verstaan, Middle Low German vorstān. Compare also English forstand.
vocabList.usage:
Ich verstehe dich nicht bei dem Lärm.
I can't understand you with this noise.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German daȥ, from Old High German daȥ, from Proto-Germanic *þat. Compare Dutch dat, Low German dat, datt, English that. Doublet of das. Distinction from das is purely orthographical convention.
vocabList.usage:
Ich habe gehört, dass du krank bist.
I was told that you are sick.

vocabList.etym: Inherited from Middle High German ander, from Old High German andar, from Proto-West Germanic *anþar.
From Middle High German saz, satz, deverbal from setzen. Compare Yiddish זעץ (zets, “a punch”).
vocabList.usage:
Dieser Satz scheint mir grammatikalisch falsch zu sein.
This sentence seems grammatically wrong to me.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German weln, from welen, wellen, from Old High German wellen, from Proto-West Germanic *walljan, from Proto-Germanic *waljaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-.
vocabList.usage:
Ich wähle diese Hose da, die mit der Bügelfalte.
I'm choosing these pants here, the ones with the crease.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German müeȥen, from Old High German muoȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *mōtan.

From Middle High German wërden, from Old High German werdan, from Proto-West Germanic *werþan, from Proto-Germanic *werþaną. Cognate with Dutch worden, obsolete English worth, Swedish varda, Norwegian Nynorsk verta, and also with Latin vertō (“to turn”).
vocabList.usage:
Ich werde nach Hause gehen.
I will go home.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German sagen, from Old High German sagēn, from Proto-West Germanic *saggjan, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ-.
vocabList.usage:
Ich habe nicht verstanden, was sie gesagt hat.
I didn't understand what she said.

vocabList.definition: to join, unite, fasten, yoke, harness, attach; esp. of the hand: to clasp, join
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 4.141-142:
[...] Ipse ante aliōs pulcherrimus omnisīnfert sē socium Aenēās atque agmina iungit.
[The Trojan leader] himself, before all others, most handsome — Aeneas comes forward as [Dido’s] companion, and also unites [their combined] ranks.
(Symbolic of personal, civic and military alliances as Dido and Aeneas, Carthaginians and Trojans, join in regal formation for the hunt.)

vocabList.definition: bad reputation or repute, ill fame, dishonor, disgrace, infamy, reproach
vocabList.etym: From īnfāmis (“infamous”), from in- (“not”) + fāma (“fame, renown”).

vocabList.definition: to use, make use of, employ
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *oitōr (with ūsus for *issus after ūtor), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₃eyt- (“to take along, fetch”). Compare the future tense οἴσω (oísō) of Ancient Greek φέρω (phérō, “carry”).
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 1.64:
Ad quem tum Iūnō supplex hīs vōcibus ūsa est:
To this one then Juno, suppliant, used these words:(Note the correlation of the indicative perfect tense verb “usa est” with the ablative plural “his vocibus”: Juno used, or that is to say, spoke “with these words”.)

vocabList.etym: From Proto-Indo-European *sm̥meh₁lom (“one time”), from *sem- (“together”) and *meh₁-lo- (“measure, time”), from *meh₁- (“to measure”). See each for cognate words.

Most likely from Proto-Italic *pro- + *prijos (“own, dear”), from Proto-Indo-European *priHós (“dear”). Since pro- can hardly be explained as a nominal prefix, Forssman (2004) explains it as having been extended to the adjective from the verb propriāre, once-attested as propriāssit. Cognate to Sanskrit प्रिय (priyá, “dear”), Russian прия́тель (prijátelʹ, “buddy, mate”) and Russian прия́тный (prijátnyj, “pleasant”), Welsh rhydd (“free”), English free.[1]
A substantivisation of the masculine plural forms of the adjective plērusque.
From valeō (“I am strong, I am healthy, I am worth”) +‎ -idus.
Univerbation of nōn (“not”) +‎ dum (“while, as, as long as”).
vocabList.usage:
Videō barbam et pallium; philosophum nōndum videō.
I see a beard and cloak; I do not yet see a philosopher.

vocabList.etym: Perfect passive participle of adigō (“drive, hurl”).
From Proto-Italic *plēros, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁-. Compare Ancient Greek πλήρης (plḗrēs).

vocabList.definition: quarrel, brawl, dispute, contest, strife, contention
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Indo-European *h₁riḱ-s-eh₂, whence also Ancient Greek ἐρείκω (ereíkō, “to rend, bruise, pound”).[1]

vocabList.definition: to bind together, connect, join, unite, yoke together, juxtapose
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 8.130:
a stirpe fores geminis coniunctus Atridis
[that] you were joined by blood to the twins of Atrides

vocabList.etym: For *provorsus, from prō + versus, vorsus (“turned”).

vocabList.definition: which is to be united, made friendly, reconciled, won over
vocabList.etym: Future passive participle (gerundive) of conciliō
Present active participle of ineō (“enter”)

From Middle High German kennen, from Old High German kennen, from Proto-West Germanic *kannijan (“to know”), from Proto-Germanic *kannijaną (“to know”), a causative form of *kunnaną formed with the suffix *-janą. Cognate to Bavarian kennan, Dutch and Low German kennen, Scots and English ken (“to know”).
From Middle High German wort. Compare Dutch woord, English word, Danish ord. Doublet of Verb.
vocabList.usage:
Im Deutschen gibt es wenig Wörter, die mit y geschrieben werden.
In German there are few words spelt with y.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German liute, from Old High German liuti, also liudi, from Proto-West Germanic *liud(i), from Proto-Germanic *liudīz (“people”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“man, people”).
Adverbialized noun Bisschen, from Bissen (“a bit, bite”) +‎ -chen (“diminutive”)

vocabList.definition: to gladden, to make glad, to make pleased
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German vrö(u)wen, vre(u)wen, from Old High German frewen, frouwen, a derivation of Old High German frō, frao (“glad”). Equivalent to froh (“glad”) +‎ -en. Compare English frolic.
vocabList.usage:
[Es] freut mich, Sie kennenzulernen.
I'm pleased to meet you. ([It] pleases me to get to know you. (formal))

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German anwalde, from Old High German anawalto, from Old English anweald.

From Middle High German ūf, from Old High German ūf, from Proto-Germanic *upp. This form with a lengthened vowel is originally Upper German. Central German forms were Middle High German uf and (western) up. Compare Dutch op, Low German op, Luxembourgish op, English up.

From Middle High German nāh, from Old High German nāh with preservation of word-final -h as -ch; thus pertaining to modern nah (“near”) (from Old High German inflected nāh-), from Proto-West Germanic *nāhw, from Proto-Germanic *nēhw. Cognate with Dutch na, English nigh.
From lang (“long”, adjective) +‎ Weile (“while”, noun). Cognate with Hunsrik langweilich.

vocabList.definition: people , folk, peeps , guys,Alternative form of Leute
vocabList.etym: Leut pl

Perfect passive participle of exerceō (“to occupy oneself, oversee; work at, practice, exercise”), from ex- (“out of”) +‎ arceō (“to ward off, protect, guard”), from Proto-Italic *arkeō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂orké-ye-ti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erk- (“to protect, guard”).

vocabList.definition: to lay, set, put or place aside or away; deposit
to finish play, cease to sport
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *eksloidō. By surface analysis, ē (“out of”) + lūdō (“play; trick”).
vocabList.usage:
59 BCE – 17 CE, Titus Livius, Ab urbe condita libri 2.48.6:
Legiōnibus Rōmānīs cēdēbant in urbem; ubi abductās sēnserant legiōnēs, agrōs incursābant, bellum quiēte quiētem bellō in vicem ēlūdentēs.
They would retreate from the Roman legions in the city; when they sensed the legions to be withdrawn, they would raid the countryside, evading war by peace and peace, in turn, by war.

vocabList.etym: Perfect passive participle of effrēnō.
From praeses (“guardian, defender”) +‎ -ium or praesideō (“to guard, defend”) +‎ -ium.
Perfect passive participle of concurrō.
From fūr (“thief”) +‎ -or.
Unknown; possibly related to Hittite 𒅕𒄩𒀸 (er-ḫa-aš /⁠erḫaš⁠/, “line, boundary”), Latvian āra, perhaps all from Proto-Indo-European *h₁erh₂- (“border, line”).[1][2]
Perfect passive participle of cōnstringō.

vocabList.definition: manner (of behaving), way (of behaving); behavior, conduct
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *mōs, a root noun interpreted as an s-stem noun, of uncertain origin. Generally believed to derive from Proto-Indo-European *moh₁-, *meh₁- (“to intend or be intent upon, to be of strong will”) (though the more common meaning of “to measure” may be the original, with “to intend” as a semantic extension),[1] whence Ancient Greek μαίομαι (maíomai, “to strive”) and perhaps Ancient Greek Μοῦσᾰ (Moûsă, “Muse”), and also English mood.

vocabList.definition: eager, desirous, passionate, fond (+ genitive or + in ablative)
vocabList.etym: From cupiō +‎ -idus.
Future participle of conciliō.
From perfidus +‎ -ia.

vocabList.definition: pity, compassion, mercy, lovingkindness, tenderness, heartedness
vocabList.etym: From misericors (“pitiful, compassionate, merciful”) +‎ -ia.

vocabList.definition: to uphold, support, prop or sustain, maintain
vocabList.etym: Frequentative verb of sustineō.
vocabList.usage:
c. 52 BCE, Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico VII.17:
Extremam famem sustentarent
They sustained the extreme hunger

vocabList.etym: From Latin concurrentia (“concurrence; competition”). Compare English concurrence.
From Proto-Indo-European *nū (“now”).
From libēns (“willing, cheerful”) +‎ -ter.

vocabList.definition: to orate, deliver a speech publicly
vocabList.etym: The etymology of this word hinges on whether Oscan urust should be accepted as cognate:
vocabList.usage:
405 CE, Hieronymus, Vulgata 1 Thessalonicenses 5:25:
Frātrēs, ōrāte prō nōbīs.
Brothers, pray for us.

vocabList.definition: to waver (in opinion), be uncertain, doubt, question, be in doubt

vocabList.etym: Future passive participle of perspiciō.
Perfect passive participle of audeō.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “paper”), with a change to the feminine gender.

vocabList.definition: to unfold, unfurl, uncoil, loosen, undo
vocabList.etym: From ex- +‎ plicō (“to fold”).
Perfect passive participle of trāiciō.
From circus (“circle, ring”) +‎ -ter.
vocabList.usage:
hunc locum circiter
close to this place

vocabList.etym: Supposed to have been earlier *priuscus, from prior, q.v. Equivalent to prius +‎ -cus; ultimately composed of Proto-Indo-European *pre- + *-yōs + *-kos.[1] Possibly cognate to English fresh.
From con- +‎ emō. Compare with its contracted form cōmō.

From Proto-Italic *tonaō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”), replacing the likely earlier form tonere (“thunder”); one of few Latin verbs (as domō) only classed in the first conjugation by the action of sound laws. Cognate with Old Norse Þórr (“Thor”), English thunder.
From Middle High German wār, wǣre, from Old High German wār, wāri, from Proto-West Germanic *wār, from Proto-Germanic *wēraz.

vocabList.definition: to place, put, set in order, assign
vocabList.etym: con- +‎ locō (“put, place, set”)
vocabList.usage:
56 BCE, Cicero, Pro Caelio 17.39:
Ob hanc causam tibi hunc puerum parens commendavit et tradidit, ut in amore atque in voluptatibus adulescentiam suam collocaret, et ut hanc tu vitam atque haec studia defenderes?
Was it for this reason that his parent entrusted and handed over this boy to you, so that he could spend his youth in love and pleasures, and so that you could defend this lifestyle and these passions?

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German drucken, from Old High German drucchen, drukken, from Proto-West Germanic *þrukkijan (“to press”). Doublet of drücken (“to press, push”) with Upper German lack of umlaut before a velar geminate; the first German printers were in the south. Established as technical term for printing in the 17th century (see also bedrucken).
From Middle High German āne (“without”), from Old High German āna, ānu, āno (“without”), from Proto-Germanic *ēnu, *ēnō (“without”).
vocabList.usage:
Ich habe viele Jahre vergeudet, ohne dir zu sagen, was du mir bedeutest.
I wasted many years without telling you what you mean to me.

vocabList.etym: einrichten +‎ -ung
mögen +‎ -lich; cognate with Hunsrik meeghlich, Dutch mogelijk.
vocabList.usage:
Es ist möglich, ungesund zu essen und trotzdem gesund zu bleiben.
It is possible to eat unhealthily and stay healthy nonetheless.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German richtunge, from Old High German rihtunga, from Proto-West Germanic *rihtungu. By surface analysis, richten +‎ -ung.
Standard +‎ mäßig
Back-formation from nequeō, itself related to the irregular verb eō.
vocabList.usage:
166 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Andria 804–805:
CRĪTŌ: Quid vōs? Quō pactō hic? Satin rēctē? MȲSĪS: Nōsne? “Sīc / ut quīmus,” aiunt, “quandō ut volumus nōn licet.”
CRITO: What about you all? How are things going here? Well enough?MYSIS: Us? “We do what we can,” as they say, “since we can’t do as we wish.”
(More literally: “since what we want is not possible.”)

vocabList.etym: Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teg- (“beam, stake”) (whence also tignum).
From ad- (“toward, to”) +‎ agō (“do, make”).

vocabList.definition: to place in command, put in charge
vocabList.etym: From prae- (“before”) +‎ faciō (“do, make”).
From Proto-Italic *relikuwos, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ-. Related to Latin linquō, itself derived from Proto-Italic *linkʷō.
Perfect participle of nancīscor
From mīrus +‎ -ficus.

vocabList.definition: to say, speak, assert, say “yes”, affirm
vocabList.usage:
Stanislaus Julien translating Mencius as Meng Tseu, p. 46:
Cōnfūcius aiēbat...
Confucius said...

vocabList.etym: Present active participle of tollō (“lift up; remove”).

For *opvortet, from Proto-Indo-European *wortéyeti, causative stem (2nd conjugation) of the root of vertō (“to turn”) (3rd conjugation). Some refer the op- to ob-, some to opus, with which compare the similar expressions opus est and operam dare.
vocabList.usage:
166 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Andria 238–239:
Uxōrem dēcrērat dare sēsē mī hodiē: nōnne oportuit / praescīsse mē ante? Nōnne priū’ commūnicātum oportuit?
He himself has decided to give me a wife today: ought I not to have known beforehand? Shouldn’t it have been communicated sooner?

vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *nepōts, from Proto-Indo-European *népōts.
From Proto-Italic *kʷot, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷóti, adverb from *kʷos, *kʷís. Cognate with Ancient Greek πόσος (pósos) and Sanskrit कति (káti).
vocabList.usage:
Quot occentabas?
How many did you serenade?

vocabList.etym: Adverbial accusative of nimius (“too great, excessive”).
For *cuter, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷóteros, from *kʷos (“which”), ultimately from *kʷ-. Cognate with Ancient Greek πότερος (póteros, “which of the two”) and English whether.
From *seksnos, equivalent to sex +‎ -nus.

vocabList.definition: severe, serious, strict, stern, stringent, austere, harsh,  grave
