From Middle High German socke, from Old High German soc, a West Germanic borrowing from Latin soccus (“a light shoe or slipper, buskin”), from Ancient Greek σύκχος (súkkhos, “a kind of shoe”), probably from Phrygian or from an Anatolian language.
From Middle High German stivel, from Old High German stival, borrowed from  Old French estivel, perhaps from Latin aestas (“summer”) or Latin stipes (“tree trunk, log”).
From Strumpf (“stocking”) +‎ Hose (“trousers”).

From Middle High German tasche, from Old High German taska, tasca. Further origin unknown. Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *taskǭ. Cognate with Dutch tas, Hunsrik Tasch, Middle Low German tasche (“bag, pouch”), Old Norse taska (“bag, purse”) (probably borrowed from Low German). Compare English tasse (“plate armor, which protects the thighs”).
From Middle High German tragen, from Old High German tragan, from Proto-West Germanic *dragan, from Proto-Germanic *draganą (“to draw, drag”).
vocabList.usage:
Sie konnten die Kiste nicht mehr tragen und mussten sie abstellen.
They couldn't carry the box any longer and had to put it down.

vocabList.etym: Training +‎ -s- +‎ Anzug (“suit”)
From unter- (“under”) +‎ Hose (“trousers”). Cognate with Hunsrik Unnerhoss.
unter- +‎ Wäsche
From Arbeit (“work”) +‎ -s- +‎ Zimmer (“room”).
From backen +‎ Ofen.
baden (“to bathe”) +‎ Wanne (“tub”)
From baden (“to bath”) +‎ Zimmer (“room”).
From Bücher +‎ Regal.

From Middle High German buode, from Old High German *buoda, from Proto-West Germanic *bōþu, from Proto-Germanic *bōþō. Probably related to *būaną (“to build”), whence German bauen.[1] Cognate with Middle Dutch boede, Middle Low German bôde, Old Norse búð, bóð, whence English booth.
From Middle High German decke, from Old High German theckī, decchī, derived from thecken (modern decken), from Proto-West Germanic *þakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną.
vocabList.usage:
unter einer Decke stecken
to be in cahoots
(literally, “be under the same blanket”)

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German dille, from Old High German dilla, from Proto-Germanic *þiljǭ. More at thill.
From doppel- (“double”) +‎ Haus (“house”).
From French douche, from Italian doccia. The word became much more common after World War II, as the native word Brausebad had developed bad connotations.
See Dusche.
vocabList.usage:
Ich dusche (mich) jeden Tag.
I shower every day.

vocabList.etym: eine (“one”) +‎ Familie (“family”) +‎ -n- +‎ Haus (“house”)
vocabList.usage:
Peter besitzt ein Einfamilienhaus.
Peter owns a family home.

vocabList.etym: Erde +‎ Geschoss
From essen (“eat”, verb) +‎ Zimmer (“room”).
From Middle High German vluor, from Old High German fluor, from Proto-Germanic *flōraz.
From Fuß (foot) +‎ Boden (bottom, ground, floor).
From Middle High German garte, from Old High German garto, from Proto-West Germanic *gardō.
From Gas (“gas”) +‎ Herd (“cooker, stove”).
Haar +‎ Bürste
From Middle High German hanttuoch, from Old High German hanttuoh. By surface analysis, Hand (“hand”) +‎ Tuch (“cloth”).
From heizen +‎ Körper.
heizen (“to heat”) +‎ -ung (nominal suffix to form nouns from verbs)
vocabList.usage:
Dreh die Heizung auf.
turn the heat up.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German kamb, camb, chamb, from Old High German chamb, from Proto-West Germanic *kamb, from Proto-Germanic *kambaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth”).
From Middle High German kemben, kemmen, from Old High German kemben, kempen, from Proto-Germanic *kambijaną (“to comb”).
vocabList.usage:
Ich kämme dir kurz die Haare.
I’ll comb / brush your hair quickly.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German keller, from Old High German kellari, from Proto-West Germanic *kellārī (“cellar, storeroom”). See Kellner.
Shortened from Klosett.
From Middle High German knopf, from Old High German knopf, from Proto-Germanic *knuppaz (“lump, clod”). Cognate with Hunsrik Knopp, Luxembourgish Knapp, Dutch knoop.
Borrowed from French commode.
Compound of kühl (“cool”) +‎ Schrank (“cabinet”).
From Middle High German lampe, from Latin lampada, from Latin lampas. Cognate with English lamp.

From Middle High German lieht (Middle German also līcht), from Old High German lioht, from Proto-West Germanic *leuht, from Proto-Germanic *leuhtą, from Proto-Indo-European *lewktom. Compare Dutch licht, English light.
Mikrowelle (“micro wave”) +‎ Herd (“oven”)
15th century, from Middle French meuble(s) (“household goods”), from Latin mobilis. At first restricted to the Moselle region, more widely attested since ca. 1600.
Möbel +‎ -iert
From Middle High German oben, obene, from Old High German obana, from Proto-West Germanic *obanā, from Proto-Germanic *ubanē. Related to über and ober-.

From north-eastern Middle High German rase, probably from Middle Low German wrāse (“sod, turf”), though the two could also be cognate forms. Further origin presumably a variant of Middle Low German wāse, from Old Saxon waso, from Proto-West Germanic *wasō (“moisture, slime, muck”) which has been inherited as German Wasen.[1]
Early 17th century, of unclear origin. Hypotheses include:[1]
From Schlaf (“sleep”) +‎ Zimmer (“room”).

From Middle High German slüȥȥel, from Old High German sluȥȥil, from Proto-West Germanic *slutil, which is derived from *sleutan (“to close”), from which also modern German schließen.
Cognate with Dutch sleutel and English slot.[1]
vocabList.usage:
Der Schlüssel passt nicht.
The key doesn't fit.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German seife, from Old High German seifa, seiffa, from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out, dribble, strain, trickle”). Cognate with Dutch zeep, Low German Seep, West Frisian sjippe, English soap.
From French sofa and Italian sofà, from Arabic صُفَّة (ṣuffa).
From spülen (“rinse, wash”) +‎ Becken (“basin”).
From spülen (“to wash”) +‎ Maschine (“machine”).
From steppen +‎ Decke.
From Middle High German stoc, from Old High German stoc, from Proto-West Germanic *stokk.
vocabList.usage:
Ich weiß nicht, wo ich den Stock gelassen habe; haben Sie ihn nicht gesehen?
I don't know where I've left the staff; haven't you seen it?

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German stuofe, from Old High German stuofa, from Proto-West Germanic *stōpā, related to the verb *stappjan (“to tread, step”).

Borrowed from French tablette.
Doublet of Tablet

15th century. From Medieval Latin tapēta f (“wall covering”), from the plural of tapētum n, itself derived from tapēte n, tapēs m, from Ancient Greek τάπης m (tápēs, “carpet, rug”), from an Iranian word.
From Middle High German teppich, tepich, teppech, tepech, tepch, teppch; from Old High German teppih, tepich, teppech; from Medieval Latin tapicus; from Latin tapes.
tiefkühlen (“to freeze”) +‎ Truhe (“chest”)
Tisch +‎ Tuch
From Toilette (“toilet”) +‎ -n- +‎ Papier (“paper”).

From Middle High German topf, from Old High German *topf, from Proto-West Germanic *dopp, from Proto-Germanic *duppaz (“hollow, bowl”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewb- (“deep, hollow”). Cognate with Dutch dop (“little cup, thimble”), Low German Dopp (“shell, pod, bowl”), Saterland Frisian Dop (“shell, pod, bowl”), English dop (“cup in which a diamond is cut”).
Attested since the 12th century, from Middle High German treppe, trappe, from Old High German trappa, from Proto-West Germanic *trappā.
From Middle High German tuoch, from Old High German tuoh, from Proto-West Germanic *dōk (“cloth”). Compare Dutch doek (“cloth, canvas”), English duck. More at duck, dook.
From Middle High German, from Old High German turi, from Proto-West Germanic *dur. Compare English door.
From Middle High German unden(e), undenen, und(e)nân, untnân, from Old High German undenân, untenân, untana. Related to unter.
From Middle High German vorhanc, vürhanc. By surface analysis, deverbal from vorhängen.
waschen +‎ Becken

From Middle High German wesche, from Old High German wesca, from Proto-West Germanic *waski ~ *waskiju (not attested outside High German). Cognate with Luxembourgish Wäsch, Vilamovian weś, etc. With a different stem formation compare Dutch was, Old High German wasca. By surface analysis, waschen (“to wash”) +‎ -e.
vocabList.usage:
Nach der Wäsche muss ich meine Hemden bügeln.
After washing I need to iron my shirts.

vocabList.etym: From waschen (“to wash, to launder”) +‎ Küche (“kitchen”)
From waschen (“to wash”) +‎ Maschine (“machine”).
From Wasser +‎ Hahn.
wecken (“to wake”) +‎ -er (suffix forming agent nouns)
From wohnen +‎ Zimmer.

From Middle High German brief, from Old High German briaf, which is borrowed from Latin breve, a neuter form of brevis (“short”). Cognates include Middle Dutch brief, Dutch brief, Old Norse bréf, Old Saxon brēf (all of them borrowed from Latin)[1][2] and English brief.
Brief (“letter”) +‎ Freund (“friend”)
From Middle High German bruoder, from Old High German bruoder, from Proto-West Germanic *brōþer, from Proto-Germanic *brōþēr, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr. Doublet of Frater.
Ca. 1600, from Middle French cousin, from Latin consobrinus.
From French dame, from Latin domina (“mistress, lady”). Cognate with English dame.
From Ehe (“marriage”) +‎ Frau (“woman”).
From Middle High German eltern, from Old High German eltirōn, from Proto-Germanic *alþizô. Compare Dutch ouders, English elders.
From Middle High German enkel, from Old High German enkil, enchil, Proto-West Germanic *ankil, *ankul, from Proto-Germanic *ankulaz (“ankle”). Cognate with Dutch enkel, English ankle.
Nominalization of erwachsen.
Borrowed from Latin familia

From Middle High German vrouwe, from Old High German frouwa (“mistress”), from Proto-West Germanic *frauwjā, from Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ, a feminine form of *frawjô (“lord”), giving Old English frēa (“lord, king; God, Christ; husband”), frēo (“woman”), from Proto-Indo-European *proHwo-, a derivation from *per- (“to go forward”).
Middle High German vrouwelīn (“mistress, young unmarried noblewoman”), equivalent to Frau +‎ -lein

Inherited from Middle High German vriunt, from Old High German friunt, from Proto-West Germanic *friund, from Proto-Germanic *frijōndz (“lit., the loving one; lover, loved one, friend”), from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *preyH-.

From Middle High German geswister, from Old High German giswëstar, equivalent to ge- +‎ Schwester. Compare Old Saxon gisustrōni (“sibling”), Old Frisian swesterne, susterne, sisterne (“siblings”), Old English ġesweostren (“maternal cousin, sister”).

From groß +‎ Vater. Cognate to Dutch grootvader, German Low German Grautvader (Paderbornisch). Displaced Middle High German eltervater, altervater (“grandfather”). Compare English grandfather, which displaced English eldfather, elderfather in a similar manner.
Fixed nominalisation of Middle High German jung (“young”), from Old High German jung (“young”).
From Middle High German liute, from Old High German liuti, also liudi, from Proto-West Germanic *liud(i), from Proto-Germanic *liudīz (“people”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“man, people”).

From Middle High German magedichīn, meidichīn, from Old High German *magadihhīn or calqued from Middle Low German mēgedeken, megedekīn, both from Proto-West Germanic *magaþukīn. Equivalent to Magd +‎ -chen.

From Middle High German manlich, from Old High German manlīh, manalīh, from Proto-West Germanic *mannlīk, from Proto-Germanic *mannlīkaz. By surface analysis, Mann +‎ lich. Cognates include Dutch mannelijk, English manly, and Old Norse mannligr (“human”) (whence Danish mandlig, Swedish manlig).

From Middle High German muoter, from Old High German muoter, from Proto-West Germanic *mōder, from Proto-Germanic *mōdēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. Compare Dutch moeder, English mother, Danish moder, Swedish moder.

From Middle High German nāchgebūr(e), from Old High German nāhgibūr(o), from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwagabūrō, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwagabūrô (“neighbour”). Equivalent to nah, nach (“near, next, after”) + Bauer (“dweller, farmer”).

From Middle High German neve, from Old High German nefo, nevo, from Proto-West Germanic *nefō, from Proto-Germanic *nefô. Cognate with Dutch neef, obsolete English neve. Further from Proto-Indo-European *népōts, whence English nephew, which see for more.
Borrowed from Middle Low German nichte, from Old Saxon *nifta, from Proto-Germanic *niftiz.
Borrowed from French oncle.
Cognate with Dutch opa. This etymology is incomplete. You can help Wiktionary by elaborating on the origins of this term.
From Middle High German swëster, from Old High German swëster, from Proto-Germanic *swestēr.
From Middle High German sun, from Old High German sunu, from Proto-West Germanic *sunu, from Proto-Germanic *sunuz, from Proto-Indo-European *suHnús.
Borrowed from French tante.
Tochter f (genitive Tochter, plural Töchter, diminutive Töchterchen n or Töchterlein n)

From Middle High German vater, from Old High German fater, from Proto-West Germanic *fader, from Proto-Germanic *fadēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr. Germanic cognates include Dutch vader, Low German Vader, English father, Danish fader, Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌳𐌰𐍂 (fadar).
vocabList.usage:
Mein Vater erklärt mir jeden Sonntag unsere neun Planeten.
My father explains to me our nine planets every Sunday.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German wīplich, from Old High German wīblīh, from Proto-Germanic *wībalīkaz, equivalent to Weib +‎ -lich. Cognate with Dutch wijfelijk, English wifely.
vocabList.usage:
Sie gehört dem weiblichen Geschlecht an.
She belongs to the female sex.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German ente, confluence of (1.) the plural and oblique singular of ant and (2.) the Old High German variant enita, both from older anut, from Proto-West Germanic *anad. Cognate with Dutch eend.

From Middle High German vüetern, from Old High German fuotiren, derived from fuotar, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“fodder”). Equivalent to Futter +‎ -n. Compare Dutch voeren (“to feed”), dialectal English to fodder.
From Middle High German has(e), from Old High German haso, from Proto-West Germanic *hasō, from Proto-Germanic *hasô, from an Indo-European root originally meaning grey.
Inherited from Middle High German hunt.

From Middle Low German kanīneken, diminutive of kanīn, konīn, itself probably through Middle Dutch connijn from Old French connin, northern variant of connil, from Latin cunīculus. Analysable as Kanin +‎ -chen. Compare English cony.
Inherited from Middle High German katze, Old High German kazza, from Proto-West Germanic *kattā. Akin to Old English catt (“cat”).
Inherited from Middle High German kuo.
From Meer (“sea”) +‎ Schwein (“pig, swine”) +‎ -chen (diminutive suffix), literally “little sea pig”, or from Meerschwein +‎ -chen. The use of Meer refers to the animal as coming from overseas.

From Middle High German phert, phærît, pherit, pferift (“riding horse”), from Old High German pherit, pfarifrit, parafred, from Late Latin paraverēdus (originally “substitute post horse”). Largely displaced the native word Ross. Compare Dutch paard and English palfrey.
vocabList.usage:
Meine Mutter hat ein Pferd und das ist sehr süß.
My mother has a horse and it is very cute.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German schâf, from Old High German scāf.
By surface analysis, compound of Schild (“shield”) +‎ Kröte (“toad”).

From Middle High German slange, from Old High German slango, from Proto-Germanic *slangô. Cognate with German Low German Slang (“snake”), Dutch slang (“snake”), West Frisian slang (“snake”). Compare also Albanian shlligë (“adder”).
From Middle High German tier, from Old High German tior, from Proto-West Germanic *deuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *deuzą, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewsóm. Cognate to English deer.

From Middle High German vogel, vagel, from Old High German fogal, fugal, from Proto-West Germanic *fugl, from Proto-Germanic *fuglaz; possibly related to *fleuganą (“to fly”) through dissimilation from earlier *fluglaz. Cognates include Low German Vagel, Dutch vogel, English fowl, Danish fugl, Swedish fågel, Gothic 𐍆𐌿𐌲𐌻𐍃 (fugls).
From Welle (“wave”) +‎ Sittich (“parakeet”), a calque of translingual Melopsittacus undulatus.
17th century, from backen +‎ Stein, a calque of Middle Low German backstên.

From Middle High German boumwolle, from Late Old High German boumwolla. By surface analysis, Baum (“tree”) +‎ Wolle (“wool”). Perhaps based on Herodotus’ description of wool-bearing trees in India; compare Ancient Greek ἐριόξυλον (erióxulon, “cotton”, literally “wood/tree-wool”) and Latin linum xylinum (“cotton”, literally “wood/tree-flax”).
Compound of Kunst +‎ Stoff.
From Middle High German lëder, from Old High German lëdar, from Proto-West Germanic *leþr, from Proto-Germanic *leþrą (“leather”). Akin to Old Saxon lethar.
From Middle High German metalle, from Latin metallum (14th century).
From Middle High German sīde, from Old High German sīda, from Proto-West Germanic *sīdā (“silk”), from sēta (“silk”), from Latin saeta (“horsehair; bristle; silk”).
From Middle High German stein, from Old High German stein, from Proto-West Germanic *stain, from Proto-Germanic *stainaz (“stone”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *steyh₂-.

First attested in the mid 17th century. Most likely borrowed from Early Modern Dutch stof, from Middle Dutch stoffe, borrowed from Old French estophe, estoffe, from estoffer (“to provide what is necessary, equip, stuff”). The word is ultimately Germanic and was borrowed into Old French from Old High German stoffōn, itself from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn, making it a doublet of stopfen (“to stuff, to plug”).
From Middle High German wolle, from Old High German wolla, from Proto-West Germanic *wullu.
From Middle High German blā (genitive blāwes), from Old High German blāo, from Proto-West Germanic *blāu, from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz.

From Middle High German bunt, probably from Latin punctus, whence also English point; this would make it a doublet of Punkt. Dutch bont seems to have somewhat earlier attestations in the relevant sense, but the phonetic form (b- for p- and Dutch -o- for -u-) could hint at Middle High German origin. It is therefore unsettled which of the two borrowed from which.
From Middle High German grā, from Old High German grāo, from Proto-West Germanic *grāu. Compare English gray, grey.
From Middle High German grüene, from Old High German gruoni, gruoen, from Proto-West Germanic *grōnī, from Proto-Germanic *grōniz. Compare Low German grön, Dutch groen, English green, Danish grøn.
From French lilas.
From Latin rosa.

From Middle High German rōt (“red, red-haired”), from Old High German rōt (“red, scarlet, purple-red, brown-red, yellow-red”), from Proto-West Germanic *raud, from Proto-Germanic *raudaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rowdʰós, from *h₁rewdʰ-.
From Middle High German swarz, from Old High German swarz, from Proto-West Germanic *swart, from Proto-Germanic *swartaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swerd- (“dirty, dark, black”).
alt (“old”) +‎ modisch (“fashionable”)
From Middle High German endern, more at anderer (“other, different”). Cognate with Hunsrik ennre.
vocabList.usage:
Früher dachte ich, Botanik sei langweilig, aber ich habe meine Meinung geändert.
I used to think Botany was boring, but I've changed my opinion.

vocabList.etym: an- +‎ probieren
From Middle High German anrihte, from the verb anrihten (“to prepare”); see anrichten for more.
an- +‎ schalten
ärgern +‎ -lich
vocabList.usage:
Der unerwartete Kurseinbruch war sehr ärgerlich für die Anleger.
The unexpected decline in share prices was very annoying for investors.

vocabList.etym: Inherited from Middle High German argern (“worsen”), from Old High German argerōn, derived from arg (“bad”). Compare English eerie.
vocabList.usage:
Die anderen Kinder ärgern ihn immer.
The other kids keep annoying him.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German ertec. Equivalent to Art +‎ -ig.
aus- +‎ schlafen
From Middle High German begiezen, from Old High German bigiozan, from Proto-West Germanic *bigeutan. Equivalent to be- +‎ gießen.
From Middle High German bīȥen, from Old High German bīȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *bītan, from Proto-Germanic *bītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéydt (“to split”).
From beziehen +‎ -ung.
From Middle High German brūt, from Old High German brūt (akin to Old Saxon brūd), from Proto-West Germanic *brūdi, from Proto-Germanic *brūdiz. Compare Dutch bruid, English bride, Danish brud.
Compound of Dach (“roof”) +‎ Boden (“floor, ground”).
From Middle High German ē, ēwe, from Old High German ēwa, from Proto-West Germanic *aiw, from Proto-Germanic *aiwǭ, *aiwaz (“law, custom”).
From Middle High German erschīnen, from Old High German irskīnan, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀskīnan. Equivalent to er- +‎ scheinen.
From Fenster +‎ Laden.
From fern (“far”) +‎ Bedienung (“handling, operation”).
From Middle High German vriuntschaft, from Old High German friuntscaf, from Proto-West Germanic *friundskapi. Equivalent to Freund (“friend”) +‎ -schaft (“-ship”).
From Gebrauch (“use”) +‎ -s- +‎ Anweisung (“instruction, direction”).
From Middle High German gevāre, gevære, from Old High German fāra, from Proto-Germanic *fērō. Cognate with English fear and Dutch gevaar.
See the verb scheiden (“to separate”)
From Middle High German wiht, gewiht, from Old High German giwihti, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *gawihtī. Compare Dutch gewicht, Danish vægt, English weight, Swedish vikt.
From Middle High German grif, from Old High German grif, from Proto-West Germanic *gripi, from Proto-Germanic *gripiz.
Inherited from Middle High German güetec. By surface analysis, Güte (“kindness”) +‎ -ig. Cognate with Dutch goedig.
From Middle High German heizen, from Old High German heizen, from Proto-West Germanic *haitijan, from Proto-Germanic *haitijaną.

From Middle High German hütte, from Old High German hutta (“hut, cottage”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *hudjǭ, though the word is originally exclusively High German. Further origin unknown. Some theories link it to Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewt- (“to deck; cover; covering; skin”). All related words in European languages are borrowings from Old High German. Compare Dutch hut, French hutte, English hut, etc.
Jahr (“year”) +‎ hundert (“one hundred”). Compare Dutch jaarhonderd.

From Middle High German kabel, which is borrowed via Middle Low German from Middle Dutch cabel (“thick rope”), itself from northern French câble. The contemporary sense is from English cable, which see for more.
From Middle High German kamîn, from Old High German kemîn, from Latin camīnus. Compare English chimney.
Klima +‎ Anlage
From Middle High German künec, from Old High German kuning (rarer kunig), from Proto-West Germanic *kuning, from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz.[1]
From Middle High German künigin, from Old High German chuningin, from Proto-West Germanic *kuningini, equivalent to König +‎ -in. Cognate with West Frisian keninginne.

From Middle High German kruoc, from Old High German kruog, from Proto-West Germanic *krōgu, from Proto-Germanic *krōguz. Immediate cognates are Middle Dutch croech, Old English crōg, of obscure origin. Possibly from a Proto-Indo-European root shared with Old Armenian կարաս (karas, “pitcher, large jar”), Ancient Greek κρωσσός (krōssós, “pitcher”), but the phonetics are problematic.  Also compare Old Irish croiccenn (“skin”).[1][2]
From Middle High German lecheln. By surface analysis, lachen +‎ -eln.
From Middle High German lecherlich. Equivalent to lachen +‎ -er- +‎ -lich.
From Middle High German nennen, nemmen, nemnen, from Old High German nemnen, from Proto-West Germanic *namnijan, from Proto-Germanic *namnijaną.

Compound of neu (“new”) +‎ gierig (“greedy”), but originally neusgierig with an adverbial genitive. A Middle Low German formation that replaced older Middle High German niugerne. Compare Dutch nieuwsgierig and Norwegian Bokmål nysgjerrig.
vocabList.usage:
Ich bin besonders neugierig auf die Sitten und Gebräuche anderer Kulturen.
I am very curious and keen to discover the customs and traditions of other cultures.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German persōnlīcheit. By surface analysis, persönlich +‎ -keit. Cognate with Dutch persoonlijkheid.
Borrowed from Latin pupa. Sense of "pupa" borrowed from New Latin.
From Quadrat (“square”) + Meter (“metre”).
From rasieren (“to shave”) +‎ Apparat (“device”).
From Middle High German rīȥen, from Old High German rīȥan (“to scratch”), from a conflation of two similar verbs:.
From reißen (“to pull apart, tear”) +‎ Verschluss (“closure, shutter”).
Borrowed from English rowdy.
From Rücksicht (“consideration”) +‎ -s- +‎ -los.
Schminke +‎ -en
vocabList.usage:
Ich schminke mich immer zu Hause vor dem Spiegel.
I always put on my make-up at home in front of the mirror.

vocabList.etym: A nominal formation related to Schopf (“tuft, crown (of feathers)”), as they were originally covered with bundles of straw. Cognate with dialectal English shippon (“cow-shed”).[1]

Schwager +‎ -in.
Cognate with Hunsrik Schwehrin.
vocabList.usage:
Ist diese Schwägerin die Frau Ihres Bruders oder die Schwester Ihrer Frau?
Is this sister-in-law your brothers’s wife or your wife’s sister?

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German swanger, from Old High German swangar, from Proto-West Germanic *swangr (“heavy”), further origin unknown.[1] Cognate with Old English swangor, Dutch zwanger (“pregnant”), and Yiddish שוואַנגער (shvanger, “pregnant”); compare also Lithuanian sunkùs (“heavy; difficult”).
vocabList.usage:
Sie ist schwanger von ihrem Mann Peter mit ihrem dritten Kind.
She is pregnant from her husband Peter with her third child.

vocabList.etym: Expanded from earlier Schwieger (“mother-in-law”), from Old High German swigar, from Proto-Germanic *swegrō, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱruh₂- (“woman's mother-in-law”) (compare *swéḱuros (“woman's father-in-law”)). By surface analysis, schwieger- +‎ Mutter.
schwieger- +‎ Vater.
From Middle High German sëlpstēnde +‎ -ig.

From Middle High German seltsām, seltzām, seltsæm, alteration (due to Middle High German -sam (“-some”)) of Middle High German seltsæn, seltsæne, from Old High German seltsāni. Cognate with Dutch zeldzaam and English seldom.
From spülen (“to rinse or wash”) +‎ Küche (“kitchen”).
stief- (“step-”) +‎ Mutter (“mother”)
From Middle High German strīt, from Old High German strīt, from Proto-West Germanic *strīd, from Proto-Germanic *strīdaz.
Sympathie +‎ -isch
From older Italian tastatura; compare tastiera. Analysable as Taste (“key, button”) +‎ -tur.

From Middle High German toup, toub, from Old High German toub, from Proto-West Germanic *daub, from Proto-Germanic *daubaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, be obscured”); cognate to English deaf, Swedish döv.
Teppich (“carpet”) +‎ Boden (“ground, floor”)
From Middle High German troum, Old High German troum, from Proto-West Germanic *draum, from Proto-Germanic *draumaz; akin to Low German Droom, Dutch droom, English dream, Danish drøm.
From Middle High German and Old High German troumen, from Proto-West Germanic *draumijan. Akin to Dutch dromen, English dream, and Swedish drömma.
ver- +‎ Antwort (“answer”) +‎ -ung.
vocabList.usage:
Diese Verantwortung kann dir niemand abnehmen.
Nobody can take this responsibility away from you.

vocabList.etym: Nominal of vergnügen.
vocabList.usage:
Es ist ein Vergnügen, Sie kennenzulernen.
It's a pleasure to meet you.

vocabList.etym: ver- +‎ größer +‎ -en
A conversion from the verb vertrauen (“to trust”) which has been used since the 1400s.
waschen +‎ Lappen

From Middle High German weinen, from Old High German weinōn (“to cry, lament, cry woe”), from Proto-Germanic *wainōną (“to cry, weep”), from Proto-Indo-European *wáy (“woe”). Related with Weh, English woe, which see. Cognate with Dutch wenen (“to weep, to cry”), Old English wānian (“to complain, lament”).
From Winter (“winter”) +‎ Garten (“garden”).
vocabList.usage:
Unsere Nachbarn haben ihren Balkon in einen Wintergarten umgewandelt.
Our neighbours converted their balcony into a conservatory.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German witewe, from Old High German wituwa, from Proto-West Germanic *widuwā, from Proto-Germanic *widuwǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂ (“widow”). Germanic cognates include Dutch weduwe, Old Saxon widowa, Old English widuwe, whence English widow, which see.
From Middle High German witewære, witewer, witwer, from Old High German wituwo.

From Early New High German zuoval, a calque of Latin accidēns; see zufallen. Attested in the 15th century.[1]
Cognate with Dutch toeval.
From Middle High German acker, from Old High German ackar (“field”), from Proto-West Germanic *akr.
Borrowed from French allée.
From Middle High German bach, from Old High German bah, from Proto-West Germanic *baki. Cognate with English beach and English beck.
From Middle High German būwen, from Old High German būan, from Proto-West Germanic *būan, from Proto-Germanic *būaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰúHt, the athematic root aorist of the root *bʰuH-.
vocabList.usage: ein Haus bauen ― to build a house

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German būre, gebūre, from Old High German būr (“peasant”), gibūr, gibūro. All these forms ultimately descend from Proto-West Germanic *būr, itself from Proto-Germanic *būraz (“inhabitant, dweller”). Compare English boor.
From compound Bauer (“farmer”) +‎ -n- +‎ Hof (“yard; enclosure”). Akin to Dutch boerenhof.

From Middle High German boum, from Old High German boum, from Proto-West Germanic *baum, from Proto-Germanic *baumaz. Akin to Dutch boom, Low German Boom, West Frisian beam, English beam. Plural umlaut by proportional analogy with terms like Gast (“guest”) to Gäste (“guests”).
vocabList.usage:
Bäume zählen zu den größten Lebensformen.
Trees are one of the biggest life forms.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German bërc, from Old High German bërg, itself from Proto-West Germanic *berg, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bergaz.

From Middle High German blat, plat, from Old High German blat, from Proto-West Germanic *blad (“leaf”), from Proto-Germanic *bladą (“leaf”); akin to Low German Blatt, Dutch blad, English blade, Danish and Swedish blad. Indo-European cognates include Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon), Latin folium.

From Middle High German boden, bodem, from Old High German bodam, from Proto-West Germanic *bodm, from Proto-Germanic *budm-, a variant of *butmaz (whence English bottom, which see for more), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn.
Bund +‎ es +‎ Straße
19th century, from Bürger (“citizen”) +‎ Steig (“footpath”). Introduced as a puristic alternative to then-predominant Trottoir (therefore unusual in Switzerland, like other purisms of that era).
vocabList.usage:
Auch auf dem Bürgersteig muss man immer die Augen auf halten.
You always have to keep your eyes open, even on the sidewalk.

vocabList.etym: From Bus (“bus”) +‎ (an)halten (“hold/stop”) +‎ Stelle (“place/location”).

From Middle High German velt, from Old High German feld, from Proto-West Germanic *felþu, from Proto-Germanic *felþą, from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂-. Cognates include Dutch veld and English field.[1]
From Middle High German vluz, from Old High German fluz, from Proto-West Germanic *fluti, from Proto-Germanic *flutiz, ultimately from the same root of fließen (“to flow”).
From Middle High German gebiet, gebiete (“jurisdiction; area of command”), from gebieten (“to command”). Compare Dutch gebied.
vocabList.usage:
Viele Bewohner hatten das bedrohte Gebiet verlassen müssen.
Many residents had to leave the threatened area.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German gebirge, from Old High German gibirgi; originally a collective noun equivalent to ge- +‎ Berg.
From Middle High German hecke, from Old High German hegga, from Proto-West Germanic *haggju, from Proto-Indo-European *kagʰyo-. Cognate with Dutch heg, English hedge.
From Middle High German hogil, diminutive of houc, from Old High German houg.
15th century, from Italian canale, from Latin canalis. The broadcasting sense is a semantic loan from English channel.
From Middle High German strāȥe, from Old High German strāȥa, from Proto-West Germanic *strātu (“street”), from Latin (via) strata.
vocabList.usage:
Das Kind überquerte die Straße.
The child crossed the street.

vocabList.etym: From Straße +‎ -n- +‎ Bahn.
From Middle High German tal, from Old High German tal. Cognate with Danish dal, Dutch dal, English dale, Swedish dal.

From Middle High German uover, ūver, ūber, possibly from northern Old High German *uofar, but usually considered a borrowing from Middle Low German ōver, ȫver, from Old Saxon *ōvar, *ōvir, from Proto-Germanic *ōferaz. Cognate with Dutch oever, Low German Över, English over (“shore, riverbank”). The native High German word for “shore” is Gestade.
From Middle High German walt, from Old High German wald, from Proto-West Germanic *walþu.
From Middle High German wonen, from Old High German wonēn, from Proto-West Germanic *wunēn, from Proto-Germanic *wunāną, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”).

From Middle High German wonunge, from Old High German wonunga, from Proto-West Germanic *wunungu, equivalent to wohnen +‎ -ung. Related to Dutch woning (“house, residence”), English woning (“dwelling-place”). More at woning.
Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē). Doublet of Bodega, Bottich, and Boutique.
From northern Middle High German becker, from Old High German beckeri, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz. By surface analysis, backen +‎ -er.
Learned borrowing from Latin bibliothēca, from Ancient Greek βῐβλῐοθήκη (bĭblĭothḗkē).
From Brief (“letter”) +‎ Kasten (“box”).
From Brief (“letter”) +‎ Marke (“mark/stamp”).
From Middle High German brucke, from Old High German brugga, brucca, from Proto-West Germanic *bruggju. The neurological sense “pons” is a semantic loan from Latin pōns.
From Middle High German buoch, from Old High German buoh, from Proto-West Germanic *bōk, from Proto-Germanic *bōks. Cognate with English book.

From Middle High German burc, from Old High German burg, from Proto-West Germanic *burg, from Proto-Germanic *burgz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰérǵʰ-s, a form of Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“fortified elevation”).

15th-century alteration (see below) of older Thum, from Middle High German and Old High German tuom, from Proto-West Germanic *dōm (whence Old Dutch duom, Middle Low German dôm), from Medieval Latin domus (literally “house”). The use probably goes back to domus episcopatus/episcopalis (“house of the bishopric”).[1][2] An alternative theory derives it from domus ecclesiae (“church house”), after Ancient Greek οἶκος τῆς ἐκκλησίας (oîkos tês ekklēsías).[3]
From French droguerie.
ein- +‎ werfen
From Gemüse +‎ Händler.
From Middle High German gescheft, from Old High German giscaft, from Proto-West Germanic *gaskafti. Cognate with Yiddish געשעפֿט (gesheft).
Probably from early modern Dutch juwelier, though the word is first attested in German. Analyzable as Juwel +‎ -ier.
From Middle High German kappelle, kapelle, from Old High German kappella, kapella, from Late Latin and Vulgar Latin cappella (“chapel”).
Clipping of Kinematograph m. Originally also used a masculine noun (der Kino).
From Middle High German kirche, from Old High German kirihha, from Proto-West Germanic *kirikā.
vocabList.usage:
Wir gehen zu der Kirche, weil es heute Sonntag ist.
We're going to church, because today is Sunday.

vocabList.etym: From Konditor +‎ -ei.

From Middle High German and Old High German kunst (“knowledge”), first attested in c. 9th century; related to the verb können. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kunstiz (“knowledge, ability”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”).
From Middle High German leben, from Old High German lebēn. Equivalent to a gerund of leben.
Leben (“life”) +‎ -s- +‎ Mittel (“means, resources”)
From Middle High German market, from Old High German marchat, from Proto-West Germanic *markat (“market”).

From Middle High German metziger, metzigære, variants of metzjer, metzjære, from Old High German meziāri, mezziāri (“butcher”), from Proto-West Germanic *mattjārī. Perhaps influenced by Old High German mezalāri, mezzilāri (“merchant, moneychanger, butcher”), from Latin macellārius (“meat trader”).
Borrowed from Italian posta, from posto, from Latin positus.
Post (“post”) +‎ leiten (“to direct”) +‎ Zahl (“number”)
From Rat (“council”) +‎ Haus (“house”).
From Middle High German sparn, from Old High German sparēn, sparōn, from Proto-West Germanic *sparēn. Compare English spare.
vocabList.usage:
Ich spare mein Geld für ein neues Auto.
I'm saving my money for a new car.

vocabList.etym: From sparen (“save”) + Kasse (“cash box”).

From Middle High German wunde, from Old High German wunta, from Proto-Germanic *wundō (“a wound”), from *wundaz (“wounded”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wen-. Compare Low German Wunn, Dutch wond, English wound, Icelandic und.
From Middle High German zan, zant, from Old High German zan, zand, from Proto-West Germanic *tanþ, from Proto-Germanic *tanþs.
From Zahn (“tooth”) +‎ Arzt (“doctor”).
Zahn (“tooth”) +‎ Bürste (“brush”)
From Zahn (“tooth”) +‎ Pasta (“paste”).
anfangen +‎ -er
From Middle High German bluoten, from Old High German bluoten, bluotēn, from Proto-West Germanic *blōdijan.
Blut (“blood”) +‎ Probe (“sample, test”)
From Middle High German brust, from Old High German brust, from Proto-West Germanic *brust, from Proto-Germanic *brusts.
15th century, from Latin chīrūrgus, from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós).
Deverbal of durchfallen (“to fall through”) as a calque of Ancient Greek δῐᾰ́ρροιᾰ (dĭắrrhoiă).
From Middle High German elenboge, from Old High German elinbogo, from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô; by surface analysis, Elle +‎ Bogen.
Deverbal from  erfolgen.
From ergeben +‎ -nis.
From Middle High German erholn, from Old High German irhalо̄n, irholо̄n. Equivalent to er- +‎ holen.
erleichtern +‎ -ung
From Middle High German vāhen, from Old High German fāhan, a strong verb with past forms fieng, gefangan, from Proto-West Germanic *fą̄han, from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną.
From Middle High German gips, from late Old High German gips, from Proto-West Germanic *gips.

From Middle High German glatz, from Old High German glaz (“braincase; weathered skull”). According to Duden and Pfeifer, derived from glatt (“smooth, sleek”), however with unexpected /ts/, perhaps from dialectal formation.
From Hand (“hand”) +‎ Gelenk (“joint”).
From Middle High German hūt, from Old High German hūt, from Proto-West Germanic *hūdi, from Proto-Germanic *hūdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH-.
Heim +‎ Weh. Originally a medical term in Switzerland. Cognate to Alemannic German Häiwee, Bavarian Haimweh (Upper Austrian), Low German Heimweih.
From Middle High German helm, from Old High German helm, from Proto-West Germanic *helm, from Proto-Germanic *helmaz. Compare Low German Helm, Dutch helm, English helm, Danish hjelm.
Heu (“hay”) +‎ Schnupfen (“nasal congestion; cold”).
From Middle High German hœhe, from Old High German hōhī. Analysable as hoch +‎ -e.
Husten +‎ Saft
From Middle High German kinne, from Old High German kinni, from Proto-West Germanic *kinnu, from Proto-Germanic *kinnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénu-, *ǵénus (“chin, jaw, cheek”).
From Middle High German meister, from Old High German meistar, from Proto-West Germanic *maistar (“master”). Doublet of Maestro, Magister, and Master.
From Old High German managī, from Proto-Germanic *managį̄ (compare English many, Swedish många). Equivalent to manch +‎ -e.
From Middle High German mezzen, from Old High German mezzen, from Proto-West Germanic *metan.

From Middle High German nacket, from Old High German nackut, from Proto-Germanic *nakwadaz, from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós (“naked, bare”). Cognate with Low German naakd, Dutch naakt, English naked, Danish nøgen, Swedish naken.

From Middle High German pfīl, from Old High German pfīl, from Proto-West Germanic *pīl, from Latin pīlum (“javelin, throwing spear”). Cognate with German Low German Piel, Dutch pijl (“arrow, dart”), English pile (“column of wood, steel or concrete”).
From Middle High German phlëgen, from Old High German plëgan, from Proto-West Germanic *plehan.
vocabList.usage: jemanden gesund pflegen ― to nurse someone back to health

vocabList.etym: 16th century, from Italian boccale.
From Röntgen (“X-ray”) +‎ Bild (“image”).
From Middle High German salbe, from Old High German salba, from Proto-West Germanic *salbu, from Proto-Germanic *salbō.
From Middle High German schaden, from Old High German scadōn, from the root of the noun Schaden (“damage, harm”).
vocabList.usage:
Es kann nicht schaden, es mal zu versuchen.
It can't hurt to give it a try.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German schade, from Old High German scado, from Proto-West Germanic *skaþō, from Proto-Germanic *skaþô. Compare Dutch schade, Low German Schaden, Schaad, English scathe, Danish skade, Swedish skada.
The second part is akin to Richter; the first part is akin to Middle High German schideman and to Old High German scidōn (“to separate, distinguish, decide”).[1]
From Middle High German slucken, from Old High German (attested in the derived noun slucko (“glutton”)), probably ultimately onomatopoeic. Cognate with Dutch slokken.
From Middle High German sige, sic, from Old High German sigu, sigi, from Proto-West Germanic *sigi, from Proto-Germanic *segaz, from Proto-Indo-European *seǵʰ- (“related to overpowering”).
From Sonne +‎ -n- +‎ Stich.

From Middle High German sorge (“sorrow; worry; care”), from Old High German sorga, sworga (“sorrow; worry”), from Proto-West Germanic *sorgu, from Proto-Germanic *surgō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swergʰ- (“watch over, worry; be ill, suffer”).
Cognate with Hunsrik Sorrich, Dutch zorg, English sorrow, Danish sorg.
From Middle High German tūchen, touchen, from Old High German -tūhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *dūkan.

From Teil (“part”) +‎ nehmen (“take”). Calque of Latin participō, whence also English participate; compare corresponding calques such as Dutch deelnemen, English take part, Icelandic taka þátt. In this expression, the noun Teil (“part”) is considered verblasst (“grammaticalized”) and thus written lowercase when separated (Ich nehme teil).

From Late Middle High German turnier, alteration (after the verb turnieren) of older turnei, tornei, from Old French tornoi, itself deverbal from Old French tornoiier, tornier (“to turn, romp, fight in a tournament”), from torner (“to turn”), from Latin tornare (“to turn”).
ver- +‎ stauchen
From Middle High German wange, from Old High German wanga. Cognate with Dutch wang, English wang. See the latter for more.
From Middle High German zēhe, from Old High German zēha, from Proto-Germanic *taihwǭ (“toe”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to point out”).
From Middle High German zunge, from Old High German zunga, from Proto-West Germanic *tungā, from Proto-Germanic *tungǭ; from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s (“tongue”).
Abend (“evening”) +‎ Essen (“meal”)

Borrowed from Old French apetit or directly from its source, Late Latin appetītus (“attack; striving, desire; appetite”), a fourth-declension noun derived from Latin appetō (“to assail; to strive after”).
From Middle High German durst, from Old High German durst, thurst, from Proto-West Germanic *þurstu, from Proto-Germanic *þurstuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”).
From Middle High German vlamme, from Old High German flamma (10th c.), from Latin flamma.

From Middle High German flasche, from Old High German flasca (“bottle”), from Proto-West Germanic *flaskā, from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ (“bottle”), from *flehtaną (“to plait, braid”), from the practice of plaiting or wrapping bottles in straw casing. Cognate to English flask. Doublet of  Fiasko and Flakon.
From Middle High German vrisch, from Old High German frisc, from Proto-West Germanic *frisk, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *preysk-.
From Middle High German gabel(e), from Old High German gabala, from Proto-West Germanic *gabulu (“fork”).
Related to gerecht.

From Middle High German geschirre (“harness, gear”), from Old High German giskirri, giscirri (literally “the trimmed (thing)”), from skeran (“to shear”), from Proto-Germanic *skeraną. Cognate with Alemannic German Geschirr.
From Middle High German getrenke, a collective noun equivalent to ge- +‎ Trank. Displaced Trank as the default word for “a drink" c. 1750. The spelling Getränk first attested c. 1650.

From Old High German glas, gles, from Proto-West Germanic *glas, from Proto-Germanic *glasą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰel- (“to shine, glimmer, glow”). Compare Low German Glas, Dutch glas, English glass, Icelandic gler.
Borrowed from English grill.

From Middle High German imbiz, imbīz, inbīz (“food, meal, snack, breakfast”), from Old High German inbiz, inbīz, imbīz (“food, meal, snack”), equivalent to in- (“in, into”) +‎ Biss (“bite”). Compare German Low German Anbiet (“meal, snack”), Dutch ontbijt (“breakfast”).
Kanne +‎ -chen
Borrowed from French cantine, from Italian cantina.
From Middle High German küche, from Old High German chuhhina, from late Proto-West Germanic *kukinā, from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.

From Middle High German lecker, from Old High German *lekkar, from Proto-West Germanic *likkr, derived from the verb Proto-West Germanic *likkōn (“to lick”). Cognate to Dutch lekker, Afrikaans lekker, Middle Low German lecker, Norwegian lekker, Swedish läcker and Danish lækker. More at lick.

15th century, from Mahl (“meal”) +‎ Zeit (“time”). The word Mahl (a spelling variant of Mal) originally meant "mealtime", but was transferred to the meal itself. The compound then assumed the sense "mealtime", but ultimately underwent the same semantic development yet again. Compare Dutch maaltijd, English mealtide, Danish måltid, Icelandic máltíð.
From Middle High German messer, mezzer, from Old High German mezzir, mezzeres, mezzirahs, mezzisahs (“knife”), from Proto-West Germanic *matisahs (“knife used for cutting food”).
Mittag (“midday”) +‎ Essen (“meal”)
From nach +‎ Tisch. The latter is used here in the otherwise archaic/obsolete sense “meal”.

From Middle High German smecken, from Old High German smecchen, from Proto-West Germanic *smakkijan (“to taste”), from Proto-West Germanic *smakku (“a taste”). Compare English smack and smatch, as well as Lithuanian smagù (“cheerful, enjoyable, pleasant”).
vocabList.usage:
Das Bier schmeckt sehr gut.
The beer tastes very good.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German snel, from Old High German snel (“nimble, brave, quick, lively”), from Proto-West Germanic *snel, from Proto-Germanic *snellaz (“active, bold, quick”). Cognate with Dutch snel, Low German snell, English snell. More at snell.
From schnell +‎ Imbiss.
From Middle High German schüȥȥel, from Old High German scuȥȥila, from Proto-West Germanic *skutilu (“small bowl, dish”).
From Selbst +‎ Bedienung.
From Speise (“meal, food”) +‎ Karte (“card”).
From Speise +‎ Wagen.
From super- +‎ Markt.

From Middle High German süezi, from Old High German suozi (akin to Old Saxon swōti), from Proto-West Germanic *swōtī, from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz, from Proto-Indo-European *swéh₂dus. Compare Bavarian siaß, Low German sööt, German Low German soit- (Paderbornisch), Hunsrik sies, Dutch zoet, English sweet, Danish sød.
From Tag +‎ -es- +‎ Karte.

Borrowed from French tasse, from Arabic طَاس (ṭās) (a shortening of طَسْت (ṭast)), from Middle Persian tšt' (tašt), ultimately from the past participle of the Proto-Iranian verb *taš- (“to make, construct; to cut”). Cognate with dialectal English tass (“cup”), Dutch tas (“cup”), Hunsrik Tass; more distantly, doublet of Text and Technologie.
Ultimately from Hokkien 茶 (tê), probably through Dutch thee. Attested since the 17th century.
Ultimately from Hokkien 茶 (tê), probably through Dutch thee. Attested since the 17th century.
From Middle High German teller (“plate”), from Middle French tailloir (“plate, cutting board”).
From Middle High German trinken, from Old High German trinkan (attested since the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *drinkan.[1]
From unter- +‎ Tasse.
From vor- +‎ Speise.

From Middle High German bier, from Old High German bior, from Proto-West Germanic *beuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *beuzą (“beer”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰews-, *bheus- (“dross, sediment, brewer's yeast”).
From the kola nut and the brandname Coca-Cola.
From Frucht +‎ Saft.

From French café, from Italian caffè, from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve), from Arabic قَهْوة (qahwa). First attested in the 17th century. The variants with -o-, which fell into disuse around 1800, are from Dutch koffie and English coffee. Doublet of Café.
Borrowed from French limonade.
From Middle High German milch, from Old High German miluh, from Proto-West Germanic *meluk, from Proto-Germanic *meluks, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-.
From Middle High German saf, saft, from Old High German saf, from Proto-West Germanic *sap (“juice, sap”).
From German Low German Snapps, originally “a sip (of liquor)”. Related to schnappen.
From sprudeln.
From Middle High German waȥȥer, from Old High German waȥȥar, from Proto-West Germanic *watar, from Proto-Germanic *watōr, from Proto-Indo-European *wédōr, collective of *wódr̥.
From Middle High German wīn, from Old High German wīn, from Proto-West Germanic *wīn.

From Middle High German apfel, from Old High German apful, from Proto-West Germanic *applu, from Proto-Germanic *apluz (compare Dutch appel, West Frisian apel, English apple), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ébōl.
Via Low German Appelsina, from Dutch appelsina (cp. appelsien, for which now usually sinaasappel). So named because of their introduction to Europe from China (Latin Sīna).

Borrowed from Dutch abrikoos, from Middle French abricots, plural of abricot, from Catalan albercoc, from Arabic اَلْبَرْقُوق (al-barqūq), from Classical Syriac ܒܰܪܩܽܘܩܳܐ (barqūqā), from Ancient Greek πραικόκιον (praikókion), from Latin praecox (“overripe”).
Deverbal from  aufschneiden (“cut into slices”).

From Middle High German bire, bir, from Old High German bira, pira, from Vulgar Latin pira, reanalysis of the plural of Latin pirum. Early Modern German birn is from the Middle High German plural and dative/genitive singular, whence a double plural birnen was formed. The contemporary Birne is a new backformation from this plural (perhaps influenced also by the older, still dialectal form bire). Thus, between Latin and modern German, the word was reformed on the basis of the plural three times. Cognate with Alemannic German Bire.
Blume (“flower”) +‎ -n- +‎ Kohl (“cabbage”)
From Bock +‎ Wurst
From Middle High German brate, from Old High German brāto, from Proto-Germanic *brēdô.
From Middle High German brāten, from Old High German brātan, from Proto-Germanic *brēdaną.
braten (“to roast, to bake, to fry”) +‎ Kartoffeln (“potatoes”)

From Middle High German brātwurst, from Old High German brātwurst. The term originally denoted a sausage (Wurst) made of Brät (Old High German brāto), but has come to be used for a sausage that is fried or is suited to being fried (braten). Kluge suggests the modern word might be a conflation of those two etymologies rather than a derivation of only the first one.[1]

From Middle High German brōt, from Old High German brōt (attested since the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *braud, from Proto-Germanic *braudą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrew- (“to seethe, to boil”).
Brot (“bread”) +‎ -chen (“diminutive”)
From Butter (“butter”) +‎ Brot (“bread”).
Borrowed from English corn flakes.

Inherited from Middle High German ei and Old High German ei, from Proto-West Germanic *aij, from Proto-Germanic *ajją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm.
Cognate with Yiddish איי (ey), Dutch ei, West Frisian aai, English ey and egg, Danish æg.

From Middle High German īs, from Old High German īs, from Proto-West Germanic *īs, from Proto-Germanic *īsą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyH-. Etymology 1 sense 2 is a semantic loan from French glace.

Equivalent to Erde +‎ Beere; from Middle High German ërtbere, from Old High German ërdberi, from Proto-Germanic *erþōbazją. Akin to Dutch aardbei, Danish jordbær. Compare Polish poziomka, Russian земляни́ка (zemljaníka) (related to земля́ (zemljá)).
From Middle High German ezzich, from  Old High German ezzih, from Proto-West Germanic *atek, metathesized variant of *aket (“vinegar”). Compare with Vilamovian essig.
From Middle High German fleisch, vleisch, from Old High German fleisk, from Proto-West Germanic *flaiski.

With irregular stress shift (as in Holunder, lebendig, etc.) from Middle High German forhel, alteration of older forhen, from Old High German forhana, from Proto-Germanic *furhnō, from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ- (“speckled”).
From Middle High German gans, from Old High German gans, from Proto-West Germanic *gans, from Proto-Germanic *gans, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns.

From Middle High German gemüese, a derivative of Old High German muos (“food, victuals, porridge”), from Proto-Germanic *mōsą (“porridge, food”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“wet, fat, dripping”). By surface analysis, ge- +‎ Mus +‎ -e. Cognate to Bavarian Gmias, Pennsylvania German Gemies, Luxembourgish Geméis, and possibly English mush.
Borrowed from Old Polish ogurek, from Byzantine Greek ἀγγούριον (angoúrion, “cucumber”).
From Hahn +‎ -chen.

By renewed adaptation to Beere from earlier and still dialectal Himper, by assimilation (as in Wimper) from Middle High German hintber, from Old High German hintberi, from Proto-West Germanic *hindibaʀi. Compare (dialectal) English hindberry, (dialectal) Dutch hennebes, hinnebes, Danish hindbær. Equivalent to Hinde (“hind, doe”) +‎ Beere (“berry”).
From Middle High German honic, honec, hönic, hünic, from Old High German honag, from Proto-West Germanic *hunag, from Proto-Germanic *hunagą. Cognate with English honey.
Kalb +‎ Fleisch.
Borrowed from French carotte, from Latin carōta, from Ancient Greek κᾰρωτόν (kărōtón).
From older Tartuffel or Tartüffel (18th c.), from Italian tartufolo, diminutive of tartufo (“truffle”), from Medieval Latin *territūberum or Latin terrae tūber (“tuber of the earth”).
Inherited from Middle High German kæse, from Old High German kāsi,[1] from Proto-West Germanic *kāsī (“cheese”).
kauen (“to chew”) +‎ Gummi (“gum, rubber”)
From Middle High German kirse, from Old High German kirsa, from Proto-West Germanic *kirsijā, from Late Latin ceresia.
Kopf +‎ Salat
Borrowed from French côtelette.
From Middle High German kuoche, from Old High German kuohho, from Proto-Germanic *kōkô. Compare Dutch koek. Doublet of Quiche.
From Middle High German lahs, from Old High German lahs, from Proto-West Germanic *lahs, from Proto-Germanic *lahsaz.
Inherited from Middle High German lamp, in the 14th century also lam, from Old High German lamb, from Proto-West Germanic *lamb, from Proto-Germanic *lambaz.
From Middle High German lëber, lëbere, from Old High German lëbera, lëbara, from Proto-West Germanic *libru; akin to Dutch lever, English liver, Danish lever.
16th century, from Middle French marmelade, from Portuguese marmelada.

From Middle High German nuȥ, from Old High German nuz, from Proto-West Germanic *hnut, from Proto-Germanic *hnuts, from Proto-Indo-European *knew-. Compare Dutch noot, English nut, Danish nød, Swedish nöt.
From Middle High German öle, ole, olei, olge, from Old High German oli, from Proto-West Germanic *oli (“olive oil”). Doublet of Oleum.

Borrowed from Dutch pompelmoes. Further origin uncertain, but the first two syllables are probably—either originally or by secondary association—the dated Dutch noun pompel (“something squat or plump”), to which compare German pummelig. Formerly, the form Pompelmuse was also used; the -a- may be due to influence by French pamplemousse, also from the Dutch.
From Middle High German pfeffer, from Old High German pfeffar, pfeffur, from Proto-West Germanic *pipar (“pepper”).
From Middle High German pfersich, from Old High German phersih, from Proto-West Germanic *persik (“peach”).
From Middle High German pflūme, from Old High German pflūma, from Proto-West Germanic *plūmā (“plum”).
Regional form with initial b → p and unrounding, from Middle High German bülez, bülz, from Old High German buliz, from Proto-West Germanic *bulit (“porcini”).
Clipping of Pommes frites with a spelling pronunciation.

From Middle High German rigel, from Old High German rigil, of unclear derivation, either related to words like Reihe (Reige), Reck, regen, or borrowed from Latin rēgula. Cognate to Dutch richel, Vilamovian rejgel.
Rind (“cow”) +‎ Fleisch (“flesh, meat”)
Rose +‎ -n- +‎ Kohl. Named after the rose-shaped vegetable part (part which is consumed as a vegetable).

Inherited from Middle High German salz, from Old High German salz (akin to Old Saxon salt, Old Dutch salt, Old English sealt, Old Norse salt), from Proto-West Germanic *salt, from Proto-Germanic *saltą, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *séh₂ls. Compare Dutch zout, English salt, Danish salt. The Internet slang sense is a semantic loan from English salt.

sauer (“sour”) +‎ Kraut (“cabbage”). The sense “cabbage” in the word Kraut is southern German. Sauerkraut is not a traditional term in northern and central Germany, but has now become predominant in these areas, too.

From Middle High German schībe, from Old High German skība, from Proto-Germanic *skībǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to cut, part, divide, separate”). Cognate with Dutch schijf, English shive, sheave, skive, Old Norse skífa.

From Middle High German schinke, from Old High German scinco, from Proto-West Germanic *skinkō, from Proto-Germanic *skinkô, *skinkō (“shank; thigh”). In the sense “tome” originally student slang (18th c.), from the use of pigskin leather to bind such books.
A compound of schlagen (“to beat”) + Sahne (“cream”).
From Schnitz (“cut-off piece”) +‎ -el. Pertaining to schneiden (“to cut”). The culinary sense spread from Austria and was therefore adopted in the regional neuter gender.
Borrowed from Dutch chocolade, from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl.
From Schwein (“pig”) +‎ Fleisch (“meat”). Compare Silesian East Central German Schweinefleesch, English swineflesh (“pig-meat, pork”).
From Middle High German spec, from Old High German spek, from Proto-West Germanic *spik, from Proto-Germanic *spiką. Cognate with Old English spic (whence English speck).
Borrowed from Italian spinace.

Borrowed from Middle Low German suppe, soppe, sope, which spread under the reinforcing influence of French soupe. Both from Proto-Germanic *supô, *suppô, *suppǭ (“broth, sop”), which is related to German saufen (“to drink”).
Toast +‎ Brot
From Middle High German trūbe, from Old High German drūbo, thrūbo, from Proto-West Germanic *þrūbō.

From trut +‎ Hahn (“rooster”). The first element is either imitative of the turkey’s call to its young (cf. the etymology of Pute) or alternatively from Middle Low German drōten (“threaten”), improperly adapted to High German, in reference to the male turkey’s seemingly aggressive behavior.[1][2]
From Middle High German wīȥ, from Old High German wīȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīt, from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweytos (“bright; shine”).
From Middle High German wurst, from Old High German wurst, from Proto-West Germanic *wursti.
15th century, from Italian citrone (older variant of cedro) as well as Middle French citron, derived from Latin citrus.

From Middle High German zucker, from Old High German zuckar, from early Italian zucchero, from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), from Persian شکر (šakar), from Sanskrit शर्करा (śárkarā, “grit, gravel; ground or candied sugar”). Cognates include Czech cukr, Hungarian cukor and Dutch suiker.
From Middle High German zwibel, zwibolle, from Old High German zwibollo, from Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.
Inherited from Middle High German bühse. Doublet of Buchse (the Upper German form).

Spread via the Lower Rhineland from Middle Low German dōse and Middle Dutch dose. Probably from Latin dosis (“dose”), with semantic shift "a small amount (dose) of medicine" > "a container of such a dose of medicine" > "containers in general".
Borrowed from French carton, from Italian cartone. Doublet of Cartoon.

From Middle High German korp, from Old High German korb, chorp, from Proto-West Germanic *korb.
The sense “rejection of a (romantic) request” is formed back from the expressions einen Korb geben (“to so reject”), einen Korb kriegen (“to be so rejected”). These derive from certain older customs, which involved a bottomless basket as a symbol of the end or inexistence of love. The further origin of this symbol seems uncertain, though it has been plausibly related to the apparent mediaeval practice of pulling a secret visitor up to one’s window in a basket. Compare the same in Dutch een korf krijgen and Swedish få korgen.
From packen +‎ -ung.

15th century, from Italian scatola, with metathesis from Latin castulum, itself a diminutive of Lombardic Old High German kasto. Hence a doublet of inherited Kasten as well as the later borrowing Schatulle. The -ch- is due to a Bavarian consonantal development, for which compare Spachtel.

Borrowed from Middle Low German tûte, tǖte (“horn, conical paper bag”). Cognate with English tote (“bag”), Dutch tuit (“spout”). Further origin unknown, though has been suggested to be part of a sound-symbolic family of words including Zitze (“teat”).
Borrowed from Latin diaeta, from Ancient Greek δίαιτα (díaita).
From Middle High German dienen, from Old High German dionōn, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōną.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vette; see fett for more.

From Old High German gifugili. The expected modern form is *Gefügel, a collective form pertaining to Vogel (“bird”), cf. similar Dutch gevogelte. The connection with Vogel was lost in German and the word was at some point re-interpreted as Geflügel, that is “creatures with wings; winged ones”. Cf. Flügel (“wing”).
From Middle High German smac, from Old High German gismac, gismah, smac from Proto-West Germanic *smakku.
From Middle High German gieȥen, from Old High German gioȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *geutan (“to pour”).
From French piquant.
From Latin probō +‎ -ieren. Doublet of proben and prüfen.
From Middle High German reichen, from Old High German reihhen, reichen, from Proto-West Germanic *raikijan, from Proto-Germanic *raikijaną. Compare Dutch reiken, English reach.
vocabList.usage:
Der Turm reicht fast bis zum Himmel.
The tower almost reaches the sky.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German scheln, schelen, from Old High German skelen, skellen, from the noun scala, from Proto-West Germanic *skalu, from Proto-Germanic *skalō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to cut, divide”) or *(s)kel- (“to cover”). Cognate with Bavarian schäin, schöln, schön, and Yiddish שיילן (sheyln).

From 15th-century Middle High German sparge, spargen, sparges, from Medieval Latin sparagus, asparagus, in part through Italian sparago, sparagio. The form in -el (16th c.) probably after such plant names as Kerbel, Kümmel.
From older Vegetarianer, a borrowing from English vegetarian.
Borrowed from French amuser.
From Ansicht (“view”) +‎ -s- +‎ Karte (“card”).
From aus- +‎ geben. Cognate with English outgive.
aus- +‎ stellen +‎ -ung

An Upper German verb, from earlier besteln, iterative of Middle High German besten, from Proto-West Germanic *bastijan. The -a- is perhaps dialectal or through readaptation to the underlying noun Bast (“bast”).
From Middle High German bestellen, from Old High German bistellen. Equivalent to be- +‎ stellen.
From Middle High German bezaln. By surface analysis, be- +‎ zahlen. Compare Dutch betalen, Danish betale etc.
From Middle High German bilde, from Old High German bilidi, biladi, from Proto-West Germanic *biliþī.
From Middle High German kōr, chōr, from Latin chorus.
Computer (“computer”) +‎ Spiel (“game, play”)
ein- +‎ kaufen
From einladen +‎ -ung.
verbal noun of eintreten
From Eis (“ice”) +‎ Bahn (“lane”).
From Middle High German fëst, derived from Latin festum. Cognate with English feast, French fête, Italian festa.[1]

From Middle High German viur, from Old High German fiur, from Proto-West Germanic *fuir, from Proto-Germanic *fōr, from Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥. Compare Dutch vuur, Low German Füer, West Frisian fjoer, English fire, Danish fyr.
From Middle High German vrî, Old High German frî, from Proto-West Germanic *frī. Compare Dutch vrij, English free, Danish fri.
frei (“free”) +‎ Zeit (“time”)
From heilig (“holy”) +‎ Abend (“evening, eve”).
From Middle High German ōsteren (plural of ōstere), from Old High German ōstarūn, a plural form of ōstara, from Proto-West Germanic *Austrā, from Proto-Germanic *Austrǭ. Compare English Easter.
From Pope Silvester I, whose feast-day has been the 31st of December since the Gregorian calendar reform of 1582. Compare Russian Сильвестров день (Silʹvestrov denʹ), Polish sylwester.
From Middle High German wīhenahten (“Christmas”), from a dative plural ze den wīhen nahten (“in the holy nights”). Compare modern weihen (“to hallow”) and Nacht.
From Weihnachten (“Christmas”) +‎ -s- +‎ Baum (“tree”).
Ca. 1800, from Funktion +‎ -ieren, likely after French fonctionner.
From Middle High German geniezen, from Old High German giniozan, from Proto-West Germanic *ganeutan, equivalent to ge- +‎ nießen. Akin to Dutch genieten, Yiddish געניסן (genisn).

Some sources claim the existence of an early English preform. Perhaps from English handie-talkie, apparently used as a Motorola product name based on walkie-talkie. Or perhaps derived from English handheld transceiver, coined by CB radio users, later informally applied to the first mobile phones, and soon found in product names.

From Middle High German hērre, hërre, from Old High German hēriro, hērro (“grey, grey-haired”), the comparative form of hēr (“noble, venerable”) (by analogy with Latin senior (“elder”)), from Proto-Germanic *hairaz (“grey”).
Cognate with Dutch heer, Old English hār, English hoar, Old Norse hárr; compare also modern German hehr (“noble, holy”), herrschen (“to rule”).
From Middle High German hërze, from Old High German hërza, from Proto-West Germanic *hertā, from Proto-Germanic *hertô (“heart”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr (“heart”).
Literally, “in the free”.
Substantivization of jugendlich (“youthful”).

From Middle High German junc, from Old High German jung, from Proto-West Germanic *jung, from Proto-Germanic *jungaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁n̥ḱós. Compare Dutch jong, English young, Danish ung.
From Latin calendārium.

From Late Middle High German karte (“stiff sheet of paper”), from Old French carte, from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs). Compare Dutch kaart, English card, Yiddish קאָרט (kort), Low German Kaart, Koort. Doublet of Charta and Karton. See also Charter.
From Middle High German koufen, from Old High German koufōn, from Proto-West Germanic *kaupōn.
From Middle High German koufhūs, from Old High German koufhūs. Equivalent to kaufen (“to buy”) +‎ Haus (“house”).
From Middle High German kosten, from Old French coster, from Latin cōnstō.
From Middle High German kus, kos, from Old High German kus, kos, from Proto-West Germanic *koss. Compare Dutch kus, English kiss, Danish kys.
From Middle High German lachen, from Old High German lahhen, from Proto-West Germanic *hlahhjan, from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną.
vocabList.usage:
über einen Witz lachen
to laugh at a joke

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German mālen, from Old High German mālōn, mālēn, denominative of māl (“spot, stain”), from Proto-West Germanic *mālijan, from Proto-Germanic *mēlijaną (compare Dutch maal), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“dark color”) (compare Lithuanian mė́las (“black”), Ancient Greek μέλας (mélas, “dark-colored, black”)).
From Middle High German, ultimately from Latin pretium.
rechnen +‎ -ung. Compare Dutch rekening, English reckoning.

From Middle High German schāch, from Arabic شاه (šāh), from Classical Persian شاه (šāh), from Middle Persian 𐭬𐭫𐭪𐭠 (mlkʾ /⁠šāh⁠/), from Old Persian 𐏋 (XŠ /⁠xšāyaθiya⁠/, “king”). Doublet of Check, Schah, and Scheck.
From Middle High German schenken, from Old High German scenken, from Proto-West Germanic *skankijan (“to pour, serve”).
vocabList.usage:
Ich schenke meiner Tochter ein Kätzchen zum Geburtstag.
I’m giving my daughter a kitten for her birthday.

vocabList.etym:
From Middle High German schicken (“to outfit oneself, fit in, arrange appropriately”), from Old High German *skihhen, from Proto-West Germanic *skikkijan, from Proto-Germanic *skikkijaną (“to order, send”). This represents the causative of Middle High German geschehen, geschēn (“to happen, rush”).
Akin to Middle English skekken (“to send forth”), Old English sċēon (“to happen”), Dutch schie- in schielijk (“hasty”). Related to English chic.
From Schluss (“end, ending, conclusion, finish”) +‎ Verkauf (“sale”).
From earlier Spasso, borrowed from Italian spasso, deverbal from spassare or spassarsela, from Vulgar Latin *expassāre, from expandō (“to stretch out”). Compare Saterland Frisian Spoas.

From Middle High German spǣte, from Old High German spāti, from Proto-West Germanic *spādī, from Proto-Germanic *spēdiz. Cognate with Hunsrik sped, from Low German späd, archaic Dutch spade (“late”). Probably related to sparen (“to spare, conserve”).

From Middle High German tiure, from Old High German tiuri, from Proto-West Germanic *diurī, from Proto-Germanic *diurijaz, akin to Old Saxon diuri, compare Dutch duur, English dear, Icelandic dýr, and Swedish dyr.
From Middle High German trëffen, from Old High German trëffan, from Proto-West Germanic *drepan, from Proto-Germanic *drepaną, whence also English drub.
vocabList.usage:
Wir treffen uns morgen.
See you tomorrow.
(literally, “We'll meet each other tomorrow.”)

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German verkoufen, from Old High German firkoufen. Equivalent to ver- +‎ kaufen. Cognate with Dutch verkopen and Yiddish פֿאַרקויפֿן (farkoyfn).
From vor- +‎ stellen. Compare Dutch voorstellen.

From Middle High German begegenen, begagenen, from Old High German bigaganen, with prefix from Proto-West Germanic *gaginijan, from Proto-Germanic *gaginjaną; equivalent to be- +‎ gegnen (“encounter”) +‎ -en. Cognate with Dutch bejegenen.

From Middle High German begleiten (14th c.), from an underlying (apparently unattested) *begeleiten, a confluence of beleiten and geleiten, both prefixed forms of leiten (“to lead”). Compare Dutch begeleiden. Sometimes reanalyzed as be- +‎ Geleit (“escort”) +‎ -en (with syncope as in begnügen from genug).
Compare English bekenned.
From bekannt.
drucken (“print”) +‎ -er

From Middle High German vūlezen (originally “to rot”), which is derived from the predecessor of German faul (“rotten; lazy”) with an intensifying suffix -ezzen (see Proto-Germanic *-atjaną). Later on -n- was infixed, either caused by or causing an association with Lenz (“spring-time”, and hence “time of joy”). Compare also the expression ein lauer Lenz (“a period of idleness”).
From Middle High German vīren, from Old High German fīrōn, derived from fīra, whence modern Feier. Compare Dutch vieren.
Fest +‎ Tag
From Middle High German gebür(e), from Old High German giburi. Deverbal from gebühren.
From Gebühr +‎ -en- +‎ frei.
From Middle High German hōchzīt, hōchgezīt, from (only plural) hōhūn gizīti (“high celebration”), equivalent to hoch (“high”) +‎ Zeit (“time”).
From Italian carnevale, from the Latin phrase carnem levāre, to put away meat.

From Middle High German kerze, from Old High German kerza, charza, from either Latin cērāta (“covered with wax”) or Latin charta (“sheet of papyrus”, in this case referring to layers of birch bark from which candles were made). The latter explanation is typically preferred, though the former is semantically more suggestive. Compare Dutch kaars, Hunsrik Kerz, Luxembourgish Käerz.
From Schaufenster (“shop window”) +‎ Bummel (“stroll”).

From Middle High German smücken, smucken (“to press against oneself, contract”), from Old High German *smucken (whence firsmucken (“to crush”)), from a formation related to modern German schmiegen (“to nestle up”); see there for more.[1]
Sitten n (proper noun, genitive Sittens or (optionally with an article) Sitten)

From Middle Low German tippen (“to touch lightly”), from Middle Low German tip (“tip, fingertip”), cognate with English tip, from Proto-Germanic *tuppijô, *tuppijǭ (“tip”), diminutive of *tuppaz (“top”).
über- +‎ raschen, compare English over, rush
verabreden +‎ -ung
veranstalten (“to organize, to arrange”) +‎ -ung
From vor- +‎ ziehen.
Block (“block”) +‎ Flöte (“flute”)
From Middle High German vloite and variants; borrowed via Middle Dutch floite from Old French fleüte.

From Middle High German gīge, from Old High German gīga, of unclear origin. Possibly from a Proto-Germanic *gīganą (“to move, wish, desire”) (based on the movement of a violinist's arms), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeyǵʰ-, *ǵʰeygʰ-, an extension of *ǵʰeh₂- (“to yawn, gape, long for, desire”),[1] though this is semantically dubious. Alternatively an independent onomatopoeic formation.[2] Cognate with Middle English gyge (“to make a creaking sound”), Old French giguer (“to play the fiddle”), English gig, English jig.
Borrowed from Spanish guitarra. See also Zither.
Borrowed from French clavier.
dokumentar(isch) +‎ Film
Borrowed from Latin cōmoedia.
Shortened from Kriminalroman (“crime story”).
Seife +‎ -n- +‎ Oper, calque of English soap opera.
From senden (“to send, transmit”) +‎ -ung.
18th century, from Latin seriēs, perhaps through French série.
From Zeichentrick +‎ Film.
an- +‎ schauen
From Middle High German and Old High German bal, from Proto-West Germanic *ballu, from Proto-Germanic *balluz.
Compound of fern +‎ sehen, derived from the noun Fernsehen.
From Middle High German hœren, from Old High German hōren. Compare Dutch horen, English hear, Danish høre.
Borrowed in the 17th century from Italian concerto, ultimately from Latin concertō (“to dispute”).

From Middle High German kopf (“drinking vessel”), from Old High German kopf, chopf, kupf (“mug, bowl, head”), from Proto-West Germanic *kopp, from Proto-Germanic *kuppaz (“round object, bowl, crown of the head”), from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to turn, bend, arch, curve”).
Cognate with German Low German Kopp (“head”), Dutch kop (“head”), Saterland Frisian Kop (“head”), Yiddish קאָפּ (kop, “head”), English cop (“the crown (of the head); the head”).
Alternatively, from or influenced by Late Latin cuppa, probably a form of Latin cūpa (“tub”) from Proto-Indo-European *kewp- (“a hollow”), related to English cup, although the form and gender make this derivation less likely.
From Middle High German liet, from Old High German liod (“song, lay, singing”), from Proto-West Germanic *leuþ (“song”), from Proto-Germanic *leuþą (“song”).
18th century, from Musik +‎ -er, after Musikus, which it has displaced.
Borrowed from Italian opera.
From French roman.
Inherited from Middle High German senger, from Old High German sangāri; Sang +‎ -er.
Schauspiel +‎ -er.
From Middle High German singen, from Old High German singan, from Proto-West Germanic *singwan, from Proto-Germanic *singwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ-.
From Middle High German tanz, from Middle Dutch dans, from Old French danse, dancier. See tanzen for more.

From Middle High German tanzen, from Old French dancer; the adapted onset t- in Upper German dialects (and standard German) proves that the word was not borrowed directly from the French word, but via Middle Low German or Middle Dutch dansen and Central German.
Tasche +‎ Buch
Ultimately from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”), from θεάομαι (theáomai, “to see, watch, observe”).

From Latin tragoedia, from Ancient Greek τραγῳδία (tragōidía, “epic play, tragedy”), from τράγος (trágos, “male goat”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”), a reference to the goat-satyrs of the theatrical plays of the Dorians.
Derived from the noun Zeichen. Compare English token (verb).

From Middle High German zeigen, from Old High German zeigōn, intensive of zīhan, whence modern zeihen (“to blame”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ-, whence also Zeichen, English teach. In Modern German, zeigen absorbed the synonymous but entirely unrelated Middle High German zöugen (cognate with Gothic ataugjan); therefore the spellings zäugen, zeugen also occurred.
vocabList.usage:
Man zeigt nicht mit dem Finger auf die Leute!
You don’t point your finger at people!

vocabList.etym: Inherited from Middle High German zīt, from Old High German zīt, from Proto-West Germanic *tīdi, from Proto-Germanic *tīdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₂itis, from *deh₂y- + *-tis.
From Zeit (“time”) +‎ Schrift (“writing”), "writings of the time".

From Middle Dutch tīdinge, whence is borrowed Middle High German zīdunge (West Central German), from Proto-West Germanic *tīdungu (“message”), from the verb *tīdōn (“to happen”), from Proto-West Germanic *tīdi (“time, interval”). From this the later Upper German form zītunge, and then the modern form.
From Bild (“picture/image”) +‎ Schirm (“screen”).
From Middle High German blāsen, Old High German blāsan, from Proto-West Germanic *blāsan.
From blasen +‎ Kapelle.
Borrowed from French garde-robe.

From Middle High German geræte (“consultation; equipment”), from Old High German girāti (“advice, consultation”), derived from rāt (“advice, council”), whence modern German Rat. The semantic development can, theoretically, be explained internally through a path “consultation” → “precaution” → “equipment”. However, the word has without doubt been influenced by another term, at hand in Old High German gireiti (“stuff, equipment”), which is related with bereit (“ready”). Both became homophonous in many Low and Central German dialects; compare Middle Low German gerēde (“consultation; equipment”), which can be cognate with either Old High German word. The Middle High German sources show that the sense “equipment” did indeed spread from the north. Cognate with Swedish geråd. Compare Dutch gerei and gereedschap.
18th century, borrowed from French parquet.
Borrowed from French rang.
From Middle High German stimme, from Old High German stimma or stimna, from Proto-West Germanic *stebnu, from Proto-Germanic *stebnō or *stamnijō from Proto-Indo-European *stomen- (“mouth, muzzle”).
From Tag (“day”) +‎ -es- +‎ Schau (“view”), formed after Wochenschau (“weekly cinema newsreel”).
From unter +‎ Titel.
From Middle High German zuoschouwe. Equivalent to zuschauen +‎ -er.
From Middle High German affe, from Old High German affo, from Proto-West Germanic *apō, from Proto-Germanic *apô.
From an- +‎ rufen (“to call, to shout”).
vocabList.usage:
Ich habe ihn gerade angerufen.
I've just called him.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German ūfzuc, verbal noun of ūfziehen.
From aus- (“out”) +‎ füllen (“to fill”).
Back-formation from Ausländer (“foreigner”), from Middle High German ūzlender, from ūzlant (“outlying fields”), which had no continuation in Early New High German. Compare English outland.
From Middle High German ūzlender, derived from ūzlant (“outlying fields”). See aus, Länder.
Derived from auswählen.
Deverbal from ausweisen.
From be- +‎ dienen.
From bedienen +‎ -ung.
From Middle High German bet, bette, from Old High German betti, from Proto-West Germanic *badi, from Proto-Germanic *badją (“plot, grave, resting-place, bed”).
Bett +‎ Wäsche
From Middle High German bedecken, from Old High German bidecken, bidekken, bithecken, from Proto-West Germanic *biþakkjan, equivalent to be- +‎ decken.
From Middle High German donern, from Old High German thonarōn, synchronically analyzed  as Donner (“thunder”) +‎ -n (“verbal suffix”).

From Middle High German tunkel, from Old High German tunkal, tuncal (“dark”), from Proto-Germanic *dunkalaz (“dark”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʷ- (“to smoke, fume”).
