The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German dunker, also dunkel). Cognate to Dutch donker (“dark”).

From Middle High German vrieren, vriesen, from Old High German friosan, from Proto-West Germanic *freusan, from Proto-Germanic *freusaną, from Proto-Indo-European *prews-. The -r- was generalised from the Middle High German past forms (as in verlieren). Cognate with German Low German freren, fresen, Dutch vriezen, English freeze, Danish fryse.

From Middle High German gewiter, gewitere, from Old High German giwitiri, from Proto-West Germanic *gawidri, from Proto-Germanic *gawidriją, documented since the 9th century AD,[1] equivalent to ge- +‎ Wetter. Cognate with Hunsrik Gewitter. Distantly cognate in structure to English aweather.
From Middle High German hagelen, synchronically analyzable as Hagel (“hail”) +‎ -n. Compare Dutch hagelen, English hail (verb).
From Middle High German and Old High German heiz, from Proto-West Germanic *hait. Akin to Old Saxon het, Dutch heet, English hot, Danish hed (“hot”).

From Middle High German heiter, from Old High German heitar, from Proto-West Germanic *haidr, from Proto-Germanic *haidraz. Compare Old Norse heiðr, Old English hador and Sanskrit चित्र (citra, “bright, wonderful, multicolored”).
From Middle High German and Old High German kalt, from Proto-West Germanic *kald.
Borrowed from Latin clima (“climate, clime”).

From Middle High German küele, Old High German kuoli, from Proto-West Germanic *kōl(ī), from Proto-Germanic *kōluz, *kōlaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gel-. Cognate with Dutch koel, English cool. Doublet of cool.
From Middle High German lewe, löuwe, lauwe, from Old High German lewo, lēo, from Proto-West Germanic *lewo, *lēwo (“lion”).

From Middle High German naz, from Old High German naz, from Proto-West Germanic *nat, from Proto-Germanic *nataz (“wet”), from Proto-Indo-European *ned- (“to be wet”). 
Cognate with Dutch nat (“wet”), Ancient Greek νοτέω (notéō, “to be wet”), νότος (nótos, “the south wind”).

From Middle High German nebel, from Old High German nebul, from Proto-Germanic *nebulaz, from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (whence also Proto-Balto-Slavic *néba, Proto-Indo-Iranian *nábʰas, Ancient Greek νεφέλη (nephélē, “cloud, mist”), Latin nebula (“mist, fog”)). More at English nuel.
From Middle High German rëgen, from Old High German rëgan, from Proto-West Germanic *regn, from Proto-Germanic *regną. Cognate with Yiddish רעגן (regn), Dutch regen, English rain, Danish regn.
From Regen (“rain”) +‎ Schirm (“screen”).
From Middle High German regenen, from Old High German reganōn, derived from the noun at hand in modern Regen (“rain”). Cognate with Hunsrik rehne.
Regen +‎ -isch
From Middle High German schūr, from Old High German scūr, from Proto-West Germanic *skūr, from Proto-Germanic *skūrō. Cognate with Dutch schoer, English shower, Swedish skur.

From Middle High German schīnen, from Old High German skīnan, from Proto-West Germanic *skīnan. Cognates include German Low German schienen, Dutch schijnen, English shine, Danish skinne, Esperanto ŝajni.
From Middle High German snê, from Old High German snēo, from Proto-West Germanic *snaiw.[1]
Inherited from Middle High German schœne, from Old High German scōni, from Proto-West Germanic *skaunī, from Proto-Germanic *skauniz.

From Middle High German sunne, from Old High German sunna, from Proto-West Germanic *sunnā, from Proto-Germanic *sunnǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *sh̥₂uén-, oblique stem of *sóh₂wl̥.
Akin to Low German Sünn, Zunne, Dutch zon, English sun, West Frisian sinne, Icelandic sunna. Further Indo-European cognates include Latin sōl, Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios), Sanskrit सूर्य (sū́rya), Russian солнце (solnce), Lithuanian saulė, Welsh haul.
From Middle High German *sunnec (suggested by derivative sunneclich), equivalent to Sonne +‎ -ig. Compare English sunny.

From Middle High German and Old High German sturm (“storm”). The retention of the u vowel is irregular; it was lowered to o due to a-mutation in all other West Germanic languages and even Old Norse, despite German being the one Germanic language where a-mutation most consistently occurred, especially of u to o.

From Middle High German wëter, from Old High German wëtar, from Proto-Germanic *wedrą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁dʰrom, from *h₂weh₁- (“to blow; wind”) +‎ *-dʰrom (instrument noun–deriving suffix). Compare German Low German Weder, Luxembourgish Wieder, Dutch weer, English weather, Danish vejr.
From Middle High German windic, equivalent to Wind +‎ -ig. Compare English windy.

From Middle High German wolken, from Old High German wolkan, from Proto-West Germanic *wolkn.
Akin to Dutch wolk, English welkin, Proto-Slavic *volga, Albanian ulmej (“to wet, dampen”).
Wolke +‎ -ig
From Middle High German blic, from Old High German blik, from Proto-Germanic *blikaz, *blikkaz (“shine, appearance, look; metal”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ- (“to shine”).

From Middle High German blīben, belīben (“to remain in the same position, pause, blin”), from Old High German bilīban (“to remain”), from Proto-Germanic *bilībaną (“to remain”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick, glue”). Cognate with Dutch blijven (“to remain”), English belive (“to remain, stay”). More at belive.
vocabList.usage:
Er blieb sein ganzes Leben ein glühender Anhänger der Monarchie.
He remained a devoted supporter of the monarchy for all his life.

vocabList.etym: In the 18th century, from French brochure.
From Camping +‎ Platz.
From Middle High German antvanc, from Old High German antfang. By surface analysis, deverbal from empfangen.
15th century, from Latin fēriae, with replacement of the Latin plural suffix -ae with German -en.
From foto- +‎ Apparat.
foto- +‎ -graf
Fund (“find”) +‎ Büro (“office”).
From Middle High German gast, from Old High German gast, from Proto-West Germanic *gasti, from Proto-Germanic *gastiz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis.
From Gast +‎ Geber.
From Middle High German gasthūs, from Old High German gasthūs, from Proto-West Germanic *gastahūs, from Proto-Germanic *gastahūsą, equivalent to Gast (“guest”) +‎ Haus (“house”). Compare Gästehaus.
From Gast (“guest”) +‎ Stätte (“place”).
From Late Middle High German gepac, synchronically analyzable as a collective nominal formation from Pack (“package, bundle”) (DWDS).
From Middle High German gültic, from gülte, from gelten. Cognate with Low German güllig.
From Middle High German insel, insele, isele, from Old High German isila, *insila, from Proto-West Germanic *isulā, *insulā, borrowed from Latin *isula, insula (“island”).
Jugend +‎ Herberge
From early modern Dutch kust(e) (“coast”), from Old French coste (“side; coast”), from Latin costa (“rib”). Compare modern French côte, English coast.

From Middle High German lant, from Old High German lant, from Proto-West Germanic *land, from Proto-Germanic *landą, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”). Compare Dutch, English, and Danish land, Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌽𐌳 (land).
From Land (“land”) +‎ Karte (“card”).
From Middle High German lantschaft, from Old High German lantskaf. By surface analysis, Land +‎ -schaft.
Borrowed from Latin lūxus (“extravagance”).
From Middle High German mere, mer, from Old High German meri, from Proto-West Germanic *mari. Doublet of Maar and Mare.
From mit- +‎ nehmen; cognate with Hunsrik mitnemme.

From Middle High German ort (“point (of a tool or weapon), corner, end point, boundary, border, site, place”), from Old High German ort (“point, tip, corner”) (8th century),  from Proto-West Germanic *oʀd, from Proto-Germanic *uzdaz (“point”).

From Early New High German pass, from Middle High German pas (“parts of a deer's entrails”) (but also West Central German "step, walk, gait, way", also "the right measure; the right, appropriate time" by influence of Middle Dutch, whence Late Middle High German pas (“"measured part, section”), compare the verb passen). Borrowed from Old French pas (“pace, step”) (partially intermediated by Middle Dutch pas), from Latin passus. 
The meaning "pass, passageway" is first recorded in the 15th century and is possibly influenced by Italian passo (“pass”). The meaning "pace of an animal" is first recorded in the 16th century.
Borrowed from French pension, ultimately from Latin pēnsiō, pēnsiōnem.
Personal (“personal or personnel”) +‎ Ausweis (“ID card”)
From Latin prospectus.
From Middle High German reise, reis, from Old High German reisa, from Proto-West Germanic *raisu.
From Reise (“journey, voyage”) +‎ Büro (“office”).
Reise +‎ Bus
From Middle High German reisen, from Old High German reisōn, from Proto-West Germanic *raisōn, further from Proto-West Germanic *raisu (akin to Proto-Germanic *raizijaną).
Reise +‎ Scheck
From Reise (“journey, voyage”) +‎ Ziel (“target”).
From Middle High German sant, from Old High German sant, from Proto-West Germanic *sand, *samd, from Proto-Germanic *sandaz, *samdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sámh₂dʰos.
Schlaf (“sleep”) +‎ Sack

From Sonne (“sun”) +‎ -n- +‎ Brand (“fire, burn”). The word originally meant the burning heat of the sun. As such it was also commonly used in the context of sunburnt skin. However, the use of Sonnenbrand to refer this skin condition itself (meaning that one can “have a sunburn”, Sonnenbrand haben) seems to be a development of the 20th century.
Sonne (“sun”) +‎ -n- +‎ Creme (“cream”)
From Middle High German strant, from Old High German *strand, from Proto-Germanic *strandō. Cognate with English strand (“shore; beach”). More at strand.
From Middle High German suochen, süechen, from Old High German suohhen, from Proto-West Germanic *sōkijan, from Proto-Germanic *sōkijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂g- (“seek out”).
vocabList.usage:
Ich suche meinen Schlüssel. / Ich suche nach meinem Schlüssel.
I’m looking for my key.

vocabList.etym: From Tasche (“pocket”) +‎ Lampe (“lamp”).
Tasche +‎ -n- +‎ Messer

From Middle High German übernahten, from Old High German ubarnahtēn (“to overnight”), from Proto-West Germanic *obarnahtēn (“to overnight”), equivalent to über- +‎ Nacht +‎ -en. Cognate with German Low German övernachten, Dutch overnachten, West Frisian oernachtsje, Saterland Frisian uurnoachtje, English overnight.
vocabList.usage:
Mama? Kann ich heute bei der Sarah übernachten?
Mum? May I sleep over at Sarah’s tonight?

vocabList.etym: From the verb unterkommen (“to find a place, find shelter”).

From older unterwegen, from Middle High German under wegen, from Old High German untar wegun. Equivalent to unter- (“under”) +‎ Weg (“way”) +‎ -s (adverbial suffix). Compare Dutch onderweg, English underway.
From wohnen (“to live, dwell, stay”) +‎ Wagen (“vehicle, wagon, car”).

From Middle High German zëlt, from Old High German zelt, from Proto-West Germanic *teld, from Proto-Germanic *teldą.
Compare Danish telt (whence English tilt + native teld from Old English teld), Middle Dutch telt, Old Norse tjald (“tent”) (whence Norwegian Bokmål tjeld).
Zelt (“tent”) + -en.

From Middle High German zimber, from Old High German zimbar, from Proto-West Germanic *timr, from Proto-Germanic *timrą, from Proto-Indo-European *dem- (“build, house”) (see Proto-Indo-European *dṓm). Cognate with English timber and Dutch timmer (“building; construction; room”).
From Zimmer +‎ Mädchen.
From Aufenthalt +‎ -s- +‎ Dauer.
aus- +‎ tauschen
From Middle High German entscheiden, equivalent to ent- +‎ scheiden. Cognate with German Low German entscheden, Dutch ontscheiden, Saterland Frisian undskede.
ent- +‎ spannen
Derived from Latin cursus. Cognate with Russian курс (kurs), French cours, French course, English course etc. Doublet of Korso.
Compound of lau +‎ warm
From Reise +‎ Führer.
Ca. 1898, from rollen (“to roll”) +‎ Treppe (“staircase”), possibly after French escalier roulant (of roughly contemporaneous attestation).

From Middle High German schate, schatwe, schatewe, schetewe, from Old High German scato, from Proto-West Germanic *skadu; akin to Old Saxon skado, Dutch schaduw, English shadow and shade. More at shadow.
From Middle High German tropfen, tropfe, from Old High German tropfo, from Proto-West Germanic *dropō, from Proto-Germanic *drupô. Akin to English drop.
From verändern.
ver- +‎ ändern
Wechsel +‎ -haft
From Middle High German abfal, abefal, equivalent to ab- (“from”) +‎ Fall (“fall”). Cognate with German Low German Offall, Dutch afval, English offal, Swedish avfall.

From Middle High German ampel, ampolle, ampulle, from Old High German ampla, ampulla (“vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *ampullā (“flask, cruse”). The sense development was vessel → hanging lamp (in or shaped like a vessel) → traffic light. Doublet of Ampulle.
an- +‎ springen
vocabList.usage:
Ich wurde von einem Hund angesprungen.
I was pounced at by a dog.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German blī, from Old High German blīo.
From Middle High German brant, from Old High German brant, from Proto-West Germanic *brand. Cognate with Bavarian Brånd and English brand.

From Middle High German ërde, from Old High German ërda, from Proto-West Germanic *erþu, from Proto-Germanic *erþō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁érteh₂ (“earth”). Compare Dutch aarde, West Frisian ierde, Low German Eerde, English earth, Danish jord, Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌸𐌰 (airþa).
Borrowed from French grade (“a grade, degree”), from Latin gradus (“a step”).

From Middle High German grenize, graniza, from Old Polish granica, from Proto-Slavic *granica (“boundary, border”). The word spread westward in the 15th century and was reinforced by Luther’s Bible. Doublet of  Granne.

From Middle High German hērlich, from Old High German hērlīh, equivalent to hehr (“sublime, noble”) +‎ -lich, with the first element remodelled after Herr already during OHG; cf. the same development in Herrschaft and herrschen. Cognate with Dutch heerlijk (“delicious, lovely, delightful”), Swedish härlig. More at hoar, -ly.
From Middle High German himel, from Old High German himil, from Proto-West Germanic *himil.

From Middle High German hōch, from Old High German hōh, from Proto-West Germanic *hauh, from Proto-Germanic *hauhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kewk-, a suffixed form of *kew-. Compare Dutch hoog, Low German hoog, English high, Swedish hög.
From Middle High German jār, from Old High German jār, from Proto-West Germanic *jār. Compare Low German Johr, Jahr, Dutch jaar, English year, Danish år. Doublet of Uhr.
From Middle High German luft m or f, from Old High German luft, from Proto-West Germanic *luftu, from Proto-Germanic *luftuz.

An originally Central and Low German word from Middle Low German mül (“dust”) and Middle High German mülle, from Old High German mulli (“waste, rubbish”), a nominal formation from mullen (“to crush, grind”), from Proto-Germanic *muljaną (“to crush”) (DWDS).
From nieder +‎ -ig; probably either borrowed or calqued from Middle Low German nēderich. Cognate to Dutch nederig (“humble”).
From German Norden.
From Ost or Old High German ostan, from Proto-Germanic *austrą, related to *ausos (“dawn”), compare Latin aurora, and Latin auster, which, probably due to a re-orientation, means "South".
Borrowed from French panne.
From parken (“to park”) +‎ Haus.
From parken +‎ Platz.
From Middle High German partīe, from Old French partie. Cognate with English party, Italian partita.[1] Doublet of Partie and Party.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin policia, from Late Latin polītīa.
Polizei (“police”) +‎ -ist (“-ist”)
Borrowed from French porte-monnaie around 1850.
From Middle High German rouchen, röuchen, from Old High German rouhhen, from Proto-West Germanic *raukijan. By surface analysis, Rauch (“smoke”) +‎ -en.
vocabList.usage:
Das abgebrannte Haus raucht noch immer.
The burned-down house is still smoking.

vocabList.etym: Recht +‎ haben
Recht (“law”) +‎ -s- +‎ Anwalt (“lawyer”)

From Middle High German rede, from Old High German redia, radia (“speech, view, opinion”), from Proto-Germanic *raþjǭ, *raþjō (“accountability, speech”); from the same root as reden (“to talk, to speak”). Cognate with Latin ratiō (“account, reason, proof”) and German Rat (“counsel”), English rede (“counsel”).

vocabList.definition: to talk, to speak, to orate
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German reden, from Old High German redōn, rediōn (“to speak”), a derivative of reda, redia (“speech, word, opinion, view, mind”), from Proto-Germanic *raþjǭ, *raþjō (“accountability, speech”). See Rede.
Stem variant of Reif, which developed weak forms in early modern German.
Reifen +‎ Panne
Beginning of the 18th century, from Latin reparātūra (literally “things about to be repaired”).
Borrowed from Latin reparō. Compare to English repair.
From Middle High German stroum, strūm, strām, from Old High German stroum, strōm, from Proto-West Germanic *straum.

From Middle Low German sūden and Middle Dutch sūden. The form is already attested in Middle High German sūden, which replaces native Middle High German sunden from Old High German sundan. However, the modern form with a preserved monophthong must be directly from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch. The latter's influence is seen in the umlaut (compare the Middle Dutch pronunciation of -ū- [yː]). All these forms are from Proto-Germanic *sunþanē, an adverb meaning "from the south". The original Proto-Germanic noun *sunþrą, whence English south and German Süd, has always been restricted chiefly to compounds in continental West Germanic.

From Middle High German verbieten, from Old High German firbiotan, from Proto-West Germanic *furibeudan, from Proto-Germanic *furibeudaną. Equivalent to ver- +‎ bieten. Compare Dutch verbieden, Low German verbeden, English forbid, Danish forbyde, Swedish förbjuda, Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌱𐌹𐌿𐌳𐌰𐌽 (faurbiudan).
From Middle High German vergëȥȥen, from Old High German firgëȥȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *fragetan.
vocabList.usage:
Diese ganzen Geschichten hatte ich ja ganz vergessen.
I'd completely forgotten all these stories.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German vorteil, voreteil, from Old High German forateila, equivalent to vor- (“before, better”) +‎ Teil (“part, piece”). Compare English foredeal (“advantage, benefit”).

Inherited from Middle High German wëlt, assimilative contraction of older wërlt, from Old High German weralt, from Proto-West Germanic *weraldi, from Proto-Germanic *weraldiz. Cognate to English world, Dutch wereld, Swedish värld.
From West.
Borrowed from French cigarette.
abschleppen (“to tow away”) +‎ Wagen (“car”)
ab- +‎ schliessen
alt +‎ Papier

Compound of an- (“on, at”) +‎ zünden (“to ignite, kindle”). Akin to
Old English ontendan, Swedish antända, Norwegian antenne.
From Middle High German ūfgeben. Equivalent to auf- (“up”) +‎ geben (“give”). Cognate with English upgive, Dutch opgeven.
From be- +‎ klagen.
From Middle High German beliuhten, from Old High German biliuhten. Equivalent to be- +‎ leuchten.
be- +‎ schädigen

From Middle High German beswæren (“to afflict, to depress, to annoy”), a merger from Old High German biswāren (“to depress, to burden”) (10th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *biswârijan; and Old High German biswārōn (“to burden”) (10th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *biswārōn. Related to swāren (“heavy”) (8th c.) whence schwer. The reflexive sense developed later in the 14th century from "to burden oneself", "to fret" to "to complain about something worrisome, burdensome".[1] Cognate with Dutch bezwaren.
From the adjective besser.
bessern (“to better, to improve”) +‎ -ung

From Middle High German diep, Old High German diob, from Proto-West Germanic *þeub, from Proto-Germanic *þeubaz. Cognate with Old Norse þýfð, Old English þēof, Dutch dief, English thief, Gothic 𐌸𐌹𐌿𐍆𐍃 (þiufs).[1]
Droge +‎ -n- +‎ süchtig, equivalent to Drogensucht +‎ -ig
From einbrechen +‎ -er.
Geld (“money”) +‎ Strafe (“punishment”)

From Middle High German gesetze, gesetzede, from Old High German gisezzida (“fixing, determination, assessment”), from sezzen (“to make sit, set, put”), from Proto-West Germanic *sattjan (“to set, put down”).
From Middle High German gewonheit, from Old High German giwonaheit. Equivalent to gewohn +‎ -heit, the former being an obsolete variant of gewohnt. Compare gewöhnlich.
Calque of English global warming.

From Middle High German liegen, from Old High German liogan, from Proto-West Germanic *leugan, from Proto-Germanic *leuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ-. Cognate with Bavarian liagn, Dutch liegen, Low German liegen, legen, lögen, English lie, Danish lyve, Swedish ljuga.
miss- +‎ Verständnis

From Middle High German māne, from Old High German māno, from Proto-West Germanic *mānō. Later forms of the Middle High German word, mānde, had a final dental due to confusion with mānōt (“month”) (modern Monat).

From Middle High German mort, from Old High German mord, from Proto-West Germanic *morþ, from Proto-Germanic *murþą. Cognate with Dutch moord, English murth, Swedish mord, Finnish murha. Also related with English murder, French meurtre.
From Middle High German nōt, from Old High German nōt, from Proto-West Germanic *naudi.
From Middle High German rāt, from Old High German rāt, from Proto-West Germanic *rād, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaz.
Borrowed from English recycle  +‎ -en.
From Latin redūcō +‎ -ieren.
From Middle High German regel, from Old High German regula, from Proto-West Germanic *regulā, from Latin regula (“rule”).
From Middle High German rettunge, equivalent to retten +‎ -ung.
Borrowed in the 16th century from older Italian risico (contemporary rischio). Further origin unsettled.
From rollen (“to roll”) +‎ Stuhl (“chair”).
From Middle High German schamen, schemen, from Old High German scamēn, from Proto-West Germanic *skamēn, from Proto-Germanic *skamāną (“to be ashamed”), equivalent to Scham (shame) +‎ -en.
Inherited from Middle High German schulden, from Old High German skuldōn, from Proto-West Germanic *skuldōn.

From Middle High German schuldec, from Old High German sculdig. Equivalent to Schuld +‎ -ig. The form shows (chiefly southern) blocking of umlaut in -ul- + consonant, as usually in modern German (exceptions gülden, gültig, Sülze). Cognate with Luxembourgish schëlleg, Dutch schuldig.

From late Middle High German schützen (“to protect”, literally “to dam up, contain”), either from the root of schießen (“to shoot (advance a barrier)”) or schütten (“to pour [pile up a protective wall]”). Cognate with English shut.
vocabList.usage:
Die Götter schützen die guten Leute.
Gods protect good people.

vocabList.etym: Inherited from Middle High German stëln, from Old High German stelan, from Proto-West Germanic *stelan, from Proto-Germanic *stelaną.
From Middle High German tōt, from Old High German tōd, from Proto-West Germanic *dauþu, from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz. Compare Old Saxon dōth, Dutch dood, English death, Danish død.
From Middle High German tœten, tœden, from Old High German *tōten, tōden, from Proto-West Germanic *daudijan ~ *dauþijan. By surface analysis, tot (“dead”) +‎ -en.
vocabList.usage:
Zehn Menschen wurden bei dem Anschlag getötet.
Ten people were killed in the attack.

vocabList.etym: From English tramp, from Middle English trampen (“to walk heavily”), from Middle Low German trampen (“to stamp”) (trampeln (“to walk with heavy steps”), see English trample) or from Middle Dutch trampen (“to stamp”), from Proto-West Germanic *trampan (“to step”).
Treibhaus (“greenhouse”) +‎ Effekt (“effect”)

From Middle High German umbekomen (“to pass by, end, die”). Analysable as um- +‎ kommen. Cognate with Middle Dutch ommecomen (“to pass by, end, die”), whence modern Dutch omkomen. Compare also ums Leben kommen, and further umbringen, ums Leben bringen. Regarding the broader semantic use in both Middle High German and Middle Dutch, it is not certain that the short verbs are mere ellipses of the phrases with Leben, though they have without doubt been influenced by them.
From um- +‎ tauschen.

From the fusion of Middle High German underschiet, underschit, Middle High German underschide, and Middle High German underscheit, unterscheid, from Old High German untarskeit, untarskeid; derived synchronically from unterscheiden. Compare Dutch onderscheid, Hunsrik Unnerschied, Low German Ünnerscheed, Saterland Frisian Unnerskeed.
ver- +‎ brauchen. Cognate to Dutch verbruiken.
From Middle High German vergiften (“to give, donate, bequeath; to poison”), formally from Old High German firgiften (“to donate; to sell”). Analysable as ver- +‎ Gift +‎ -en or ver- +‎ giften.
ver- +‎ haften

vocabList.definition: to lose one’s way/ to get lost
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German verirren, from Old High German firirrо̄n, from Proto-West Germanic *farirʀijōn. Equivalent to ver- +‎ irren.
Schmutz +‎ ver- -en
From Middle High German versichern. Equivalen to ver- +‎ sichern. The insurance sense (17th c.) is a calque of Italian assicurare.
From weg- +‎ werfen. Compare Dutch wegwerpen.
From Middle High German zerstören, from Old High German zistōren, zirstōren, from Proto-West Germanic *staurijan. Equivalent to zer- +‎ stören.
vocabList.usage:
Der Alkohol hat seine Gesundheit zerstört.
Alcohol has destroyed his health.

vocabList.etym: Attested since the 1890s. A shortening of Abiturium n, itself short for Latin exāmen abiturium—in formal German of the 19th century rather found as Abiturientenexamen—, from abituriō (“I wish to leave”), desiderative construction of abeō (“I leave, go off”). For more, see also Abiturient. Compare Physikum.

From Middle High German ūfgābe, ultimately a verbal noun from the ancestor of aufgeben. By surface analysis, auf (“up”) +‎ Gabe (“gift, giving”). Compare also Dutch opgave, which may have borrowed the meaning "task" from the German.
auf- +‎ räumen
Borrowed from Latin aula.
From doppel- (“double”) +‎ Stunde (“hour, lesson”).

From Middle High German gebūwede, from the Old High German gibūidi (literally “that which has been built”),[1][2][3] originally a collective noun to bauen. See there for more. By surface analysis, ge- +‎ Bau +‎ -de, related to bauen. Doublet of Gebäu. Cognate with Yiddish געבײַדע (gebayde)

From Middle High German gespræche, gesprēche, from Old High German gisprāchi, from Proto-Germanic *gasprakją. Cognates with Low German Gespreek, Hunsrik Gesprech, Luxembourgish Gespréich, Dutch gesprek, Old English gesprecan.

Borrowed from French groupe, from Italian gruppo, groppo, from Vulgar Latin *cruppus, (cf. Renaissance Latin grupus), from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz (“lump, group, body, crop”), from Proto-Indo-European *grewb- (“to crumple, bend, crawl”).[1][2] Doublet of Kropf.
From Middle High German hūs, from Old High German hūs, from Proto-West Germanic *hūs, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą.
Haus (“house”) +‎ Meister (“master”)
Haus (“house”) +‎ Tür (“door”)
Borrowed from French intéressant.
From Middle High German kint, from Old High German kind, from Proto-West Germanic *kind, from Proto-Germanic *kindą, *kinþą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to give birth”).
Ultimately from Latin classis, probably via French classe.
From Klasse (“form, class”) +‎ Arbeit (“work”).
From Klasse (“class”) +‎ -n- +‎ Zimmer (“room”). The use of the word Zimmer is slightly unusual in this compound because it is chiefly used for private rooms.
From Middle High German corrigieren, from Latin corrigere.
Clipping of Laboratorium, from Latin labōrātōrium.

From Middle High German lēren, from Old High German lēren, from Proto-West Germanic *laiʀijan, from *laizō (“lore”), from Proto-Germanic *laizijaną, from *lizaną +‎ *-janą, stative from the root *leys- (“track, furrow, trace, trail”).
From Middle High German lērer, lērære, from Old High German lērāri; equivalent to lehren +‎ -er.
lehren +‎ -ling. Compare Dutch leerling.

From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German līht, from Proto-West Germanic *lį̄ht, from Proto-Germanic *linhtaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-. Compare English light, Dutch licht, Danish let.
Ultimately from Latin nota (“mark, sign, remark, note”).

From Middle High German nœtic, nœtec, nōtic, nōtec, nōdic, from Old High German nōtag (“forced, urgent, needy”), from Proto-West Germanic *naudag (“obligatory, needful”), from Proto-Germanic *naudagaz, equivalent to Not +‎ -ig. Cognate with German Low German nödig, English needy, Swedish nödig.
From Middle High German nützelich, from Old High German nuzzilīh (“useful”), equivalent to Nutzen +‎ -lich. Compare Hunsrik nitzlich, Old English nytlīċ.
From Middle High German pūse, borrowed from Middle French pause (14st), from Latin pausa.
From Middle High German plaz, from Old French place, from Latin platēa, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), shortening of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”). Cognate with English place.
From prüfen +‎ -ung; cognate with Hunsrik Priefung.
From Middle High German punct, Late Latin pūnctus. Doublet of bunt.
Punkt +‎ -lich. Further from Latin punctus (p.p.p. of pungō), whence also English point, punctual.
From Middle High German rihtec, from Old High German rihtīg, from reht (“right”) + -ig. Equivalent to recht +‎ -ig. Originally only an adjective; adverb developed later.

From Middle High German sal, from Old High German sal, sali, seli, from Proto-West Germanic *sali, from Proto-Germanic *saliz, *salą, from Proto-Indo-European *sel- (“human settlement, village, dwelling”).
From Middle High German schrīben, from Old High German scrīban, from Proto-West Germanic *skrīban (“to write”), from Latin scrībō.
schreiben (“write”) +‎ Papier (“paper”)
From Middle High German schuole, from Old High German scuola.
From Middle High German schuolære, from Old High German scuolāri, from Medieval Latin scholaris; analyzable as Schule +‎ -er.
From Schüler +‎ Austausch.
From Middle High German swach, from Old High German *swah, from Proto-West Germanic *swak. Cognate with Dutch zwak, Scots swack, also English dialectal swack.
From Middle High German swær, from Old High German swār, from Proto-West Germanic *swār, from Proto-Germanic *swēraz, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy, grave, serious”).
From Middle High German swiric, sweric (“full of boils”), a derivative of Schwäre. Cognate to dated Dutch zwerig (“full of boils”).
Borrowed from Latin sēmēstris.
From Middle High German studente, from Medieval Latin studēns.
From Middle High German studieren, from Latin studeō +‎ -ieren.
vocabList.usage:
Sie studiert Chemie.
She studies chemistry.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German stunde, from Old High German stunta, from Proto-West Germanic *stundu, from Proto-Germanic *stundō (“point in time, hour”).
Stunde +‎ Plan
From Middle High German tavel, tavele, from Old High German tavala, tabela, from Proto-West Germanic *tabulā.
Inherited from Middle High German tac, from Old High German tag, from Proto-West Germanic *dag, from Proto-Germanic *dagaz, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ-.
From Tag (“day”) +‎ -e- +‎ Buch (“book”).
From unterrichten; from Middle High German underrihten; unter- +‎ richten.
From Middle High German underrihten, equivalent to unter- +‎ richten. Cognate with Middle Low German underrichten (whence German Low German unnerrichten), Saterland Frisian unnergjuchte.
From Middle High German versuoch (“striving, undertaking, test, examination”), from Old High German firsuoh (“test, experiment”). See versuchen (“to try, attempt”).
From ver- +‎ suchen. Compare English forseek.
vocabList.usage:
Bitte sei still, ich versuche zu schlafen.
Please be quiet, I'm trying to sleep.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German wale, from Old High German wala, from Proto-West Germanic *walu, from Proto-Germanic *walą.
From Middle High German wiȥȥen and Old High German wiȥȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *witan, from Proto-Germanic *witaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyde (“to see, to know”).
vocabList.usage:
Ich weiß, wo du bist.
I know where you are.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German woche, from Old High German wohha, alteration of older wëhha, from Proto-West Germanic *wikā, from Proto-Germanic *wikǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *weyg- (“to bend, wind, turn, yield”). Compare English week, Yiddish וואָך (vokh), Dutch week, West Frisian wike, Danish uge, Swedish vecka.

Compound of Woche (“week”) +‎ -n- +‎ Ende (“end”). In the older language sporadically for “end of the week”. The modern sense since the 19th century after English weekend, in general use since ca. 1920.
zu- +‎ hören
From Blei (“lead”) +‎ Stift (“pen”).
18th century, from French étui.
From Filz +‎ Stift.
From Middle High German vüllen, from Old High German fullen. Compare Dutch vullen, English fill, Danish fylde, Swedish fylla.
From füllen (“to fill”) +‎ -er (“-er”).
From Middle High German gummi (13th c.), from Medieval Latin gummi, byform of older cummi(s), which see.
Kugel (“ball”) +‎ Schreiber (“writer”)
15th century, learned borrowing from Latin līneāle.
Notiz (“note”) +‎ Buch (“book”)
From Middle High German papier, from Old French papier.
radieren (“to rub out”) +‎ Gummi (“gum”)

From Middle High German sache, from Old High German sahha, from Proto-West Germanic *saku, from Proto-Germanic *sakō.
Cognate with Bavarian Såch, Yiddish זאַך (zakh), German Low German Sake, Low German Sake, Dutch zaak, Afrikaans saak, English sake, Danish sag, Swedish sak.

From Middle High German stift / steft, from Old High German stift / steft, from Proto-West Germanic *stift, from Proto-Germanic *stiftaz (“pin, nail”); likely derived from the Proto-Indo-European root *steyp- (“stiff, erect”), whence also German steif (“stiff”). Cognate with German Low German Stift.

Inherited from Middle High German stücke, from Old High German stucki, from Proto-West Germanic *stukkī, from Proto-Germanic *stukkiją. Cognate with Hunsrik Stick, Dutch stuk, Luxembourgish Stéck, Yiddish שטיק (shtik), dialectal English steck (“piece”). Doublet of  Stuck.
Tasche (“pocket”) +‎ -n- +‎ Rechner (“calculator”)
Tasche (“pocket”) +‎ Tuch (“cloth”).

From Early New High German zeddel, zedel, from Middle High German zedele, zedel, a loan from Italian cedola, from Medieval Latin cedula, schedula, the diminutive of scheda, scida (“strip of papyrus”) ultimately from Ancient Greek σχίδη (skhídē, “splinter, fragment”). Cognate to Low German Zeddel, Palatine Rhine Franconian Zeddel, English schedule.
18th century, from Erde +‎ -kunde, a calque of Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).
From Middle High German vach, from Old High German fah, from Proto-West Germanic *fak, from Proto-Germanic *faką.
From fremd (“foreign”) +‎ Sprache (“language”).

From Middle High German geschicht(e) (“event, struggle, story, history”), from Old High German gisciht, from the verb Proto-Germanic *skehaną, whence German geschehen. Unrelated to Schicht. Cognate with Vilamovian gyśicht.
From Information +‎ -ik
Clipping of  Mathematik.
From Pflicht (“obligation”) +‎ Fach (“subject”).
Borrowed from Latin religio.
turnen (“to do gymnastics”) +‎ Halle (“hall”)
From Beruf (“profession”) +‎ -s- +‎ Schule (“school”).
gesamt +‎ Schule
grund- (“basic/elementary”) +‎ Schule (“school”).
Borrowed from Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion, “exercise, school”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”).
haupt- +‎ Schule
Borrowed from French internat.
Kind (“child”) +‎ -er- +‎ Garten (“garden”). Coined in 1840 by Friedrich Fröbel in the metaphorical sense of “place where children can grow in a natural way”, not in the literal sense of “garden”.[1]
privat +‎ Schule
From real +‎ Schule.
Borrowed from Latin ūniversitās. Compare Dutch universiteit.
From Middle High German ūfsaz; analyzable as a back-formation from aufsetzen. Cognate with Luxembourgish Opsaz, Dutch opstel.
From Middle High German benëmen, from Old High German bineman, from Proto-West Germanic *bineman, from Proto-Germanic *binemaną. Equivalent to be- +‎ nehmen. Compare English benim.
Betrieb +‎ -s- +‎ Wirtschaft
From Middle High German bildunge, from Old High German bildunga. By surface analysis, bilden +‎ -ung.
From French brave.

From Middle High German bret, from Old High German bret, from Proto-West Germanic *bred, from Proto-Germanic *bredą, an e-grade byform of *burdą (“board, plank”). Cognate with Old English bred and Yiddish ברעט (bret).
From durch- +‎ fallen.
vocabList.usage:
Das Gitter war zu weitmaschig. Der Ball ist einfach durchgefallen.
The grating was too wide-meshed. The ball simply fell through.

vocabList.etym: ein- +‎ reichen
From fort- +‎ Schritt, a calque of Latin prōgressus. See also fortschreiten.
From Middle High German ganc, from Old High German gang, from Proto-West Germanic *gang. Cognate with English gang.
From Middle High German lōnen, from Old High German lōnōn. By surface analysis, Lohn +‎ -en.
From Middle High German meinen, from Old High German meinen, from Proto-Germanic *mainijaną (“to mean, think; lament”).
vocabList.usage:
Ich meine, das war letztes oder vorletztes Jahr.
I think it was last year or the year before.

vocabList.etym: Mund +‎ -lich
nach- +‎ denken; cognate with Hunsrik nohdenke, Dutch nadenken.
vocabList.usage:
Ich dachte darüber nach und beschloss, das Auto zu kaufen.
I thought about it and decided to buy the car.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German rechenen, from Old High German rehhanōn (akin to Old Saxon *rekenen), from Proto-West Germanic *rekanōn. Compare Hunsrik rechne, Low German rekenen, Dutch rekenen and English reckon. Indirectly derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-.
15th century, from Old French rolle, probably through Middle Dutch rolle (as also the verb rollen). Further from Latin rotula, rotulus. The sense “role” from the modern French descendant rôle.
Schrift +‎ -lich

Literally, “to stay sitting”. The school sense is from situations where proceeding to the next year meant going to another classroom or row of seats. The marriage sense is from the notion of not being picked, e.g. at a dance. Compare Dutch blijven zitten.
vocabList.usage:
Bleib sitzen! Ich komme zu dir rüber.
Keep your seat! I’m coming over to you.

vocabList.etym: 16th century, from über- (“over”) +‎ setzen (“to set”), probably modeled on Latin trādūcere, perhaps through Middle Low German ōversetten (15th c.).
vocabList.usage:
Sie übersetzt Lyrik ins Deutsche.
She translates poetry into German.

vocabList.etym: ver- +‎ bessern
From versammeln +‎ -ung.

From Middle High German zel(e)n, zellen, from Old High German zellan, from Proto-West Germanic *talljan, from Proto-Germanic *taljaną. The modern long vowel continues the 2nd and 3rd persons singular of the present (where West Germanic gemination did not occur); it was reinforced also by the lengthened vowel in Zahl (Middle High German zale).
vocabList.usage:
Die Stadt zählt etwa 13.000 Einwohner.
The town has approximately 13,000 inhabitants.

vocabList.etym: Akte (“file, papers”) +‎ -n- +‎ Tasche (“bag”)

From Middle High German arbeit, from Old High German arbeit, from Proto-West Germanic *arbaiþi, from Proto-Germanic *arbaidiz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan, servant, slave”), from which English orphan is also derived. Cognate with Yiddish אַרבעט (arbet), Middle English arveth.

From Old High German arbeiten, from Proto-Germanic *arbaidijaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan”), from which English orphan is also derived. Cognates include Dutch arbeiden, Old Saxon arvedian, Gothic 𐌰𐍂𐌱𐌰𐌹𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (arbaidjan).
From Middle High German arbeiter. By surface analysis, arbeiten (“to work”) +‎ -er (agentive suffix).
From aus- +‎ Bildung or ausbilden +‎ -ung.
Brief +‎ Tasche.
Ca. 1700, from French bureau (“desk, office”), which see.

Feier (“celebration”) +‎ Abend (“evening”). Originally related to Vorabend (“evening before”), it took on its current meaning in the 16th century.
Compound of Feier +‎ Tag.
Borrowed from Italian firma. Cognate with English firm.
From Middle High German gelt, from Old High German gelt, kelt, from Proto-West Germanic *geld, from Proto-Germanic *geldą (“reward, gift, money”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeldʰ- (“to pay”).
Borrowed from Italian cassa, from Latin capsa.
From klein (“small”) +‎ Geld (“money”).
Borrowed from Italian conto (“calculation”).
From Middle High German kunde, from Old High German cundo, from Proto-West Germanic *kunþō. Cognate with Old English cūþa and Middle Dutch konde (“acquaintance, friend”).
From Middle High German münze, from Old High German muniz, munizza, from Proto-West Germanic *munit.

From Middle High German pfunt, phunt, from Old High German pfunt, phunt, from Proto-West Germanic *pund, from Proto-Germanic *pundą, a borrowing from Latin pondō (“by weight”, adverb) or Latin pondus (“weight”, noun).
Borrowed from French réclame. Cognate with English reclaim.

From Middle High German schīn, Old High German scīn, skīn (“shine, brightness, light, ray”), from Proto-West Germanic *skīn, from Proto-Germanic *skīną. Cognate with Old Norse skína, Old Saxon scīnan, Old English sċīn (“phantom, ghost”), Dutch schijn, English shine, Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌴𐌹𐌽𐌰𐌽 (skeinan).[1]
Back-formation from stellen, verb.

Compound of Telefon (“telephone”) +‎ Zelle (“cell”).
From Latin terminus (“boundary, limit, end”).

Originally “cupboard, safe for the cash box”. From Low Franconian and West Central German dialects (attested early 16th century), probably through Middle Dutch teke (compare dated modern Dutch teek), from Latin thēca, from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē). The word was introduced into modern standard German in the 19th century and remains more common in western Germany than elsewhere.
From Middle High German trincgelt. Equivalent to trinken (“to drink”) +‎ Geld (“money”), meaning an extra to buy drinks with.
From Middle High German underschrīben, originally with separable prefix. Synchronically analyzable as unter- (“under”) +‎ schreiben (“write”). Calque of Latin subscrībere.
vocabList.usage:
Unterschreiben Sie bitte auf der punktierten Linie.
Please sign on the dotted line.

vocabList.etym: Derived from the verb unterschreiben (“to underwrite, sign”), equivalent to unter- +‎ Schrift, literally “underwrit”. Cognate with Hunsrik Unnerschrift, German Low German Unnerschrift (“signature”).
From Middle High German verdienen, from Old High German firdionōn, firthiniōn. Equivalent to ver- +‎ dienen, calque of Latin deservio.
vor- +‎ Wahl

From Middle High German zuokunft, zuokumft, zuokumpft, from Old High German zuokumft. See zukommen. Cognate with Middle Low German tôkumpst (whence German Low German Tokumst, Tokunft, Tokummst), Dutch toekomst, Saterland Frisian Toukumst.
From Arbeit +‎ -s- +‎ -los.
Early 16th century, borrowed from Middle French armee. Compare Modern French armée, English army.
From Middle High German arzet, arzāt, from Old High German arzat, from Latin archīāter (“physician”), from Ancient Greek ἀρχίατρος (arkhíatros), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + ἰατρός (iatrós).
Borrowed from English babysit.
From Brief +‎ tragen +‎ -er resp. Brief +‎ Träger.
Unadapted borrowing from French chef (“head, boss”). Compare English chief and Spanish jefe.
From Feuer (“fire”) +‎ Wehr (“defense”).
Feuerwehr (“fire brigade”) +‎ Mann (“man”)
From Geschäft (“business”) +‎ -s- +‎ Mann (“man”).
From handeln +‎ -er.
Borrowed from French ingénieur.

From Middle High German kelnære, from Old High German kelnere, from Medieval Latin cellenarius (“(wine) cellar administrator”), from Late Latin cellārium (“pantry”), with influence of Keller, itself ultimately from the same Latin source.
An originally Central and Low German word, derived from Middle Low German klampe (“clamp”).
From Middle High German koch, from Old High German choch, from Proto-West Germanic *kok (“a cook”).
Kunst (“art”) +‎ -ler; cognate with Hunsrik Kinstler, Luxembourgish Kënschtler
From Middle High German laden, lade (“board; plank; shutter; shop”), from Old High German *lado, from Proto-Germanic *laþô. Probably akin to German Latte, English lath. Unrelated to Lade.
From Middle High German leiter(e), from Old High German (h)leitara, from Proto-Germanic *hlaidrijō.
From Middle High German mūrære, from Old High German mūrāri. By surface analysis, Mauer (“wall”) +‎ -er.

programmieren (“to program”) +‎ -er (“-er”)

From Arbeit (“work”) + geben (“to give”).
From Arbeit (“work”) +‎ -s- +‎ Amt (“office”).
From arbeitslos (“unemployed”) +‎ -igkeit.
From Middle High German bewerben, from Old High German biwerban, from Proto-West Germanic *bihwerban. Equivalent to be- +‎ werben.
From Bewerbung +‎ -s- +‎ Gespräch.
From French Jura
From Leben +‎ -s- +‎ Lauf, a calque of Latin curriculum vītae. Similar to Dutch levensloop.
From Middle High German leisten, from Old High German leisten, from Proto-West Germanic *laistijan. Cognate with English last.
vocabList.usage:
Wir haben gute Arbeit geleistet.
We did a good job.

vocabList.etym: Borrowed from Dutch matroos, from Middle French matelots, from Old French matenot (“sailor, bunkmate”), most likely from Middle Dutch mattenoot (“bunk fellow”) or less likely Old Norse mǫtunautr (“food companion”).
Borrowed from French pension, ultimately from Latin pēnsiō, pēnsiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin personale.

vocabList.definition: a receipt,  an undersigned document issued to someone to enable him with evidence that his party has performed upon an obligation
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German quittunge, quitunge, formed quiten +‎ -unge, the former verb deadjectival from what is now quitt.
Borrowed from Old French rente, from Early Medieval Latin rendita.
From Universität +‎ -s- +‎ Abschluss.
vor- +‎ haben
vocabList.usage:
Ich weiß, was du vorhast.
I know what you're planning.

vocabList.etym:
From Middle High German vürslac. By surface analysis, deverbal from  vorschlagen or vor- +‎ Schlag.
Compare the noun Vorschlagen, gerund of the verb vorschlagen, and Luxembourgish Virschlag.
From Vorstellung +‎ -s- +‎ Gespräch
pellō +‎ -sus (action noun)

vocabList.definition: long, a long while, a while, for long, for a long time
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *djowe, from Proto-Indo-European *dyéw(i) (“during the day”), locative case of *dyḗws, with d possibly imported from diēs. Cognate with Old Armenian տիւ (tiw), Sanskrit दिवा (divā, “by day”).
Perfect passive participle of dēcernō.
From summa +‎ -ātim.

vocabList.definition: to exhibit, make public, show clearly
vocabList.etym: From manifestus (“apparent, palpable, manifest”) +‎ -ō.
vocabList.usage:
397 CE – 401 CE, Aurelius Augustinus Hipponensis, Confessiones 7.12.18:
Et manifestatum est mihi quoniam bona sunt quae corrumpuntur.
And it was made clear to me that all things are good even if they are corrupted.

vocabList.etym: By surface analysis, Feuer (“fire”) +‎ Zeug (“stuff”) / erzeugen (“to create”). Historically, from Middle High German viurziuc.
From Middle High German müede, muode, from Old High German muodi, from Proto-West Germanic *mōþī. Cognate to Dutch moe.
From Middle High German durfen, dürfen, from Old High German durfan, from Proto-West Germanic *þurban, cognate with Ancient Greek τέρπω (térpō, “I delight, please”), English tharf.

From Middle High German zimber, from Old High German zimbar, from Proto-West Germanic *timr, from Proto-Germanic *timrą, from Proto-Indo-European *dem- (“build, house”) (see Proto-Indo-European *dṓm). Cognate with English timber and Dutch timmer (“building; construction; room”).
From fūcus (“seaweed, orchil, pretense”) +‎ -ō.

From Proto-Italic *weneznom (“lust, desire”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive, wish, love”). See also Sanskrit वनति (vanati, “gain, wish, erotic lust”), Latin Venus, veneror, venia, vēnor and English wish.

vocabList.definition: to tell, to narrate, to recount
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German erzellen, from Old High German irzellen. Equivalent to er- +‎ zählen.
vocabList.usage:
Erzähl mir ein Märchen.
Tell me a fairytale.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German īlen, from Old High German īlen, from Proto-West Germanic *īlijan (“to make haste, hasten”).
vocabList.usage: jemandem zu Hilfe eilen ― to rush to someone's aid

vocabList.definition: to cross while driving, to traverse, to drive through
vocabList.etym: durch- +‎ führen.
vocabList.usage:
Die Inspektorin führte ihre Untersuchung im Januar durch.
The inspector conducted her investigation in January.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German par, from Old High German par, from Latin pār.
From Middle High German strëben, from Old High German strëbēn, from Proto-West Germanic *stribēn, from Proto-Germanic *stribāną.
vocabList.usage:
Sie strebte danach, ihr Examen möglichst erfolgreich zu bestehen.
She strove to pass her exam as successfully as possible.

vocabList.definition: to hide, conceal, keep secret, cover, suppress, sheathe
vocabList.etym: From ab- (“away”) +‎ -dō (“put”).
vocabList.usage:
27 BCE – 25 BCE, Titus Livius, Ab Urbe Condita 7.13:
[…] ; quamquam de gloria vix dicere ausim, si nos et hostes haud secus quam feminas abditos intra vallum omnibus contumeliis eludunt, et […]
[…] ; though I had as lief not to speak of glory, when the enemy jeers us with much abuse as if women concealing behind walls, and […]

vocabList.etym: From octō (“eight”) + centum (“hundred”). Influenced by septingentī.
Perfect active participle of cōnspicor (“see, observe, notice”).
Of Celtic origin, from Gaulish asseda, from Proto-Celtic *eks-dī-sedo-, the root of which is from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“sit”); cognate with Old Breton assedam.

vocabList.definition: to crowd or press together, compress
vocabList.etym: According to De Vaan, a denominative from an adjective *stīpos (“erect, rigid”), itself from Proto-Indo-European *stéyp-os, which may also be attested in Proto-Germanic *stīfaz (“stiff”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steyp- (“to be stiff, erect”).
From dis- (“assunder, apart, utterly”) +‎ tendō (“stretch”).
From mel (“honey”).
From in- +‎ (g)nāvus.
From praesaepiō (“barricade, fence in”).

vocabList.definition: to emit a scent or odor
vocabList.etym: From red- +‎ oleō (“smell”).
From Proto-Italic *farstjagjom, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰérstis, from *bʰers- (“tip”). Compare Middle Irish brostaim (“I goad, spur”), English bristle, Polish barszcz (“hogweed”).
Stern +‎ Stunde
Waschbrett (“washboard”) +‎ Bauch (“belly”)
From Rabe (“raven”) +‎ -n- +‎ Mutter (“mother”).

From earlier eira (Plautus), from Proto-Italic *eizā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eys- (compare Ancient Greek οἶστρος (oîstros), Lithuanian aistrà (“violent passion”), Avestan 𐬀𐬉𐬴𐬨𐬀 (aēṣ̌ma, “anger”)).
Borrowed from Middle Low German swōl, swūl (“sultry, hot and humid”) (17th century), adopted into Standard German as schwül in the 18th century, ultimately from the root of schwelen (“to smoulder”).
Trotz +‎ -en

dem Sturm trotzen
to brave the storm

vocabList.etym: 16th century, from be- +‎ fördern. Compare German Low German beföddern, befördern (from Middle Low German bevȫrderen), Dutch bevorderen. Compare also Middle High German gefordern, from Old High German gifordarōn.
er- +‎ kunden, from kund.

vocabList.definition: cow, bull, ox, head of cattle
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German rint, from Old High German rind, hrind, from Proto-West Germanic *hrinþ, from Proto-Germanic *hrinþaz. Cognate with Middle Dutch rint. Also related with modern Dutch rund (from Middle Dutch runt), English rother.
Gipfel +‎ -en.
Perfect passive participle of summittō.
Perfect passive participle of collocō.
From per- +‎ exig(ō) (“to demand”) +‎ -uus.
Perfect passive participle of intermittō.
From spatium +‎ -ō. Compare spatior.
From per- +‎ rumpō.

From Middle High German enphencnisse, from Old High German intfangnissa. Equivalent to empfangen +‎ -nis. Originally synonymous with Empfang. In modern German, the two nouns have come to be distinguished semantically.

vocabList.definition: soft, smooth, gentle, moderate, mild, calm
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *lēnis (“soft, mild”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁- (“lazy, slow; soft”).[1]

May be from Proto-Indo-European *ksew-, extended from *kes- (“to scratch, itch”). Cognates with novācula, sentis, Ancient Greek ξέω (xéō), ξύω (xúō, “to scrape”), ξαίνω (xaínō), Old English besnyþian.
From caecus +‎ -ō.
From Proto-Italic *karpō, from Proto-Indo-European *kerp-.
vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Metamorphoses 9.380–381:
Stāgna tamen timeat, nec carpat ab arbore flōrēs,et fruticēs omnēs corpus putet esse deārum.
May he fear the ponds, and may he not pick flowers from the trees,
and may he think all trees to be bodies of goddesses.

vocabList.definition: to be favorable, to be well disposed or inclined towards, to favor, promote, befriend, countenance, protect
vocabList.etym: Uncertain.
vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Fasti 6.249–250:
Vesta, favē! tibi nunc operāta resolvimus ōra,ad tua sī nōbīs sacra venīre licet.
Vesta, be favorable! Devoted to you, we now unbind our lips; [that is], if we are permitted to come to your sacrifices.
(See Vesta (mythology); Vestalia.)

8 CE, Ovidius, Fasti 1.204:
pāscēbatque suās ipse senātor ovēs
and the senator himself was tending his own sheep

vocabList.etym: From quī +‎ -cumque; quīcunque is a later development reflecting the assimilated pronunciation.

vocabList.definition: to touch on all sides, take hold of, come into contact with
vocabList.etym: From con- (“together”) +‎ tangō (“touch”).
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 2.238–239:
“[...] Puerī circum innūptaeque puellaesacra canunt, fūnemque manū contingere gaudent.”
“Around [the wooden horse], boys and unwedded girls chant hymns, and delight to touch a rope by hand.”
(The Trojans pull the wooden horse using heavy ropes while their children celebrate it as a sacred effigy.)

vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *kʷoizā, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys- (“to heed”).
Chiefly from haplology of Middle High German ērer, from Old High German ēriro, from Proto-Germanic *airizô. Compare Dutch eerder.

From Middle High German verlāzen, Old High German firlāzan, from Proto-West Germanic *fralātan, from Proto-Germanic *fralētaną. Cognate with Dutch verlaten, archaic and/or dialectal English forlet, and Middle Low German vorlaten. Equivalent to ver- (“for-”) +‎ lassen (“let, leave”).
vocabList.usage:
Die Ratten verlassen das sinkende Schiff.
The rats are abandoning the sinking ship.

vocabList.etym: From French graduer.
genau +‎ -igkeit

From Middle High German schōne (“beautifully; appropriately; completely”), from Old High German scōno (“beautifully”), adverb of scōni, whence German schön (“beautiful”). [1] For sense development from "beautiful" to "indeed, surely; already" compare English pretty.
gleich + Gewicht. Compare Norwegian Bokmål likevekt, Norwegian Nynorsk likevekt, Danish ligevægt.
Borrowed from French baser.
From Middle High German tapfer, from Old High German tapfar, from Proto-Germanic *dapraz.
From Middle High German pūse, borrowed from Middle French pause (14st), from Latin pausa.
fahren +‎ Preis

vocabList.usage:
106 BCE – 43 BCE, Cicero, Cato Maior de Senectute 12.42:
Quōrsus hoc? Ut intellegerētis, sī voluptātem aspernārī ratiōne et sapientiā nōn possēmus, magnam habendam esse senectūtī grātiam, quae efficeret: ut id nōn libēret, quod nōn opertēret.
To what [end] is this [discussion]? It is so that you might understand, that if we are unable to reject [the lure of] sensual pleasure through reason and wisdom, we must owe a great [debt of] gratitude to old age, for what it will bring about: that [sensual pleasure] will no [longer] be pleasing [to us], due to its being improper [to advanced age].(Nota bene: Be sure not to confuse libet, libēre, “to please,” with līberō, līberāre, “to set free.”)

If they chose to make a second trial, he was ready to encounter them again; but if they chose to enjoy peace, it was unfair to refuse the tribute, which of their own free-will they had paid up to that time.

412 CE – 426 CE, Aurelius Augustinus Hipponensis, De civitate Dei 12.1:
Sīcut ergō, cum vitium oculōrum dīcitur caecitās, id ostenditur, quod ad nātūram oculōrum pertinet vīsus; et cum vitium aurium dīcitur surditās, ad eārum nātūram pertinēre dēmōnstrātur audītus: ita, cum vitium creātūrae angelicae dīcitur, quō nōn adhaeret Deō, hinc apertissimē dēclārātur, eius nātūrae ut Deō adhaereat convenīre.
As, then, when we say that blindness is a defect of the eyes, we prove that sight belongs to the nature of the eyes; and when we say that deafness is a defect of the ears, hearing is thereby proved to belong to their nature;—so, when we say that it is a fault of the angelic creature that it does not cleave to God, we hereby most plainly declare that it pertained to its nature to cleave to God.

vocabList.etym: From incolō (“to inhabit, dwell in”) +‎ -a (agent noun), from in + colō (“dwell, inhabit”).
From properus (“hasty”) +‎ -ē (adverbial ending).
From in- +‎ pendeō (“to be suspended, hang”).
vocabList.usage:
c. 42 BCE, Gaius Sallustius Crispus, Bellum Catilinae 28.2–3:
Curius ubi intellegit, quantum periculum consuli inpendeat, propere per Fulviam Ciceroni dolum, qui parabatur, enuntiat. Ita illi ianua prohibiti tantum facinus frustra susceperant.
When Curius learnt how great the danger which threatened the consul was, he hastily reported to Cicero, through Fulvia, the trap which was being prepared. When the men were thus turned away from the door, they had undertaken such a great crime in vain.

vocabList.definition: deception, deceit, fraud, guile, treachery, trickery
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Indo-European *dolh₁os. Cognate to Oscan [script needed] (dolom, “intention, ruse”) and Ancient Greek δόλος (dólos),[1] but the Italic terms may be borrowings from the latter.
From ē- +‎ nūntiō
Perhaps originally from the ablative singular of *frūstra, rebracketed from frūstrum, or from a rebracketed adverbial accusative of the same; by surface analysis, fraus (“harm, injury”) +‎ -tra.[1]

vocabList.definition: to consult, seek counsel from, take counsel from
vocabList.usage:
27 BCE – 25 BCE, Titus Livius, Ab Urbe Condita 26.1:
Cn. Fuluius Centumalus P. Sulpicius Galba consules cum idibus Martiis magistratum inissent, senatu in Capitolium uocato, de re publica, de administratione belli, de prouinciis exercitibusque patres consuluerunt.
When the consuls Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus and Publius Sulpicius Galba took up the magistracy on the Ides of March, they summoned the senate to the Capitoline Hill and consulted the senators on issues regarding the state, the handling of the war, the provinces and the armies.

vocabList.definition: any double-doored entrance (e.g. a domestic door or a gate to a temple or city)
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂- (“to go, go in, travel”). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic ꙗдо (jado, “to travel”) and Sanskrit यान (yāna, “path”).

vocabList.definition: to dig (thoroughly), dig up or over, dig round about, turn over (of land), prepare by digging
vocabList.etym: From con- (“with, together”) +‎ fodiō (“dig; thrust, stab”).
From im- (“without, not”) + paratus (“prepared, ready”).

vocabList.definition: public green area, site, park, garden
vocabList.etym: From anlegen (“to attach, apply, build, create, ...”).
From handeln, later specialized to its current meaning.
From herein- +‎ lassen.

vocabList.definition: A league in which clubs from the entire country participate.
vocabList.etym: From Bund (“federation”) +‎ -es- +‎ Liga (“league”), thus “federal league”, in the sense of “nationwide league”.
From Middle High German gelegenheit. By surface analysis, gelegen +‎ -heit.
Stadt +‎ -isch

From Middle High German stōzen, from Old High German stōzan, from Proto-West Germanic *stautan, from Proto-Germanic *stautaną, from Proto-Indo-European *stówd-e-ti, an o-grade intensive formation from *(s)tewd- (“to hit, push”).

vocabList.definition:
to put down, to set down
 to place, to leave

 to put away

 to park, to leave

to put away from
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German abestellen. Equivalent to ab- +‎ stellen.
From Middle High German vorvar, from vorvaren (“to go ahead, to precede”).[1]
aus- +‎ wandern
From erwarten +‎ -ung.
einwandern +‎ -er
From minder +‎ -heit.

vocabList.definition: to pursue, to follow, to hunt
vocabList.etym: ver- +‎ folgen. A calque of Latin persequor or its Romance descendants.

From Middle Low German knap, probably related to Old Norse hneppr (“button”) and hneppa (“pinch”), all from Proto-Germanic *knappô, *knappa-, which is perhaps related to Proto-West Germanic *knappō (“knob, boy”) or Proto-Germanic *knuppaz (“lump, clod”), though the semantic gaps are non-trivial.[1] Cognate with Dutch knap, but of uncertain ultimate origin. Also compare Danish næppe (“hardly at all”).[2]

From Middle High German vellic, vellec, from Old High German fellīg (“staggering, dilapidated, inclined to fall, obliged to yield or pay”), equivalent to Fall +‎ -ig. Cognate with Middle Low German vellich, Middle Dutch vellich, vallich.
From Middle High German gesamt, gesament, from Old High German gisamanōt, from samanōn (“to gather, collect”), from Proto-West Germanic *samnōn, from Proto-Germanic *samnōną (“to bring together”).
Deverbal from aufnehmen.
From kurz + Frist.
Inherited from Middle High German ūfvüeren. By surface analysis, auf- +‎ führen.
Early 19th century, from ur- +‎ Wald.
Serie +‎ Mörder

From Middle High German dræjen, dræhen, from Old High German drāen (akin to Old Saxon thrāian), from Proto-West Germanic *þrāan, from Proto-Germanic *þrēaną. Cognate with Bavarian drahn, Dutch draaien and English throw.
vocabList.usage:
Dreh den Spiegel etwas nach links!
Turn the mirror a little to the left!

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German burse, from Old High German bursa, from Late Latin bursa.
innerlich +‎ ver- -en
From Middle High German bestān, bestēn, from Old High German bistān, from Proto-Germanic *bistandaną, *bistāną. Equivalent to be- +‎ stehen (“to stand, be on one's feet”).
vocabList.usage:
Er hat die Prüfung bestanden.
He has passed the exam.

vocabList.definition: to bear, to stand, to endure, to take, to suffer, to tolerate, to handle
vocabList.etym: er- +‎ tragen
vocabList.usage:
Ich kann die neue Freundin von meinem Bruder nicht ertragen.
I can’t stand my brother’s new girlfriend.

vocabList.etym: From Medieval Latin rabiatus.

vocabList.definition: at the top of one's voice
vocabList.etym: Borrowed from German Low German luudhals. By surface analysis, laut (“loud”) +‎ Hals (“neck; throat”).
From Bavarian goschert
Uncertain. Kluge and Pfeifer put forward a possible relation to greinen (“to cry, whine”).
From Middle High German stetes, from Proto-Germanic *stēdi-; cognate with Dutch steeds. Synchronically analyzed as an adverbial formation  stet (“steady, constant”) +‎ -s; see there for more.
Obsolete perfect passive participle of erheben.

From Middle High German nüehtern, from Old High German nuohtarn, nuohturn, from Latin nocturnus (“nocturnal”). The word was probably originally used among monks in monasteries, with sense development "nocturnal" > "of dawn (the edge of night and day)" > "not having consumed any sustenance yet" > "sober". Compare Danish nøgtern, Hunsrik nichter, English nocturnal.

From Middle High German drücken, from Old High German drucchen, from Proto-West Germanic *þrukkijan. Doublet of drucken (“to print”), which was originally a southern variant, later standardized in a specialized sense.
Fläche +‎ deckend
From an- +‎ werben.
vocabList.usage:
Er kündigte zwei Wochen nachdem er angeworben wurde.
He quit two week after he was recruited.

vocabList.etym: einführen +‎ -ung
From Middle High German verslahen, from Old High German firslahan, from Proto-West Germanic *fraslahan. By surface analysis, ver- +‎ schlagen. Cognate with Old English forslēan and Dutch verslaan.
From Middle High German belegen, from Old High German bileggen. By surface analysis, be- +‎ legen. Cognate with English belay.
einschränken +‎ -ung
From Middle High German iedoch, idoch, ēdoch, from Old High German iodoh, iothoh. Equivalent to je +‎ doch. Compare Dutch edoch.
Grund +‎ Lage

First attested in the 15th century as undersuochen. This form suggests it already existed in Middle High German. The existence of an unattested Old High German form *untarsuohhen is probable, compare Old Saxon undarsōkian (whence Low German ünnersöken), Old Dutch undersuoken (whence Dutch onderzoeken), and Old English undersecan (whence English underseek), all from Proto-West Germanic *undersōkijan (literally “to search under or between”). Equivalent to unter- +‎ suchen.
From Middle High German ervorschen, from Old High German irforskōn. Equivalent to er- +‎ forschen.
15th century, from Latin chīrūrgus, from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós).

From Sack (“sack”), which was used in the 19th century to refer to an unwaisted jacket; compare English sack coat. This name was due to the loose fitting, possibly reinforced by the idea of it being unpretentious and humble (compare Sack und Asche, English sackcloth). The later alteration of the form on the basis of Italian sacco was intended to have the opposite effect, namely to make it sound fashionable.
From Middle High German verstecken, from Old High German firstekken. Equivalent to ver- +‎ stecken. Cognate with Dutch versteken (“to hide”).
vocabList.usage:
Der Dieb versteckte die Gegenstände vor der Polizei.
The thief hid the items from the police.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German zwīvel, from Old High German zwīfal, from Proto-West Germanic *twīfl n, related to root of zwei. Doublet of Doppel.

From Middle Low German gēgenēre, which is derived from a verb gēgenen (“to face, encounter”). Compare German begegnen. Ultimately pertaining to gegen (“against”). Cognate to Dutch jegener (“opponent”). Compare English gainer.
From Middle High German weren, from Old High German werien, from Proto-West Germanic *warjan, from Proto-Germanic *warjaną.
vocabList.usage: sich gegen Vorwürfe wehren ― to defend oneself against accusations

vocabList.etym:
From Middle High German biderbe (also bederbe and shortened bider), from Old High German biderbi, piderpi, pidarpi, cognate with Bedarf.
The derogatory sense arises in the 19th century. The compound Biedermann in origin means "brave, honest or capable man", but today has a meaning of "boring person, petty bourgeios".
Back-formation from wahnsinnig. Not related to Wahn.
From ewig +‎ -keit.

vocabList.definition: to acknowledge, to recognize, to accept
vocabList.etym: an- +‎ erkennen
vocabList.usage:
Obwohl Sie von der Sache nicht so viel verstehen, müssen wir Ihre Leistung anerkennen.
Even though you aren't very knowledgeable about the subject, we must acknowledge your effort.

vocabList.etym: an- +‎ nehmen
vocabList.usage:
Mein Fehler. Ich nahm an, sie sei ledig.
My mistake. I assumed she was single.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German antrac.
From Middle High German armuot, armuote, from Old High German armuoti, from Proto-West Germanic *armōdī (“poverty”).[1][2]
Derived from zustehen, equivalent to zu- +‎ Stand.
Aufenthalt +‎ -s- +‎ Erlaubnis
Dauer +‎ -haft
From Middle High German vürhten, from Old High German furihtan. Synchronically analyzed as Furcht +‎ -en.
From Middle High German sulich, from Old High German sulīh, from Proto-Germanic *swalīkaz.
um- +‎ wandeln
From waschen +‎ Salon.
From the verb ablaufen.

From Middle High German brūwen, briuwen, from Old High German briuwan. The form shows the Central German development of Middle High German -iuw- → -ūw-, which is only sporadically reflected in the modern standard language (compare kauen).
From Gewächs +‎ Haus.
From Middle High German brīe, brī, from Old High German brīo, from Proto-West Germanic *brīw. Cognate with Yiddish ברײַ (bray).
Antrag +‎ Steller
From vergangen +‎ -heit.
From bescheiden (“to announce a decision”).

From Middle High German betriegen, from Old High German bitriogan, from Proto-West Germanic *bidreugan. Equivalent to be- +‎ trügen. The modern -ü- in this verb chiefly follows the development in the rhyming word lügen (“to lie”). It was reinforced by the noun Betrug and by the 2nd and 3rd person-singular forms (as in lügen itself, which compare).
vocabList.usage:
Sie betrügt dich mit ihrer falschen Fürsorge.
She deceives you with her disingenuous care for you.

vocabList.etym: heim- +‎ kehren
From Heirat (“marriage”) +‎ -s- +‎ Antrag (“application”).
ohne 'without' + hin 'thither, there'

From Middle High German welle, from Old High German wella, from Proto-West Germanic *wallijā, from Proto-Germanic *wallijǭ (“wave, swirl”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn, coil”). Cognate to Old English wealca (“billow”), Albanian valë (“wave”).

From Middle High German gewalt, from Old High German giwalt, from Proto-West Germanic *gawald, from Proto-Germanic *gawaldą, from *ga- +‎ *waldą (“power, authority”). Cognate with Yiddish געוואַלד (gevald), Dutch geweld, English wald.
From Middle High German nu, nū, nuo with a secondary final -n, already occasionally in Middle High German nuon, from Old High German nu, from Proto-West Germanic *nū.
From Middle High German entverren. Analysable as ent- +‎ fern + -en.
vocabList.usage:
Der Hausmeister entfernt die Graffitis von der Wand.
The caretaker is removing the graffiti from the wall.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German vernihten, from nihten, from niht. By surface analysis, ver- +‎ nicht +‎ -en.
From Frau +‎ -en- +‎ Stimme.

vocabList.definition: to stand out, to be noticeable
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German ūfvallen, ūffallen, equivalent to auf- +‎ fallen. Cognate with Middle Low German upvallen.
vocabList.usage:
Keine Sorge, der Pickel fällt nicht auf.
Don't worry, the pimple isn't noticeable.

vocabList.etym: From her +‎ vor.

vocabList.definition: to disappear, to vanish, to move out of view
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German verswinden, from Old High German firswintan, farswindan. Cognate with Middle Low German vorswinden, Dutch verzwinden. Equivalent to ver- +‎ schwinden.
vocabList.usage:
Die Sonne verschwindet hinter Wolken.
The sun is disappearing behind clouds.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German spannen, from Old High German spannan, from Proto-Germanic *spannaną.

vocabList.definition: for there to be a lack
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German vælen, velen, valen, from Old French faillir, from Latin fallō. Cognate with English fail.
vocabList.usage:
Der Suppe fehlt es an Geschmack.
The soup lacks flavor.

vocabList.etym: Borrowed from Latin fīliālis (“filial”) (DWDS), as branches of an organization are akin to "sons and daughters" of the organization.
From Middle High German bedürfen, bedurfen, from Old High German bidurfan (“need, require”). By surface analysis, be- +‎ dürfen.
vocabList.usage:
Wir bedürfen eines starken Mannes.
We need a strong man.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German getreide, contracted from getregede, from late Old High German gitregidi (“produce, income”), a collective derived from tragen (“to bear; to bear fruit”) (DWDS).
From Middle High German holz, from Old High German holz, from Proto-West Germanic *holt, from Proto-Germanic *hultą. Compare English holt (“thicket, copse; an otter's den”).
From ver +‎ sorgen.
Deverbal from beitragen (“contribute”).

From Middle High German geringe, from Old High German giringi, ringi (“low, plain, simple, light, easy”), from Proto-Germanic *ringwaz (“small, light, quick”), of uncertain origin, though possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wrengʷʰ- (“to squeeze, wring”) and cognate with Proto-Germanic *wringaną (“to squeeze, wring”), Ancient Greek ῥίμφα (rhímpha, “fast, quickly”). Cognate with Yiddish גרינג (gring, “light, easy”) (DWDS).

From Low German and Middle Low German bedarf, the present stem of bedörven (“to need”), from Old Saxon bi- + tharvōn (“to need, lack, want”). Morphologically identical to the present singular of Middle High German and German bedürfen.

vocabList.definition: to build, to construct, to erect
vocabList.etym: auf- +‎ bauen
From denken (“to think”) +‎ Mal (“symbol, sign”).
Borrowed from Italian soldato.

From Middle High German umbekomen (“to pass by, end, die”). Analysable as um- +‎ kommen. Cognate with Middle Dutch ommecomen (“to pass by, end, die”), whence modern Dutch omkomen. Compare also ums Leben kommen, and further umbringen, ums Leben bringen. Regarding the broader semantic use in both Middle High German and Middle Dutch, it is not certain that the short verbs are mere ellipses of the phrases with Leben, though they have without doubt been influenced by them.
er- +‎ weitern (“to extend, to expand”, obsolete, derived from the comparative of weit).
Univerbation of so +‎ wohl
un- +‎ eingeschränkt
From Middle High German vergenüegen (zufriedenstellen), derived from genug.
über- +‎ nehmen

From Middle High German enthalten, equivalent to ent- +‎ halten. Influenced by innehalten, einhalten (literally “to hold inside”). This is clearest in the sense “to contain”, compare Inhalt (“contents”); but it is possible even in the sense “to abstain”, compare mit etwas einhalten (“to stop”), sich einhalten (“to restrain oneself”). Cognate with Dutch onthouden (“to remember, withhold”) and inhouden (“to contain”), Middle Low German enthōlden, inhōlden.
vocabList.usage:
Diese Gerichte enthalten wenig Fett.
These dishes contain little fat.

vocabList.usage:
Worauf bezieht sich dieser Satz?
What does this sentence refer to?

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German wërken, from Old High German werkōn, werhōn, from Proto-Germanic *werkōną. Cognate with Old Saxon werkōn, Old Dutch wirkon.
From hören +‎ Buch, literally “hear book”.
From einstufen +‎ -ung.
erhalten +‎ -lich
From the verb verhalten (“to behave”).

Freizeit +‎ Beschäftigung
einstellen +‎ -ung
From gleichgültig +‎ -keit, since the second half of the 17th century.
Back-formation from ausgleichen.

vocabList.definition: to freak out, to snap, to panic [auxiliary sein]
vocabList.etym: From durch- +‎ drehen.

vocabList.definition: to avoid, bypass, to go around
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German umbegēn, umbegān, from Old High German umbigēn, umbigān, from Proto-West Germanic *umbigān, from Proto-Germanic *umbigāną. Equivalent to um- +‎ gehen.
vocabList.usage:
Sie wollten die Stadtmitte umgehen.
They wanted to avoid [going through] the middle of town.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German sorcveltic, sorgeveltic. By surface analysis, Sorgfalt +‎ -ig. Cognate with Dutch zorgvuldig.
From Middle High German ūfhalten. Equivalent to auf- +‎ halten. Cognates include Dutch ophouden and English uphold.
From Middle High German undersagen, from Old High German untarsagēn. Equivalent to unter- +‎ sagen.

vocabList.definition: to determine, to ascertain, to establish, to find, to see
vocabList.etym: fest- +‎ stellen
vocabList.usage:
Ich werde nun feststellen, wie gut das Gerät funktioniert.
I will now determine how well the device works.

vocabList.etym: Analysable as einschließen +‎ -lich.
Ausnahme +‎ Fall
From Middle High German diupstāle, compound of diep (“thief”) (modern Dieb) and stāle, deverbal noun from stëln (“to steal”) (modern stehlen), from Old High German stëlan.

From Middle High German vorsehen, from Old High German forasehan, from Proto-West Germanic *forēsehwan. Equivalent to vor- +‎ sehen. Cognate with Dutch voorzien, English foresee (from Old English foresēon).
From auf- +‎ stellen.
Wert +‎ Sache
auf- +‎ bewahren
From Middle High German haftunge, from Old High German haftunga. By surface analysis, haften (“to be liable, to stick”) +‎ -ung (“-ing”).
From Middle High German verschieben, from Old High German firskioban. Equivalent to ver- +‎ schieben.

From Middle High German gebærde, from Old High German gibārida, gibāridī (“demeanor, behavior, character”), from Proto-Germanic *gabērijaną, *gabarjaną (“to conduct oneself, behave”); see the related *gaberaną (“to bear, beget”) for more. Cognate with dialectal German Bärde, German Low German Gebarr, Dutch gebaarde, Middle English bærde, beard, beorde (“conduct, bearing”).

vocabList.definition: to fill with enthusiasm, to enthuse, to thrill

verhalten +‎ -nis
verzeichnen +‎ -nis.
From Middle High German schrīten, from Old High German skrītan, from Proto-West Germanic *skrīþan (“to step; stride”).
ob- +‎ Acht

163 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Heauton Timorumenos 1.77:
Homō sum, hūmānī nihil ā mē aliēnum putō.
I am a human, I consider nothing that is human alien to me.

vocabList.definition: time free from activity: leisure, free time
vocabList.etym: Uncertain;[1] perhaps from Proto-Italic *autiom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewtyom (“forlorn, deserted”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew (“off, away from”).
From ante- +‎ pōnō.
Univerbation of et (“and, also”) +‎ iam (“now, already”).
Present active participle of surgō (“[I] get up, arise”).

From Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁ro- (“derelict”), from the root *ǵʰeh₁- (“to leave behind, abandon”). Cognate with Ancient Greek χήρα (khḗra, “widow”). (This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium. Particularly: “-ēd-?”)
From the root of celer, from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to drive, force to move quickly”).

vocabList.definition:
(of textures or forms) thin, slender, slim, lank; especially:


(with anima or umbra) synonym of mānēs, the manes[4]
vocabList.etym: Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *ténh₂us (“thin”).[1][2][3] Original u-stem adjectives are regularly extended into i-stem ones in Latin, compare gravis, brevis, dulcis, etc.
From ex- (“out of”) +‎ vānēscō (“disappear”).
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 4.276–278:
[...] Tālī Cyllēnius ōre locūtusmortālis vīsus mediō sermōne relīquit,
et procul in tenuem ex oculīs ēvānuit auram.
Having uttered such [words] from his lips, the Cyllenian [god] – [still] in the midst of speaking – abandoned mortal visibility, and from before the eyes [of Aeneas, Mercury] vanished into thin air.
(Mercury had been born on Mount Cyllene; his divine apparition appears suddenly, rebukes Aeneas, and disappears abruptly.)

vocabList.definition: to lose one's speech, become dumb
vocabList.etym: From ob- +‎ mūtus +‎ -ēscō.
From ā- (prefix denoting absence) +‎ mēns (“mind, reason”).

vocabList.definition: looked at, beheld, having been looked at
vocabList.etym: Perfect passive participle of aspiciō (“behold, see; catch sight of”).

vocabList.etym: From arrigō (“I set up, erect”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κόμη (kómē, “hair of the head”). For sense 2, compare crīniō (“to cover with leaves, or hair”).

vocabList.usage:
63 BCE, Cicero, Catiline Orations Oratio in Catilinam Prima in Senatu Habita.13:
Quod prīvātārum rērum dēdecus nōn haeret in fāmā?
What disgrace regarding [your] private affairs does not cling to [your] reputation?

vocabList.definition: (literal) the upper part of a throat; a throat, pharynx, gullet
vocabList.etym: Plural of faux, of unknown etymology.[1]

vocabList.usage:
27 BCE – 25 BCE, Titus Livius, Ab Urbe Condita 22.1.8–9:
Augēbant metum prōdigia ex plūribus simul locīs nūntiāta: […] et Praeneste ārdentēs lapidēs caelō cecidisse, […]
