to depart, go away, go off, exit


 to pass away

to retire from office

 to set
vocabList.usage:
c. 270 BCE – c. 201 BCE, Gnaeus Naevius, Bellum Punicum 5–7:
Ambōrum uxōrēsnoctū Troiād exībant capitibus opertīs,
flentēs ambae abeuntēs lacrimīs cum multīs.
The wives of both
were leaving Troy at night with covered heads,
both weeping while departing with many tears.

vocabList.etym: Perfect passive participle of attonō.
Perfect passive participle of moneō (“warn, remind”).

vocabList.definition: to speak to, address, accost, implore

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German swermen (“to swarm”), from Old High German swermen (“to swarm”), derived from swarm (“swarm of bees”), whence modern German Schwarm (“swarm; flock of birds”). The figurative senses developed in Early Modern German via “to deviate from the established dogma or school of thought”.
vocabList.usage:
Die Bienen schwärmen.
The bees swarm.

vocabList.etym: los- +‎ gehen; cognate with Hunsrik losgehn
From gestalt(en) (“to form, shape”) +‎ -ung.
From Middle High German esel, from Old High German esil, from late Proto-West Germanic *asil, which is borrowed from Late Latin asellus.
From Middle High German dringen, from Old High German dringan. Akin to drängen and Drang. Cognate with dialectal English thring and, more distantly, with English throng.
zutragen +‎ -lich.
From ankommen.

vocabList.definition: to put off, drive off, scare off
vocabList.etym: 20th century, from ver- +‎ graulen (“to be scared”, rare or regional). The latter is from earlier graueln, a variant of (also rare) gräueln, from Middle High German griuweln, grūweln, whence the noun Gräuel (“horror”). The form with -ūw- (modern -au-) probably shows the same Central German development as in brauen, kauen. The change from -eln to -len is unremarkable (in fact, many speakers merge these entirely).
Zusatz +‎ -lich
From Behinderter +‎ -n- +‎ feindlich.

From Middle High German gereht, from Old High German gireht, from Proto-Germanic *garehtaz, from *ga- + *rehtaz. Compare Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍄𐍃 (garaihts), Old English geriht, Dutch gerecht. Doublet of korrekt.
Zufall (“chance, coincidence, randomness”) +‎ -ig
From Middle High German almehlich. By surface analysis, all- +‎ mählich (“slow”), from Proto-Germanic *makaz; related to Old Norse makligr.

vocabList.definition: to scrutinize, to examine, to inspect, to look over, to eye
vocabList.etym: From the noun Muster.
Borrowed from French cravate. Compare English cravat and Spanish corbata. Doublet of Kroate (“Croat”).
From ab- +‎ driften.
From be- +‎ Mühe +‎ -en. Compare Dutch bemoeien.
16th century, alteration of earlier gewähnen, from Middle High German gewähenen, gewahen, from Old High German giwahanen, giwahan, from Proto-West Germanic *gawahwan (“to say, mention”).
vocabList.usage:
Ich glaube, er hat das mal erwähnt, aber ich weiß es nicht mehr genau.
I believe he mentioned it at some point, but I don’t quite know exactly.

vocabList.etym: 15th century, from Mahl (“meal”) +‎ Zeit (“time”). The word Mahl (a spelling variant of Mal) originally meant "mealtime", but was transferred to the meal itself. The compound then assumed the sense "mealtime", but ultimately underwent the same semantic development yet again. Compare Dutch maaltijd, English mealtide, Danish måltid, Icelandic máltíð.
vor- +‎ wiegen (“weigh”)
er- +‎ ganz
From Middle High German âventiure, borrowed from Old French aventure and like the latter originally feminine. The neuter gender is from Middle Low German.
From Riese (“giant”) +‎ -ig.
aus- +‎ steigen
rum- +‎ laufen
üben +‎ -lich
Reihe +‎ -n- +‎ Haus

From Middle High German rîter, rîtære, from Old High German rîtari. Not of Proto-Germanic age, but an OHG formation from the verb rītan "to ride" (Anglo-Saxon rîdere and Old Icelandic ríðari are loans from OHG).

vocabList.definition: sometimes, occasionally, from time to time, now and then
to give away, to throw away
vocabList.etym: ver- +‎ schenken

From bestecken (“to provide a thing by inserting it into another thing”), from be- +‎ stecken. Originally referred to a case into which a set of tools was put, later shifting to refer to the tools themselves.
From Middle High German ūȥschuȥ, synchronically analyzed as a deverbal from ausschießen (“to stand out”); see aus- (“out-”) +‎ schießen (“to shoot”) for more.

vocabList.definition: to accept, to promise to come
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German zuosagen. Equivalent to zu- +‎ sagen.
From Middle High German geslechte, from Old High German gislahti, a collective formation from slahta, from Proto-Germanic *slahtō, related to *slahaną (“to strike, hit”).[1]
From Middle High German gestaten, Old High German gistatōn,[1] related to Status (“status”); see there for more.[2]

From two separate but related verbs. From Middle High German verwīzen, Old High German firwīzan, from Proto-West Germanic *frawītan, from Proto-Germanic *frawītaną and the second verb from Middle High German verwīsen, from unattested Old High German *firwīsan, from Proto-West Germanic *frawīsijan, from Proto-Germanic *frawīsijaną.  By surface analysis, ver- +‎ weisen.
From Middle High German gelende, from Old High German gilenti; originally a collective noun equivalent to ge- +‎ Land.
From Middle High German erahten, from Old High German irahtōn. Equivalent to er- +‎ achten.
Literally, “to tell information”.

From Middle High German überwinden, from Old High German ubarwintan, an originally Upper German form besides Central German überwinnen, ubarwinnan. This latter is from Proto-West Germanic *ubarwinnan. Cognate with Dutch overwinnen, English overwin. Equivalent to über- + winnen (“to win”, simplex of gewinnen). The form with -nd- is analysable as über- +‎ winden (“to wind, twist”). It is uncertain whether this is a mere phonetic alteration of the nn-form or an actual derivation from the verb. For the latter possibility compare isolated Middle High German uses like anewinden (“to attack”), widerwinden (“to repulse”).
From Middle High German vūl, from Old High German fūl, from Proto-West Germanic *fūl, from Proto-Germanic *fūlaz, from Proto-Indo-European *puH-lo-s (“rotten, putrid”).
ein- +‎ sitzen
From ausschenken. Cognate with German Low German Utschank.
From Middle High German īngān, from Old High German ingān, from Proto-West Germanic *ingān. Analyzable as ein- +‎ gehen.
einig +‎ -keit
Middle High German loube, from Old High German louba, from Proto-West Germanic *laubijā.

vocabList.definition: to move in a quiet and inconspicuous manner, hence often slowly and/or ducked: to crawl, to sneak, to steal, to prowl, to creep, to slither
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German slīchen, from Old High German slīhhan. Compare English slink.
From Middle High German fūst, vūst, voust, from Old High German fūst.
From Middle High German stoc, from Old High German stoc, from Proto-West Germanic *stokk.

16th century, from Middle Low German hāst, from Middle Dutch haest, a borrowing from Old French haste, itself borrowed from Frankish *hai(f)st, from Proto-Germanic *haifstiz. See English haste for more.
From Middle High German erweichen, from Old High German irweihhēn. Equivalent to er- +‎ weich +‎ -en.
From Middle High German geschehen, geschēn, geschegen, from Old High German giskehan, scehan, from Proto-West Germanic *skehan (“to spring, come up, emerge, happen”). Cognate to Dutch geschieden.
vocabList.usage:
Wie konnte das nur geschehen?
How could that have happened?

vocabList.etym: From Middle Low German vet, from Old Saxon *fētid, from Proto-West Germanic *faitid. Doublet of feist. In the colloquial sense perhaps a calque of English phat via hip-hop culture.

From Middle High German vorekomen, forekomen, vurekomen, vürekomen, from Old High German furaqueman, furakweman, furiqueman, furikweman, from Proto-West Germanic *forakweman, from Proto-Germanic *furaikwemaną, equivalent to vor- +‎ kommen. Cognate with English forecome.
vocabList.usage:
Irene Adler ist eine der bemerkenswertesten Figuren in der Sherlock-Holmes-Serie, obwohl sie nur in einer einzigen Geschichte vorkommt.
Irene Adler is one of the most notable characters in the Sherlock Holmes series, despite appearing in only one story.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German rīhe, from Old High German *rīha, from Proto-West Germanic *rīhu, *rīgu, akin to Old High German riga. More at row.
From Middle High German schrien, from Old High German scrian, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *skrīan. Compare English scream.[1]
vocabList.usage:
Warum schreist du?
Why are you shouting?

vocabList.etym: stimmen +‎ -ung.
um +‎ kippen

vocabList.definition: to hiss, to spit, to growl
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German pfūchen, phūchen, from Old High German *pfūhhan (“to spit, puff”), from Proto-Germanic *pukaną (“to spit, puff”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew- (“to blow, swell”). The modern onset f- instead of pf- is from East Central German. Compare English puke.
From Middle High German vuoter, from Old High German fuotar (“fodder”). Compare Dutch voer, voeder, English fodder, Danish foder.
From Middle High German slāfen, from Old High German slāfan, from Proto-West Germanic *slāpan. Compare Low German slapen, Dutch slapen, English sleep.
vocabList.usage:
Ich habe diese Nacht gut geschlafen.
I slept well last night.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German kevje, from Old High German chevia, from Latin cavea (“cage”).

From Middle High German switzen, from Old High German swizzen, from Proto-West Germanic *swittjan, from Proto-Germanic *switjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *swidyéti (“to sweat”). Cognates (without gemination): Dutch zweten, Danish svede, English sweat.
From Middle High German vervaʒʒunge; by surface analysis, verfassen +‎ -ung.
From Land (“land, country, state”) +‎ -es- +‎ weit (“wide, far”).
er- +‎ läutern
fort- +‎ setzen
vocabList.usage:
Er setzt sein Studium in Berlin fort.
He is continuing his studies in Berlin.

vocabList.etym: be- +‎ stimmen
From Lager +‎ Feuer.

From Middle High German materaz, from Old French materas, from Arabic مَطْرَح (maṭraḥ). The modern German form was influenced by older Italian materazzo and/or Medieval Latin matracium, from the same Arabic source. (The Old French form may have been borrowed via Italian, too.)

vocabList.definition: a fine for a non-criminal act

vocabList.etym: verstopfen +‎ -ung
From Middle High German vermīden, from Old High German firmīdan. Equivalent to ver- +‎ meiden.
vocabList.usage:
Ich möchte vermeiden, denselben Fehler noch einmal zu machen.
I want to avoid making the same mistake again.

vocabList.definition: to gain insight into, comprehend, understand, recognize, realize, accept, convince oneself
vocabList.etym: ein- +‎ sehen
vocabList.usage:
Sieh es endlich ein! Das funktioniert so nicht.
Just accept it already! It doesn't work that way.

vocabList.etym: be- +‎ Seite +‎ -igen
From Middle High German pfīfen, from Old High German pfīfōn, from Proto-West Germanic *pīpōn (“to play a flute; to whistle”). Cognate with Hunsrik peife, Yiddish פֿײַפֿן (fayfn).
From an- +‎ pfeifen.
From Middle High German wol, wole, from Old High German wola (“well”), from Proto-Germanic *wela, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-. Compare Dutch wel, English well, Danish vel, Swedish väl.
From Middle High German tump, from Old High German tumb, from Proto-West Germanic *dumb, from Proto-Germanic *dumbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-.

vocabList.definition:
short saying, expression or dictum that is remembered or is meaningful in itself
stock phrase
slogan

sharp remark or repartee
 witticism, witty quote

proverb, saying

popular verse or short poem
particular kind of medieval lyric poem
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German spruch, from Old High German *spruh, from Proto-West Germanic *spruki (“saying”), related to the verb *sprekan (“to speak”). Cognate with Dutch spreuk, German Low German Spröök.
From lehren +‎ Gang.

The modern form is from German Low German pusten, from Middle Low German pûsten, borrowed during the 18th century and spread in this Low German form after that. Ultimately of imitative origin (lautmalend), though it is unclear if the word goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root.[1]

From Middle High German gegende, equivalent to gegen +‎ -de, which is an alteration of older gegenōte, from Old High German geginōti, probably after Old French contree, whence also English country. Compare Dutch jegenode.

From Middle High German geverte (“way, ride, walk, behaviour”), from Old High German *giferti (attested as giverte, etc.), from faran, whence modern fahren. The contemporary sense (17th c.) after cognate Middle Low German gevērde.

From Middle High German narre, from Old High German narro, further etymology unknown. Cognates include Yiddish נאַר (nar), Bavarian Noar, German Low German Narr, Dutch nar, West Frisian nar, Saterland Frisian Naar, Danish nar, Swedish narr.

vocabList.definition: to suit, to be apt for
vocabList.etym: From Middle High German eigenen, Old High German eiganen, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *aiginōną. Compare English own, Swedish ägna. Related to eigen.
vocabList.usage:
Ich eigne mich, aufgrund meiner schwach ausgeprägten Muskeln, nicht als Bauarbeiter.
Because of my weak muscles, I am not suitable as a construction worker.

vocabList.etym: Betrüger +‎ -isch
From Ekel +‎ -ig.
Dreck +‎ -ig

vocabList.definition: to speed, to whiz, to rush

groß +‎ Schreibung

From Middle High German helt (genitive heldes), from Old High German helid, from Proto-West Germanic *haliþ (“hero”).
From betreuen +‎ -ung.

vocabList.definition: to deal, to manage, to procure
vocabList.etym: From be- +‎ sorgen. Already Middle High German besorgen, Old High German bisorgēn.
vocabList.usage:
Seine Geschäfte wurden durch einen Stellvertreter besorgt.
His operations have been managed by a proxy.

c. 37 BCE – 30 BCE, Vergilius, Georgicon 2.519:
Venit hiems: teritur Sicyonia baca trapetis,glande sues laeti redeunt, dant arbuta silvae;
et varios ponit fetus autumnus et alte
mitis in apricis coquitur vindemia saxis.
  • Translation by James B. Greenough
    Winter is come: in olive-mills they bruise
    The Sicyonian berry; acorn-cheered
    The swine troop homeward; woods their arbutes yield;
    So, various fruit sheds Autumn, and high up
    On sunny rocks the mellowing vintage bakes.

vocabList.definition: time free from activity: leisure, free time
vocabList.etym: Uncertain;[1] perhaps from Proto-Italic *autiom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewtyom (“forlorn, deserted”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew (“off, away from”).

vocabList.usage:
39 CE – 65 CE, Lucanus, Bellum Civile 1.592–593:
Mox iubet et tōtam pavidīs ā cīvibus urbemambīrī […]
He soon orders the whole city by the terrified citizens
to be marched around […]

vocabList.etym: From exōrdior.

vocabList.definition: to take, take up, catch, assume, seize, claim, arrogate
vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Fasti 6.537–538:
parva mora est, caelum vātēs ac nūmina sūmitfitque suī tōtō pectore plēna deī
There is a brief pause; the prophetess assumes the divine powers of heaven, and in all her soul she is made full of her deity.
(The prophetess is Carmenta.)

vocabList.etym: From Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to drive”). Probably cognate with Ancient Greek κέλλω (kéllō), Ancient Greek κέλης (kélēs).

vocabList.definition: to this, to this, tothis subject/matter
vocabList.etym: Probably from the Old Latin locative hoi + -ce, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰe and Proto-Indo-European *ḱe (“here”), according to De Vaan (2008). Compare the mostly pre-Classical hōc (“to this place, for this reason”), which De Vaan says is from an instrumental case form.

vocabList.definition: to turn often, keep turning, handle, whirl about, turn over
vocabList.etym: Frequentative verb of vertō.
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 4.285–286:
Atque animum nunc hūc celerem nunc dīvidit illūc,in partīsque rapit variās perque omnia versat.
And his swift mind parses now this [idea], now that [one], picks among varied options, and thinks through them all.
(Aeneas considers how to end his relationship with Dido and leave Carthage.)

vocabList.etym: Present participle of furō.

vocabList.definition: if only!, I wish that!, oh that!, would that!, would to heaven!
vocabList.etym: From ut +‎ -nam.
From Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse, treasure”).

vocabList.definition: to conceal, hide, or dissimulate a state of mind
vocabList.etym: From dissimilis (“unlike”) +‎ -ō, with i changed to u before a thick l.
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 1.516:
Dissimulant et nūbe cavā speculantur amictī
They hide their feelings and, veiled by the hollow cloud, they watch.(Aeneas and Achates are hiding themselves within a divine cloud of mist, yet also concealing their emotions upon seeing fellow Trojans thought lost at sea.)

29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 4.305–6:
dissimulare etiam sperasti, perfide, tantum posse nefas tacitusque mea decedere terra?
Did you hope to even be able to conceal such a great wrong, treacherous man, and to leave my lands silently?

vocabList.definition: to withdraw, retire, depart, leave or go away
vocabList.etym: From dē- +‎ cēdō.
From mōlēs (“a pile, heap”).
vocabList.usage:

Nihil agis, nihil mōlīris, nihil cōgitās quod nōn ego nōn modo audiam sed etiam videam plānēque sentiam.
You do nothing, you plan nothing, you think of nothing which I not only do not hear, but which I do not see and know every particular of.

vocabList.definition: to sit down, to seat oneself, to settle

vocabList.etym: Substantivized neuter of arvus.

vocabList.etym: From alius (“other, another”) +‎ -ēnus.
Perfect passive participle of ignōscō. Compare Ancient Greek ἄγνωτος (ágnōtos).

manticam meam umerō exuō
I take off my sack from my shoulder

vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *preks, from Proto-Indo-European *preḱ- (“to request, ask”).
From quis +‎ -quam (“any”). Compare to quisque.
Present participle of lābor.
From auf- +‎ lösen. Compare Dutch oplossen.

From weg- +‎ schmeißen.

vocabList.usage:
Sie schmeißt mit Kastanien auf die anderen Kinder.
She’s throwing chestnuts at the other children.

vocabList.etym: From auf- +‎ munter.
Deverbal nominal form of unterhalten (“to maintain”).
From unterhalten +‎ -ung.
From Middle High German besliezen, from Old High German bisliozan, from Proto-West Germanic *bisleutan. Equivalent to be- +‎ schließen. Cognate with Dutch besluiten.
ver- +‎ schonen

I cannot spare you from the questioning; everyone at the presidium must give a personal statement.

ab- +‎ Stand. Cognate with English offstand (“offset, restitution”).

From Middle High German wirbel, from Old High German wirbil, from Proto-Germanic *hwirbilaz.

From Middle High German and Old High German banc, bank (“height”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz. Related to Old Saxon bank.
zustellen +‎ -er

From Middle High German stricken (“to tie, to knit”), from Old High German stricken (“to tie”), derived from the noun stric, whence modern Strick (“short rope for binding”). Compare Dutch strikken. Derivative of ausführen (“to execute”) +‎ -ung. Equivalent to Swedish utförande.

vocabList.definition:
to set upon, to attack suddenly 

 to assail, overwhelm

Einmal hat mich im Wald ein Wildschwein angefallen.
I was once attacked by a wild boar in the forest.

From Middle High German verlangen, equivalent to ver- +‎ langen. Cognate with English forlong.

The ice caused a few accidents.

Als sie am Bahnhof wartete, wurde sie ihres Schmucks beraubt.
As she waited at the train station, she was robbed of her jewelry.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German ātem, from Old High German ātum, from Proto-West Germanic *ādm, *āþm, from Proto-Germanic *ēþmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eh₁tmén-. Cognate with Dutch adem and Old English ǣþm. Doublet of Odem.

From Middle High German stum, from Old High German stum, from Proto-West Germanic *stumm. Cognate with Dutch stom.
schulen +‎ -ung First attested in the 19th century.

From Middle High German erreichen, from Old High German irreihhen, irreihhōn. Equivalent to er- +‎ reichen.

Onomatopoeic. Compare Dutch kletsen and English clash.

From Middle High German valden, valten, from Old High German faldan, faltan, from Proto-West Germanic *falþan. The irregular forms with -t- arose through early levelling of Grammatischer Wechsel, but remained rare in both Old and Middle High German. From Middle High German ginen, from Old High German ginēn, from Proto-West Germanic *gīnan.

From Middle High German lōnen, from Old High German lōnōn. By surface analysis, Lohn +‎ -en.
From Middle High German gedæhtnisse, gedæhtnüsse, from Old High German githehtnissī. By surface analysis, gedacht +‎ -nis. Cognate with Dutch gedachtenis.

From absichern +‎ -ung.

voraus- +‎ sagen

vocabList.etym: stellen +‎ Platz.

vocabList.etym: From sīc +‎ -ne (“focusing particle”).

From Proto-Italic *weneznom (“lust, desire”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive, wish, love”). See also Sanskrit वनति (vanati, “gain, wish, erotic lust”), Latin Venus, veneror, venia, vēnor and English wish.

Of uncertain origin. Equated with a supposed second element of Younger Avestan 𐬐𐬀𐬞𐬀𐬯𐬙𐬌𐬱 (kapastiš), the name of an illness,[1][2] which beside ka-pastiš has its morphological boundaries also rendered kap-astiš and been identified with Persian کبست (kabast, “colocynth; deadly poison”), with seemingly the suffix as Persian دهمست (dahmast, “laurel”) if not اسپست (aspest, “lucerne”).
pretium +‎ -ō

vocabList.definition: to press, push, force, drive, urge (forward); to stimulate
vocabList.etym: Disputed.
vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Fasti 2.858:
Mārsque citōs iūnctīs curribus urget equōs
and Mars, with chariots harnessed, drives swift horses(Translations of Ovid's Fasti, by H.T. Riley, James G. Frazer, and Anne and Peter Wiseman, all give Mars one harnessed or yoked chariot in the singular; however, ‘‘iunctis curribus’’ is plural. The plural seems appropriate if the poet’s meaning is understood to be that of Mars menacing with an army of charioteers. Ovid’s verse is an imaginative segue as he closes his book on February and introduces the month of March, named in honor of the war god.)

to be radiant, shine, look bright, glitter, sparkle, glisten
vocabList.etym: Probably from a past participle Proto-Italic *nitos (“made bright”), from a root Proto-Indo-European *ney- (“to shine”).[1] Potential cognates would include Middle Irish níam (“splendor, gleam”), níamda (“shining”), as well as Sanskrit नील (nī́la, “dark-colored, dark blue”).
From lost *ūveō, from Proto-Indo-European *wegʷ-, whence also attested are ūvor and ūvēns.

vocabList.definition: to separate, set apart, divide, part

vocabList.definition: to become acquainted with something, learn about it, to be aware of
vocabList.usage:
c. 45 BCE, Cicero, Tusculanae Disputationes 1.52:
Cum igitur "nosce te" dicit, hoc dicit: "nosce animum tuum". Nam corpus quidem quasi vas est aut aliquod animi receptaculum.
Therefore when he [the Pythian Apollo] says, "Know thyself", this is what it means: "Know your mind". The body is of course like a vase, or some other container for the mind.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German urteilen, denominative from Urteil +‎ -en, displacing synonymous erteilen.
An early modern German formation: Not (“need”) +‎ wendig (“maneuverable, agile”), originally “necessary to avert the distress”, compare die Not abwenden.

vocabList.definition: to give up, to go without, to live without, to make do without, to do without, to forgo, to dispense with
vocabList.etym: 18th century, denominal from Verzicht +‎ -en, displacing related sich (einer Sache) verzeihen. The significantly earlier attestation of Middle Low German vortichten, Middle Dutch vertichten (15th c.) makes it likely that the High German formation is based on these.
vocabList.usage:
Viele Menschen verzichten gerne auf ihr Auto, wenn der öffentliche Verkehr gut ist.
Many people gladly give up their car if public transportation is good.

vocabList.etym: Inherited from Middle High German messe, from Old High German missa, itself from Latin missa.

vocabList.definition: (chiefly in the plural) deity, god, goddess
vocabList.etym: From caelum (“heaven, sky”) +‎ -es (“-faring”), from eō (“I fare, go”). Compare pedes, eques, āles.

vocabList.etym: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μοιχός (moikhós).

When Curius learnt how great the danger which threatened the consul was, he hastily reported to Cicero, through Fulvia, the trap which was being prepared. When the men were thus turned away from the door, they had undertaken such a great crime in vain.

From puerīlis (“boyish, childish”) +‎ -ter.

Eorum una pars, quam Gallos obtinere dictum est
Another part of the country, which has already been said to contain the Gauls.

While [one’s attention] is scattered, life rushes past.[Alternatively, in context:]
While [our moral improvement] is delayed, life runs away.

166 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Andria 670–672:

DAVUS: This didn’t succeed; we’ll try another way. Unless you think that because at first it made so little progress, this bad situation cannot now be turned to a favorable outcome.

vocabList.etym: From in- +‎ tueor (“look at; guard”).

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German jāmern, jāmeren, from Old High German jāmarōn, from Proto-West Germanic *jāmarōn, from Proto-Germanic *jēmarōną. Compare English yammer.
Borrowed from Yiddish פּליטה (pleyte, “escape, getaway”), via Rotwelsch, 19th c.

Deverbal from spritzen (“to spray, inject”).

From con- +‎ queror.

vocabList.definition: (uncountable) dictates of religion, divine law (opp. iūs, human law), or an obligation thereunder
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *fās, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂os (“utterance, saying”), a derivative of the root *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”), whence also for, fārī. However, Beekes thinks there is "no convincing etymology" for Latin fās and Ancient Greek ὁσία (hosía).

vocabList.definition: so, so much, to such an extent, to such a degree
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *sei, from Proto-Indo-European *téh₂m, accusative of *séh₂, feminine of *só. Compare with its masculine form Latin tum, as in cum-quam.[1]
Perfect passive participle of perferō.

Unclear. A traditional reconstruction is Proto-Indo-European *perh₂- (“to exchange, sell”), comparing Ancient Greek πέρνημι (pérnēmi) etc. and Lithuanian pirkti; but this accounts badly for the /a(ː)/. De Vaan suggests *peh₂s- (“to watch (over), see?”), linking Latin pāreō.[1] All possibilities nonetheless suffer semantic problems. Others refrain from assigning an Indo-European root.

vocabList.definition: a period of two years, biennium
vocabList.etym: Synchronically, from biennis +‎ -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).

vocabList.definition: any one of the five divisions into which Servius Tullius divided the Roman citizenry
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *klāssis, from Proto-Indo-European *klh₁-d⁽ʰ⁾-ti- (“a call”), from *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”). Cognate with Latin calō, clāmō, clārus, concilium, Ancient Greek καλέω (kaléō). De Vaan notes that simplification of the Proto-Italic *-ss- would be expected following long *-ā-. He suggests that, semantically, the term evolved from referring to a “calling out” to a “class of soldiers being called out” to a “social class.”[1]

vocabList.definition: to feel, to sense, to perceive (with the senses)
vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Metamorphoses 1.553:
Hanc quoque Phoebus amat positāque in stīpite dextrāsentit adhūc trepidāre novō sub cortice pectus.
But yet Phoebus loves her in this form and pressing his right hand
he feels still the trembling heart under the bark.

vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *spernō, from Proto-Indo-European *sperH-. The perfect stem of the term may have been innovatively formed within Latin, perhaps according to the model of terms such as pleō. Alternatively, the zero-grade of an original root aorist may have produced the form *spera-, which perhaps evolved into *sprā-. Afterwards, the term may have then been reshaped into *sprē-.
vocabList.usage: Spernunt dīvitiās et voluptātēs. ― They despise riches and pleasures.

vocabList.etym: Perfect active participle of circumvehor.

vocabList.definition: to prefer, want more or instead; to wish rather, choose rather
vocabList.etym: From magis +‎ volō, literally "I more greatly wish for".
vocabList.usage:
166 BCE, Publius Terentius Afer, Andria 428–430:
BYRRHIA: Ego illam vīdī: virginem fōrma bona, / meminī vidērī. Quō aequior sum Pamphilō, / sī sē illam in somnīs quam illum amplectī māluit.
BYRRHIA: I saw her: [she was] a good-looking girl, as I recall. That’s why I’m more partial to Pamphilus, if he himself prefers [to be the one who] holds her in his sleep instead of that [other man].

vocabList.etym: Probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)treg- (“to be stiff, rigid, strong”), itself perhaps extended from *ster- (“stiff”). See strena (“auspicious sign”) for more.

vocabList.definition: to place in command, put in charge
vocabList.etym: From prae- (“before”) +‎ faciō (“do, make”).

vocabList.definition: which is to be snatched, taken away

From an unattested *fatis (“weariness”), of uncertain origin, + -igō, the latter a suffixal form of agō (“to do, act”).[1] De Vaan rejects Walde and Hoffmann's derivation of *fatis from a Proto-Indo-European *dʰH- (“to vanish”), whence supposedly Old Irish ded (“to vanish”), Old Norse dási (“slow”), and Middle English dasen (“to deafen, daze”), for vague semantics and phonology. Connected with affatim, fatīscō, fessus; confer also fūstīgō.
Via German Low German from North Frisian Hallich, of unknown origin.

vocabList.definition: intertidal zone, foreshore, especially the vast mudflats at the North Sea coast
vocabList.etym: Borrowed from Middle Low German wat, from Proto-Germanic *wadą.

Originally the same word as Teich (“pond”). The sense “dike” spread via Low German, for which reason the form Deich is most often regarded as an artificial adaptation of Middle Low German dīk (“dike”) to the phonetic system of standard German. However, Deich is also the form natively developed in West Central German and it does mean “dike, dam, weir system” in most dialects of the Rhineland, particularly along the Lower Rhine. The supposition of an artificial adaptation is therefore possible but not inevitable. Cognate to Dutch dijk and West Frisian dyk.

From Middle High German rūch, from Old High German rūh, from Proto-Germanic *rūhwaz. Though etymologically justified, the silent h was abolished in 1996 because rauh was the only word in which it was used after the diphthong -au-. Cognate with Dutch ruig and ruw, English rough (which see).
Laden (“shop”) +‎ Hüter (“keeper”)

From Middle High German bræchen/præchen (“to press in, to depict”), from Old High German giprāhhan/prāhhan (“to press in or scratch by breaking the surface”), from the 1st and 3rd person plural preterite forms of prēchan/prāchun (“to break”); likely related to brechen.

From the plural of Middle High German gezīt (“particular time, such as a feast or prayer time”), from Old High German gizit (“passage of time”), from gi- + zit. The modern sense is loaned from cognate Middle Low German getīde, whence also Tide.  Related to Zeit.
From fliehen (“to flee”) +‎ Kraft (“force”).
From Middle High German waten, from Old High German watan, from Proto-Germanic *wadaną. The form is East Central German with open-syllable lengthening before -t-; compare the variants above.

From either Middle Low German slam or Middle High German slam, which Pfeifer derives from a Proto-Germanic *slambaz, to which he considers schlemmen and Schlampe related. He further derives the term from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lembʰ- (“to hang limply”),[1] for which see Proto-Germanic *limpaną (“to glide, hang down”) for more.
From Middle High German ūzeren, that is, "making out (one's thoughts, etc.)"; see the related aus (“out”) for more.

Chiefly a backformation from vorsichtig, from Middle High German vorsihtec, vürsihtec, from Old High German foresihtig, derived from foresiht, a calque of Latin providentia and provisio. By surface analysis, vor- +‎ Sicht. Doublet of Vorsehung. Although the noun must underlie the adjective, the former is not attested again (after Notker) before the 15th century; it remained rare until ca. 1650.  Compare Dutch voorzicht, English foresight.
From Middle High German anen, from Old High German *anōn, from Proto-West Germanic *anōn, from *ana (“on”, preposition), from Proto-Germanic *an (“on”).
vocabList.usage:
Sag ihr die Wahrheit, da sie bereits etwas ahnt.
Tell her the truth since she already suspects something.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German rasch, rasche, from Old High German reski, rasco (adverb). Cognate with Swedish rask, Danish rask, English rash; see the latter for more.
an- +‎ schließen
vocabList.usage:
Die Kamera kann direkt an einen Monitor angeschlossen werden.
The camera can be directly connected to a monitor.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German kündec, kündic, from Old High German kundīg, from Proto-West Germanic *kunþīg, from Proto-Germanic *kunþīgaz, from Proto-Germanic *kunþaz, originally the past participle of *kunnaną, whose modern form is können. Equivalent to kund +‎ -ig.
From Middle High German ragen, from Old High German hragēn, from Proto-Germanic *hragōną.

los- +‎ marschieren

According to De Vaan, from Proto-Italic *pe-arkō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epo (“off”) + *h₂erk- (“to hold, guard”) (whence arceō).[1] The linguist Michael Weiss suggests that the Proto-Indo-European compound *pe-h₂erk- became *pe-h₂ark-, then *peh₂ark-, whence *pah₂ark-, which became *pārk-, and then *park- via Osthoff's law. Weiss suggests that the pre-form *pe-h₂erk- may also be continued by Hittite 𒁉𒂊𒄯𒍣 (pé-e-ḫar-zi)[2] The LIV, however, derives the term from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥k-é-ti, itself from the putative root *perk-.[3] De Vaan rejects this theory, arguing that it is semantically unconvincing.[1]

These roots are however disputed and more likely reflect Mediterranean substrate words or Wanderwörter, while Latin lāridum is thought to be a borrowing from Ancient Greek.
From dē- +‎ prōmō.
From per- (“through, along; during”) +‎ mittō (“let go, release; send out; throw”).

vocabList.definition: to spread, stretch out, spread out
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Italic *stornō, from Proto-Indo-European *str̥néh₃ti, n-infix present of the root *sterh₃- (“to spread, extend”).[1] Cognate with Sanskrit आस्तॄ (āstṝ, “spread”), Avestan 𐬯𐬙𐬆𐬭𐬆𐬥𐬁𐬌𐬙𐬌 (stərənāiti, “spread, extend”), Ancient Greek στόρνυμι (stórnumi, “scatter”), στρατός (stratós, “army, people, body of men”), Old Church Slavonic прострѣти (prostrěti, “stretch, expand”), просторъ (prostorŭ, “spaciousness”), Old English strewian (English strew), Old Norse strá.
vocabList.usage:
27 BCE – 25 BCE, Titus Livius, Ab Urbe Condita XXIV.38:
cum toga signum dedero, tum mihi undique clamore sublato turbam inuadite ac sternite omnia ferro;
when I give the signal with my toga, raise a loud shout and make an attack on the crowd from all sides and cut everything down with the sword

vocabList.etym: From ferveō +‎ -idus.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κῠπᾰ́ρῐσσος (kŭpắrĭssos).

vocabList.definition: the ancients, men of old, forefathers
vocabList.etym: From vetus (“old”).

vocabList.definition: a mountain ash tree, rowan tree
vocabList.etym: From Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃s-. Cognate with Old English æsc (“ash tree; spear (poetic)”). See also English ash.

vocabList.definition: to act, behave, do, or make persistently or unremittingly
vocabList.usage:
43 BCE – c. 17 CE, Ovidius, Heroides 7:
mare, quale vides agitāri nunc quoque ventis.
The sea, the sort you now see, also churned up by the winds.

vocabList.definition: having knowledge of a thing; acquainted with a thing., skillful, practiced
vocabList.etym: Ultimately from a Proto-Italic *gnāros, from the Proto-Indo-European root *ǵneh₃- (“to know”). Cognate with Attic Classical Greek root  aorist of γιγνώσκω ("I get to know"), ἔγνων (egnōn, "I got to know") and its participle form γνούς, γνοῦσα, γνόν (gnous, gnousa, gnon, "Having got to know")
Perfect passive participle of solvō
vocabList.usage:
8 CE, Ovidius, Fasti 6.451–452:
‘sī scelus est, in mē commissī poena redundet:sit capitis damnō Rōma solūta meī.’
“If it is a crime, let the punishment of its commission fall on me:
I condemn my head, may Rome be acquitted.”
(The Temple of Vesta ablaze, Lucius Caecilius Metellus (consul 251 BC) admits the impropriety of any man – even the pontifex maximus – entering the sacred temple of Vesta (mythology).)

vocabList.etym: Present participle of incolō.
Perfect passive participle of inferō (“carry or bring into somewhere; bury; conclude”).
From cōps +‎ -ia.
vocabList.usage:
c. 52 BCE, Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 6.6:
Caesar partītīs cōpiīs cum Gāiō Fabiō lēgātō et Mārcō Crassō quaestōre celeriterque effectīs pontibus adit tripertītō, aedificia vīcōsque incendit, magnō pecoris atque hominum numerō potītur.
Caesar, having divided his forces with C. Fabius, his lieutenant, and M. Crassus his questor, and having hastily constructed some bridges, enters their country in three divisions, burns their houses and villages, and gains possession of a large number of cattle and men.

vocabList.etym: From Middle High German sweifen, from Old High German sweifan, from Proto-West Germanic *swaipan, from Proto-Germanic *swaipaną.

vocabList.definition: to cause to stand; to set; to place
vocabList.usage:
29 BCE – 19 BCE, Vergilius, Aeneis 8.84-85:
quam pius Aeneas tibi enim, tibi, maxima Iuno, mactat sacra ferens et cum grege sistit ad aram.
  • Translation by H. Rushton Fairclough
    good Aeneas offers her in sacrifice to you, indeed to you, most mighty Juno, and sets her with her young before your altar.

vocabList.etym: From Ziegel +‎ Stein.
From the verb klingen.
From Middle High German edel, adel, from Old High German adal, from Proto-West Germanic *aþal, Proto-Germanic *aþalaz, see also Old English æþel- (> English athel), Old Norse aðall.
From late Middle High German winzic, an intensification of wenig (“little, few”); further origin uncertain. First attested in the 14th century.
Compound of Streichholz +‎ Schachtel.
Ca. 1800, from French loupe.

From Middle High German viuchte, from Old High German fūht, from Proto-West Germanic *fų̄ht, from Proto-Germanic *funhtijaz (“humid, wet, damp”). Cognate with the Dutch noun vocht (“liquid; dampness”).
From ab- +‎ schirmen.

vocabList.definition: to orate, deliver a speech publicly

vocabList.usage:
405 CE, Hieronymus, Vulgata 1 Thessalonicenses 5:25:
Frātrēs, ōrāte prō nōbīs.
Brothers, pray for us.
